short_answer: The apostolic fathers and their teacher-student chain make that skepticism very hard to sustain.
expanded_answer: Early church writers form a chain of teachers and students reaching back toward the apostles. Polycarp knew John, Clement of Rome knew Paul, and the apostles knew Jesus. In this argument, denying the apostles or the early Christian movement requires dismissing that linked testimony.

question: Does anyone doubt Socrates lived?
short_answer: No, even though the evidence mainly comes through Plato and Xenophon; the comparison highlights stronger skepticism about Christian figures.
expanded_answer: Socrates is generally accepted even though the core evidence comes through Plato and Xenophon, both students of Socrates. The comparison argues that skepticism about Jesus or Paul often exceeds the standards applied to other ancient figures, even when scholars may still debate embellishment or interpretation.

question: Did ancient Egyptian women have equal rights to men of the same social class?
short_answer: Egyptian women had unusually broad rights for the ancient Near East, including divorce, property, adoption, and economic options, with exceptions based on status.
expanded_answer: Rights were curtailed for enslaved women, women regarded as insane, and royal daughters. Other Egyptian women could initiate divorce, retain their share of property, work, serve in temples, and adopt children without a husband's permission. Some also used legal loopholes involving slavery, adoption, and remarriage. Their legal and economic agency was broad for the region, although inheritance rights were not absolute.

question: Are there good books on disturbing Old Testament passages besides Paul Copan?
short_answer: Copan fills an important niche, older broad works such as Gleason Archer's and the McDowells' attempts have problems, and slavery-law literature is more specialized.
expanded_answer: Slavery law has a large specialized literature. Richard Averbeck was the one author named, and Falk noted that the field is outside his focus. For broad treatments, Copan fills a difficult niche. Gleason Archer's work is not recommended because its single answers are often weak, while the McDowells' kitchen-sink approach lists views without enough evaluation.

question: What about the claim that Old Testament sacrifices purified holy spaces while Jesus forgives sins, and that New Testament authors confused this?
short_answer: It is partly true but partly mistaken: purification sacrifices and sin forgiveness are distinct categories, yet Jesus' sacrifice also covers the broader sacrificial system.
expanded_answer: Old Testament sacrifices cover several categories, including sin, purification, vows, and thanksgiving, so purification and forgiveness should not be collapsed into the same category. At the same time, Jesus' final sacrifice relates to the whole sacrificial system, so the quote was half right in keeping categories distinct but wrong if it excluded Jesus' sacrifice from covering those other sacrificial functions.

question: Do the great cloud of witnesses see believers' lives and what they have done?
short_answer: They are portrayed as watching and cheering believers on, which can feel unsettling but should also be encouraging.
expanded_answer: The follow-up returns to the earlier heaven discussion. The cloud of witnesses is described as interested in believers' lives and urging them to finish the race well, so their attention is both personally uncomfortable when failures are exposed and comforting because they are on the believer's side.

question: Did Tertullian believe the Spirit and Son were created first but temporary and would one day cease?
short_answer: The exact source and context are needed because Tertullian is often misquoted, especially when he quotes and then refutes modalist opponents.
expanded_answer: The claim needs a precise citation before it can be accepted. Tertullian often quotes opponents at length, so a reader who stops there can mistake a modalist position associated with Noetus for Tertullian's own view even though he later refutes it.

question: What are his thoughts on Total War: Pharaoh?
short_answer: He had not seen or played it yet, but the described setting sounded like late Dynasty 19 or early Dynasty 20, and he welcomed more Egypt-themed games.
expanded_answer: He had neither seen a trailer nor ordered or played the game, so he could not review it. Based on the description, the setting might fall near the end of Dynasty 19 or the start of Dynasty 20, with Pi-Ramesses, Memphis, or Thebes among the relevant places. He welcomed more Egypt-themed games because they bring ancient Egypt into popular culture.

question: What can be used instead of Strong's Concordance?
short_answer: Recommended replacements include HALOT for Hebrew and Aramaic, BDAG for New Testament Greek, and Holladay's concise Hebrew-Aramaic lexicon as a cheaper Old Testament option.
expanded_answer: Strong's is an outdated word list that treats language synchronically and does not distinguish changes from Classical to Middle to Late Hebrew. HALOT and BDAG are the standard choices for serious work. Holladay's concise Hebrew and Aramaic lexicon is a cheaper Old Testament option, although no similarly strong budget substitute was offered for BDAG.

question: Who is the naked young man in Mark 14:51-52?
short_answer: The text does not identify him. Falk leans toward a literary Gestalt for the fleeing disciples while allowing that he could have been a real person.
expanded_answer: Identifying the young man with Mark is unlikely because Mark was probably not among the original disciples. His naked flight could be a literary device that compresses the disciples' shameful flight into one figure. Falk considers a strange but real event equally possible, though he leans toward the literary reading.

question: What is his view of Michael Heiser's argument that the tribes under the conquest ban were Nephilim tribes?
short_answer: The spy report is exaggerated, Heiser conflates Nephilim and Rephaim, and the biblical text does not require that identification even if Second Temple literature supports it.
expanded_answer: Numbers 13 labels the spies' report as bad, and their description of all the inhabitants as giants is treated as exaggeration. Rephaim are very tall humans in this reading. Heiser's identification of Rephaim with Nephilim has support in later Second Temple traditions but is not required by the biblical text itself.

question: How does Christianity influence David and Kiara's lives?
short_answer: Christianity led Falk to give up a high-paying career, pursue ministry and education work, and see God's provision through difficult turns.
expanded_answer: Kiara did not answer directly. Speaking for himself, Falk tied Christianity to his whole vocation: leaving a six-figure career, pursuing seminary and doctoral work, and dedicating himself to educating the church. His examples included selling possessions, living through financial uncertainty, starting the channel unexpectedly during the pandemic, and seeing God's provision and guidance through both scarcity and opportunity. He also stressed that an ordinary Christian life is no less honorable; not everyone is called to the same upheaval.

question: What are his thoughts on Builders of Egypt?
short_answer: He did not know whether it was a game or video series and could not comment because he had not seen or played it.
expanded_answer: He did not know what Builders of Egypt was and explicitly declined to give an opinion. If it was a game or video series, he had neither seen nor played it, so he could not comment responsibly.

question: What did he think of Rob's Mount Ebal short?
short_answer: He thought it was well done and funny, but the image of Scott Stripling dancing was burned into his memory and he wished he had not seen it.
expanded_answer: The short was well executed and funny. The image of Scott Stripling dancing was the one gag he said he could not forget, so his praise came with a joking wish that he had never seen it.

question: Does Heiser's view provide a strong apologetic for conquest allegations compared with human-Nephilim views?
short_answer: No; even if Heiser were right, it would not solve the genocide objection, and genre and lexical issues provide better explanations.
expanded_answer: Heiser's view would not answer the moral objection if the claim is still that Israel wiped out whole peoples, even if those peoples were defined as Nephilim. Gigantism is rare, and archaeology has not produced remains showing whole unusually tall Canaanite or Philistine populations. Explanations based on ancient Near Eastern warfare genre, hyperbolic language, and lexical issues around the ban make the Nephilim apologetic unnecessary.

question: What were the most distant regions or peoples ancient Egyptians had contact with in Europe, Asia, and Africa?
short_answer: Egyptian trade contacts changed by period but reached Punt/Ethiopia, Cyprus and the Greek islands, Anatolia, Spain's Atlantic coast, India, and by Dynasty 20 possibly China.
expanded_answer: Egyptian trade contacts depend on period because Egypt's trade networks expanded over time. Examples include Punt or Ethiopia to the south, Cyprus, the Greek islands, and Anatolia to the north, scarabs reaching Spain's Atlantic coast to the west, goods from Afghanistan and India in Dynasty 18 contexts, and possible silk from China by Dynasty 20.

question: Is the idea that demons are spirits of dead Nephilim unbiblical?
short_answer: It is not directly contradicted but is unsupported or non-biblical, and the evidence leans against it.
expanded_answer: "Unbiblical" would mean the Bible directly contradicts the idea; "non-biblical" better describes a claim the Bible does not support. The no-marriage statement about the afterlife was used to argue against spirits procreating. The evidence also leans against demons as dead Nephilim because demonic beings are treated as existing from the beginning of creation and the Second Temple framing behind half-demonic Nephilim is rejected.

question: Could Jude and Enoch be quoting a shared tradition rather than Jude quoting Enoch, and could the prophecy be separate from the rest of Enoch?
short_answer: Either Jude quoting Enoch or both drawing from a shared tradition is possible, but the question remains speculative and hard to prove.
expanded_answer: A shared tradition or predecessor document is possible, and Jude could also be quoting Enoch directly because of the verbal similarities. Falk takes no firm position because hypothetical source relationships are difficult to prove and can move quickly from evidence into speculation.

question: Are there relations between Israelite timekeeping and the calendars of Canaanites or Egyptians?
short_answer: Israel's calendar began as lunar, adopted features from neighboring systems over time, used regnal dating under Egyptian influence, and later absorbed Mesopotamian intercalation.
expanded_answer: Israel's early calendar was lunar and similar in some ways to regional systems, with months divided into weeks and regnal dating affected by whoever held hegemony. Israelite practice shifted over time, later incorporating Mesopotamian intercalation, while Egyptian calendars themselves could drift because they lacked intercalation until much later.

question: Could Goliath have suffered from the same pituitary-gland problem as Robert Wadlow?
short_answer: The same medical explanation is doubtful because Goliath and related giants are portrayed as accomplished warriors, unlike most modern pituitary-gigantism cases, but skeletons would be needed to know.
expanded_answer: Most modern pituitary-gigantism cases involve serious health and mobility issues, whereas Goliath and related figures are portrayed as capable warriors. The same medical explanation is therefore doubtful, but the question cannot be settled without skeletal evidence showing how such ancient giantism manifested.

question: Does 2 John still apply if heretical missionaries such as Mormons or Jehovah's Witnesses come to a home?
short_answer: The passage concerns giving false teachers a platform in a house church, not ordinary hospitality or evangelistic conversation, so the application depends on whether they are being allowed to teach.
expanded_answer: "Receiving" in 2 John is about admitting false teachers into the house church or giving them a recognized teaching platform, not about letting a plumber, unbelieving guest, or missionary into the house for conversation. Hospitality and evangelistic discussion can be appropriate, but hosting their Bible study or granting them authority to teach would violate the passage.

question: Should Christians still celebrate the Sabbath?
short_answer: Christians are not under the Sinai covenant requirement, but taking a Sabbath rest can still be healthy and beneficial.
expanded_answer: The Sabbath functioned as a sign of the Sinai covenant, while Christians are under the new covenant. A Sabbath rest may still be healthy and may be observed on any day. Its purpose is to benefit people, not burden them with legalism.

question: How are ancient dates dated when dates can be unreliable, such as for the late Exodus period?
short_answer: Chronologists use king lists and synchronisms such as battles, letters, marriages, and royal gifts to align rulers and rule out impossible date schemes.
expanded_answer: Some dates can be fixed by several independent sources, while earlier periods rely on king lists and synchronisms. A synchronism shows that two rulers or events overlap. Diplomatic letters, battles, marriages, commemorative scarabs, and royal gifts can provide this evidence, and enough of these links can rule out chronologies that place rulers in impossible relationships.

question: How serious was the insubordination of the Egyptian midwives in Exodus 1?
short_answer: Pharaoh's order violated Egyptian justice traditions, so their refusal probably did not count as serious insubordination, though they likely were beaten before questioning.
expanded_answer: Egypt lacked written law for much of its history but had a strong tradition of justice, and Pharaoh's order to murder infants violated that tradition. The midwives' excuse was probably not believed. In this account, Egyptian questioning began with a beating, so they likely were beaten before appearing before Pharaoh and might have been beaten again. Refusing the unjust order probably brought no greater penalty.

question: In Egyptian naming magic, what was a person's real name, and did Egyptians understand the arbitrariness of names?
short_answer: Egyptians distinguished a public name from a hidden true name that functioned like a magical key to control a being.
expanded_answer: Egyptians understood that ordinary names could be arbitrary, but they also believed that gods, humans, and spirits had hidden true names. A true name reflected an attribute that magic could use to control the being, so a curse needed that name rather than the public one. The true name might be secret even from the person who bore it and had to be sought through divination or other magical means.

question: Did Egyptians during the Late Period learn to speak Greek, and how did they communicate with foreigners about trade, armies, and intelligence?
short_answer: Egyptian scribes learned diplomatic languages, including Greek in the Late Period, and served as interpreters for rulers, commanders, and diplomats.
expanded_answer: Greek was added to the scribal language repertoire in the Late Period because Egypt used Greek mercenaries and paid them in Greek coinage. Commanders and kings could continue speaking Egyptian while trained scribes translated, just as earlier scribes had used Akkadian and later Aramaic for diplomacy; many diplomats also came from that scribal class.

question: Why did the Minoans import so much from ancient Egypt?
short_answer: Egyptian goods and symbols were prestigious, useful, and culturally attractive, so Minoan borrowing was partly simple desirability.
expanded_answer: The borrowing was a mixture of practical trade and attraction to Egyptian material culture. Minoans needed goods such as papyrus, grain, flax, and linen, and trade also brought scarabs, Hathor mirrors, idols, and other objects whose value was aesthetic, symbolic, or social, much like later Egyptomania.

question: Would a full manuscript of Manetho or Berossus significantly change our picture of Egypt or Mesopotamia?
short_answer: It would clarify major historiographical questions, especially disputed passages, but not revolutionize everything by itself.
expanded_answer: The main value would be recovering a less-mediated version of texts now preserved through later writers. A full Manetho, for example, could clarify whether Exodus-related king lists came from Manetho himself, later Jewish or Christian users, or variant manuscript traditions, but it would still be evidence to weigh rather than automatic proof.

question: What are his thoughts on Catholicism?
short_answer: He considers Catholics Christian brothers and sisters, though he disagrees with some doctrines.
expanded_answer: In his view, Catholics hold the essentials of the Christian faith and should be treated as brothers and sisters in Christ. He still evaluates doctrine case by case against the Bible. Roman Catholicism is also a large, varied tradition with official teachings, exceptions, and broad internal diversity, so an individual Catholic's exact beliefs should not be assumed.

question: Are there any early-date Exodus proponents he actually likes?
short_answer: Randall Price is someone he likes personally and respects in some work, while still strongly disagreeing with Price's Exodus dating.
expanded_answer: Personal regard is distinct from agreement on chronology. Randall Price is the example of an early-date proponent whose company and some archaeological work he respects, even though Price's Exodus date is rejected and the broader early-date debate has been made more hostile by groups such as ABR.

question: Has he thought about interviewing other scholars?
short_answer: He has considered interviews, but sees teaching and answering questions as a better fit for his strengths.
expanded_answer: He describes himself as a strong introvert and does not think interviewing fits his strengths. Some other hosts have a knack for it, while this channel is built around teaching, answering questions, and making instruction engaging for its existing audience.

question: Is there evidence that pharaohs Griffith treats as concurrent ruled the same city, and would that undermine the city-dynasty hypothesis?
short_answer: Yes; overlapping administrative centers, biographies, and synchronistic data make the city-dynasty hypothesis untenable.
expanded_answer: Administrative and biographical data create fatal problems for the city-dynasty hypothesis: multiple dynasties are tied to the same centers such as Itjtawy and Memphis, and officials' biographies point to overlapping administration. Two kings with separate armies and administrations in the same place would quickly conflict, and synchronisms point against the proposed scheme.

question: What are his thoughts on Christopher Rollston's interview with Sean McDowell?
short_answer: He praised Rollston's evidential approach, agreed that the Mount Ebal amulet lacked visible writing, and criticized treating weak and strong views as equally credible.
expanded_answer: He praised Rollston as an evidentialist and agreed that epigraphers normally debate what an inscription says, rather than whether writing is present at all. In his assessment, the Mount Ebal object showed no real writing. He criticized McDowell for offering Stripling ways to save face and treating unequal arguments as though they deserved equal standing. The announced re-examination of the epigraphy showed that the controversy was still unfolding.

question: Are there any developments with the Amorite tablet discussed in the Mana Machine Alert?
short_answer: No new developments had appeared since the full publication, but future work was expected to test the grammar against other inscriptions.
expanded_answer: The full publication had already appeared and there had not yet been later developments. The likely next step is scholarly testing: the new grammar may be applied to other inscriptions or scripts, and peer review will include disagreement and refinement as scholars digest the material.

question: Does the lack of Genesis 1-11 references in early prophetic texts imply those chapters are late?
short_answer: No; absence of mention is not positive evidence for late composition.
expanded_answer: The inference is an argument from silence. The Balaam example shows that a figure once treated as legendary because of limited references could be reassessed when an inscription appeared, so the lack of earlier prophetic mentions cannot by itself show Genesis 1-11 was late; positive evidence is needed.

question: Does he know PhD reading lists for Egyptology or Old Testament self-study, and are online MAs a path to becoming a scholar?
short_answer: He does not recommend online MAs as preparation for scholarship because graduate study depends on relationships and recommendations. Old Testament reading lists are easier to find than Egyptology lists.
expanded_answer: Online MAs can provide information, but he considers them weak preparation for scholarship because graduate study also builds the relationships and recommendation letters needed for PhD admission. Public syllabi and reading lists are useful for self-study. Old Testament study has abundant secondary literature, while advanced Egyptology focuses more on primary texts, languages, and translation.

question: What are his thoughts on historian David Miano and World of Antiquity?
short_answer: David Miano and World of Antiquity were unfamiliar to him, unlike channels such as Metatron that he had seen and liked.
expanded_answer: David Miano and World of Antiquity cannot be judged here because he had not watched them. By contrast, Metatron's classical-history and language work is appreciated, including the channel's entertainment value and grounding in languages such as Greek, Hebrew, Latin, and some Egyptian.

question: Did Hike badly misinterpret Tertullian's `Against Praxeas` by treating 1 Corinthians 15:28 as saying the Trinity will cease?
short_answer: The claim fits a common problem: Tertullian is often misread when readers lose track of whether Tertullian or an opponent is speaking.
expanded_answer: Tertullian is easy to misuse because long stretches quote opponents, so readers must track whether Tertullian, Noetus, or someone else is speaking. Jehovah's Witness misuse of church-father quotations is a similar problem, and patristics requires careful acclimatization to style, context, and argument flow.

question: Is there any way to show the Bible hints that Adam's 930 years means the age of a clan rather than one individual?
short_answer: Patriarchal ages, the Abraham/Terah problem, Exodus 6, and the Old Testament's focus on clans support a clan-identity reading.
expanded_answer: Some biblical genealogical data make better sense as clan identity than as strict individual lifespan. Abraham's surprise at fathering a child at 100, the compressed genealogy of Moses in Exodus 6, and the Old Testament's frequent clan language all suggest that names can represent lines or houses that continue beyond one person's life.

question: What does the `tribute of people` in Numbers 31:40 mean?
short_answer: It belongs in the context of war spoils and the Midianite campaign, not as proof of temple prostitution.
expanded_answer: Numbers 31:40 is part of the division of Midianite war captives and other spoils. The small number given as the Lord's portion would likely have been assigned to Eleazar and the tabernacle for menial service such as fetching water or wood, not for a sacred sexual role.

question: Will the Mount Ebal tablet be the beginning of the end for ABR?
short_answer: No. In his view, ABR's support base in churches and donor networks insulates it from academic embarrassment.
expanded_answer: He argued that ABR has survived prior academic embarrassments because its church speaking circuit, seminary ties, donors, and continuity of leadership matter more than academic approval. In his view, even unsuccessful claims can still attract donations and excitement if the organization appears to be generating results.

question: What are good books for starting research on Egyptian chronology and Middle Eastern synchronisms?
short_answer: Hornung and Warburton's Egyptian chronology work is a starting point, and primary sources such as Mesopotamian chronicles and Amarna letters are essential.
expanded_answer: The Egyptian chronology volume associated with Hornung and Warburton is recommended as a starting primer, but synchronisms require primary sources. Examples named include Mesopotamian Chronicles, Sasson's work with chronicle material, and the Amarna letters, because chronology work depends on tracing synchronisms through texts.

question: When should laymen trust the academic consensus, and when should they not?
short_answer: Consensus grounded in evidence deserves more trust, while consensus resting mainly on theory or interpretation should be weighed cautiously against the data.
expanded_answer: Consensus is strongest when it rests on new data or clear evidence, and weaker when it rests mainly on theoretical interpretation. The guiding rule is to follow evidence even when it changes the picture, while treating interpretations and working hypotheses with caution until their reasoning has been tested.

question: Would the documentary hypothesis fall into the category of interpretation rather than direct data?
short_answer: Yes; it is a theory built on interpretations, and some of its middle premises fail against the data.
expanded_answer: The documentary hypothesis is an overarching interpretive theory, not direct data. For example, treating doublets as editorial reduplication is itself an interpretation; if that middle premise is faulty, the larger theoretical conclusion is weakened, so the evidence has to be weighed rather than the consensus accepted automatically.

question: Is there proof that Shamash is Zedek, Kittu, or Isar?
short_answer: The terms and intended identifications were unclear, so he could not answer directly. He could only note that deities may arise independently or be absorbed into larger pantheons.
expanded_answer: The question did not give enough context to establish whether Shamash meant the Mesopotamian sun god or whether "Isar" was intended to mean Osiris. He therefore could not address the proposed identifications. His limited general point was that cultures may borrow deities, while local gods can also arise independently and later be incorporated into larger city-state or imperial pantheons.

question: Is Franck Goddio for real, or is he another Ron Wyatt?
short_answer: Goddio and Heracleion were outside his knowledge, but underwater cities can be real when earthquake subsidence or similar processes lower land.
expanded_answer: Goddio and Heracleion were not familiar enough for him to judge the person or claim. The limited point is that underwater cities are plausible in principle, citing Alexandria and earthquake subsidence or land-level changes that can submerge settlements over months, years, or decades.

question: What was the process of starting a new cult in Egypt, who was allowed to do it, and how was a new deity welcomed into the religious structure?
short_answer: New cults usually grew from existing traditions, divine attributes, or relationships among gods. Kings held primary authority to install a deity, while priests could sometimes erect or relocate statues.
expanded_answer: New Egyptian cults usually did not appear from nothing; they tended to divide from an existing deity, develop from an attribute or instrument, or join an established divine family. Installing a deity meant placing its image or bark in a temple, where it received the usual daily care. The king had broad authority to add a god or move its cult image. Priests could sometimes erect or relocate statues, and priesthoods could resist royal changes. The transcript does not identify commoners as having comparable authority.

question: Did monotheism, or something close to it, exist in cultures besides Israel?
short_answer: Monolatry, henotheism, and monotheism are distinct. In this account, Israel provides the first clear example of true monotheism, while other cultures often come closer to monolatry.
expanded_answer: Worshiping one god exclusively differs from believing that only one true God exists. Monolatry and henotheism can occur within broader polytheistic systems. Atenism is described as closer to monolatrous pantheism than full monotheism. In this account, Israel is the first clear example of true monotheism, developing from Sinai onward.

question: What about native African religions and monotheism?
short_answer: Some may get close, but the examples he had encountered looked more monolatrous than clearly monotheistic, and he avoided a definitive claim outside his expertise.
expanded_answer: Outside Egypt, African religions are not his field. Some examples may approach monotheism, but the ones presented to him looked more like monolatry because they emphasized the practice of worshiping one deity rather than a full doctrine of the nature of divinity; he leaves room for exceptions he has not studied.

question: Why were pharaohs worried about peasant revolts caused by priests choking the food supply if peasants lacked military skill and technology?
short_answer: Priests could affect food supplies for both peasants and the military, and kings sometimes broke up priestly or regional land power to keep control centralized.
expanded_answer: Control of food threatened more than peasants: soldiers also depend on food, and unpaid or hungry forces can riot. This connects to kings breaking up priestly, temple, or nomarch land grants, especially in periods such as the Middle Kingdom, so food and military power would be centralized under the crown rather than regional elites.

question: On the clan-interpretation view, what does `begot` mean?
short_answer: It means a line of descent, not necessarily an immediate father-son relationship, because Hebrew genealogies can skip generations.
expanded_answer: Israelite genealogies do not function like modern Western genealogies. A son can be a grandson or later descendant, a father can be an ancestor, and Hebrew has no separate ordinary genealogical categories for grandson and great-grandson, so "begot" can identify descent through a line with omitted intermediaries.

question: How can local churches, especially more fundamentalist-leaning ones, become more interested in scholarly research and academics?
short_answer: Start with poetry and symbolism to loosen a rigid literal-or-error mindset before moving into more contested scholarly questions.
expanded_answer: The first obstacle is the black-and-white assumption that the Bible is either literal or wrong. Recommended starting points are Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, or Song of Solomon, where people can practice symbolism, literary devices, and multiple possible readings before applying that habit to history or scholarship.

question: Why would the king of Shinar go all the way to the Dead Sea for a raid if the trip cost exceeded the loot value?
short_answer: Mesopotamian armies looted everything along the route, so the campaign was not only about the final target and its costs were offset by accumulated plunder.
expanded_answer: The campaign should be imagined as a moving looting party, not a single destination raid. Mesopotamian armies could take food, clothing, captives, livestock, furniture, wood, oil, wine, and anything transportable along the route, which also explains why Abraham could catch up with a force slowed by goods and animals.

question: Would Egypt have been strong enough to fight the Mesopotamian looters if they headed to Egypt?
short_answer: Egypt under the 13th Dynasty, especially under strong kings such as Neferhotep I and Sobekhotep IV, likely could have repelled them.
expanded_answer: The question is placed around the 13th Dynasty, when Egypt still had enough strength under kings such as Neferhotep I and Sobekhotep IV to stop such a coalition. Possible Mesopotamian-Egyptian diplomatic contact also means treaty or gift-exchange relationships could have discouraged raiding Egypt.

question: Why are there no reported clashes between the Israelites and Egyptian mining parties in Sinai?
short_answer: The Israelites likely took a different route while the mining operations were small, localized, and away from their main path.
expanded_answer: The main mining site, Serabit el-Khadim, was up in the mountains while the Israelites were moving down the west coast of Sinai and then through Wadi Feiran. The mining camp was small, seasonal, and work-focused, perhaps only dozens of miners, guards, administrators, and priests, so it was unlikely to seek a clash even if aware of movement below.

question: Were decorative and lewd graffiti like those at Hatshepsut's temple common in ancient Egypt, and what did common people think of her?
short_answer: Graffiti was widespread after temples were abandoned; common opinion of Hatshepsut is mostly unknown, while Thutmose III's monument damage was state-sponsored and personal.
expanded_answer: Temples were kept pristine only while their cults were supplied; once abandoned, people could enter and write on the walls, and technologies such as DStretch now reveal widespread faded graffiti. Hatshepsut's common reputation is mostly unknowable, though palace gossip may have existed, while the chiseled attacks on her images were state-sponsored action by Thutmose III rather than ordinary graffiti.

question: How long before the Rollston interview is taken down like Falk's debate was?
short_answer: He considered removal unlikely because taking down the interview after criticism of the Mount Ebal amulet would look like a cover-up.
expanded_answer: He considered removal possible but unlikely because Rollston is a major scholar, was congenial despite being blunt, and taking the interview down after the earlier debate removal would make the controversy look even more like censorship or a cover-up. In his view, the interview also looked like an attempt to get ahead of bad publicity.

question: What is his opinion of `Crystal Blade`?
short_answer: He had not read the novel, though the cover used his artwork and fans of the book like it.
expanded_answer: Copies are in his possession because the cover uses a photograph of a crystal dagger he made as an art jeweler, but the young-adult fantasy novel had not been read and cannot be recommended from experience. The cover artwork is his own work, and the book appears to have devoted fans.

question: Have more conservative-leaning scholars written responses to the Levite hypothesis?
short_answer: Most responses he had seen were in the `Five Views` book or in book reviews, because conservative scholars are less likely to engage that hypothesis directly in journals.
expanded_answer: In his assessment, the Levite hypothesis rests heavily on the documentary hypothesis and redaction criticism, subjects many conservative scholars are not eager to engage in journal articles. He therefore expected most conservative interaction to appear in the `Five Views` volume or in book reviews, where reviewer assignment is somewhat random.

question: If the Hyksos numbered around 500,000 and Egypt had about 2.1 million people around 1600 BC, why did that influx not collapse Egypt's food supply?
short_answer: The population number is contested, the Delta and Faiyum were highly productive, and the Hyksos presence grew over centuries rather than arriving all at once.
expanded_answer: The 500,000 figure is disputed and may only be possible if counting broadly across the Delta, while Avaris itself is usually estimated much lower. Food pressure was mitigated by fertile Delta land, Middle Kingdom agricultural expansion in the Faiyum, and gradual immigration over centuries by groups whose herds and population grew slowly rather than arriving in one sudden wave.

question: Are the songs of Miriam and Deborah written in an older form of Hebrew, and can their language help date them to the 11th century BC?
short_answer: Poetic sections may preserve older features, but poetry is hard to date securely; Hebrew was also updated over time, so linguistic dating has limits.
expanded_answer: Most scholars treat poetic sections such as Judges 5 as older than surrounding prose, but this is hard to prove because poetry and prose can look different even when they are contemporary. Hebrew vocabulary and forms changed over time, yet the lack of a strong baseline makes the songs difficult to date securely.

question: Are there any fringe history views that you hold or think are plausible?
short_answer: He did not endorse a fringe-history view; he described his approach as generally conventional and evidence-driven.
expanded_answer: He finds fringe views interesting because they reveal how people reason, but he does not find them historically plausible when they are detached from data. He takes minority positions when he thinks the evidence supports them, as in biblical maximalism debates, but did not endorse a fringe-history view.

question: Will we ever find evidence for a historical Moses outside the Bible?
short_answer: Probably not; Moses' Egyptian connection would be hard to identify archaeologically.
expanded_answer: Moses was probably not high enough in Egyptian status before leaving to have dedication stelae or inscriptions that would preserve his name. Joseph is a more promising archaeological target because his Egyptian rank would have made statues or inscriptions more plausible.

question: Could anyone besides Joshua and the Israelites have destroyed Jericho and its walls?
short_answer: Egypt is unlikely, and neighboring city-states are possible but less compelling; the Israelites remain the strongest remaining explanation.
expanded_answer: The chronology rules out Egypt, and no other major power fits the destruction horizon. A nearby Levantine city-state remains possible, but the region's Late Bronze Age depopulation makes that less persuasive. The case for the Israelites is probabilistic rather than absolute.

question: Is the Septuagint based on an older Hebrew text, and is it closer to the originals than the Masoretic Text?
short_answer: Yes to an older Hebrew Vorlage, but not always closer; textual decisions have to be made verse by verse.
expanded_answer: The Septuagint reflects an older Hebrew text, but lower textual criticism does not make one textual family closest to the original in every case. The Dead Sea Scrolls show that original readings can surprise scholars, so the answer requires comparing each verse across available witnesses.

question: Were the Trojans the Sea Peoples after Troy, or did they become the Romans?
short_answer: No; in this account, the Sea Peoples were Greek or Anatolian Greek groups that pressured Troy, not Trojans or Romans.
expanded_answer: The Trojans were distinct from the Sea Peoples, and the Sea Peoples were not Romans. He connects the Sea Peoples with Greek-speaking or Anatolian Greek populations moving southward, pressuring Troy, and contributing to the background from which the Philistines emerged.

question: Is there evidence of a seven-year famine in Egypt, and would that help date the Exodus?
short_answer: Egypt has many recorded famines across long periods, so famine evidence does not narrowly date the Exodus.
expanded_answer: Egyptian records preserve recurring low-Nile and famine conditions from the Old Kingdom through later periods, including evidence connected with nilometer readings. Because famine was common enough across Egypt's history, even a documented famine would not by itself pinpoint the Exodus.

question: Did sites like Gobekli Tepe and Catalhoyuk leave a legacy in the ancient Near East, such as excarnation as a precursor to resurrection beliefs?
short_answer: That is possible only in a broad sense, but there is no clear direct line, and this is outside his main specialty.
expanded_answer: Resurrection-like concerns could appear widely because humans think about death and future life, but written evidence is lacking for those very early sites. Without language, the specific beliefs behind the material culture remain uncertain, so any direct line to later ancient Near Eastern religion is speculative.

question: Does the Exodus point to an early date for the Pentateuch?
short_answer: Yes; itinerary details plus Egyptian vocabulary, names, customs, and loanwords support an early written setting.
expanded_answer: The support comes from obscure itinerary details such as Pi-Hahiroth, Egyptian practices involving bread bowls, and loanwords that fit a particular stage of Egyptian. Those features would be difficult to explain if the Pentateuch were composed hundreds of years later without early Egyptian memory.

question: What are your thoughts on the "house of kettle" reading of the Tel Dan Stele?
short_answer: He dismissed the reading as ridiculous; he did not read the Tel Dan Stele as "house of kettle."
expanded_answer: His answer was brief and dismissive. He regarded the proposal as an attempt to get a reaction rather than a serious interpretation of the Tel Dan Stele.

question: What evidence places Joseph in Egypt during the 15th rather than the 12th dynasty, and can we rule out chariots in the 12th dynasty?
short_answer: Chariot warfare fits the 15th dynasty much better; the 12th dynasty lacks the horse-breeding, military, and pictorial evidence expected for chariot armies.
expanded_answer: The 12th dynasty has abundant warfare reliefs but no chariots, and it lacks a horse-breeding program. At Avaris, the 15th dynasty evidence includes horse burials, bridles and bits, and Hyksos-linked chariot technology.

question: Were there two Judean campaigns by Sennacherib, and why did the Rabshakeh come if Hezekiah had already paid tribute?
short_answer: He had not yet looked into that enough to give a firm answer.
expanded_answer: He tentatively suggested that Sennacherib may have become greedy and returned for more tribute, but explicitly deferred judgment. He left open whether there were two campaigns or one campaign in which Sennacherib was dissatisfied with the tribute.

question: What books are a good starting point for Middle Kingdom history and culture?
short_answer: Start with Ian Shaw; he also mentioned Leprohon and Quirke, while identifying himself as a New Kingdom specialist.
expanded_answer: He recommended Ian Shaw's Oxford history volume as a general starting point for Egyptian history. For the Middle Kingdom specifically, he mentioned Leprohon and Quirke but did not supply a particular title because his own specialty is the New Kingdom.

question: Is Pepi II's reported 94-year reign plausible?
short_answer: Yes; it is well documented and plausible, though very long reigns tend to weaken kingdoms politically.
expanded_answer: Pepi II's reign was unusually long but is well attested through multiple generations at court and the ubiquity of his cartouche. He linked exceptionally long reigns with political weakness, comparing Pepi II with Ramesses II and modern monarchic succession problems.

question: What would you recommend for beginners in Egyptian history, including primary texts and general surveys?
short_answer: Start with Ian Shaw. Barry Kemp remains useful but dated, and William Kelly Simpson is a good source for primary texts.
expanded_answer: He recommended Ian Shaw's Egyptian history volume as a strong primer suitable even for first-year students. Barry Kemp's *Anatomy of a Civilization* remains useful but needs caution because it is dated, while William Kelly Simpson's anthology provides translations of ancient Egyptian literary texts.

question: What realistic evidence could overturn major scholarly opinion on the Exodus or conquest, and could biblical minimalism change its mind?
short_answer: More ostraca, texts, and excavation data could shift opinion, especially from the Wadi Tumilat and Israel, though some skeptical settings may resist changing.
expanded_answer: He expected new texts and excavation results to keep refining the field, especially from the Wadi Tumilat, sites such as Tell el-Retaba and Tell el-Maskhuta, and work in Israel on Middle and Late Bronze Age contexts. Minimalist opinion may shift in some places, but institutions that prize skepticism may resist evidence-driven change.

question: What should we make of the claim that Joseph's sarcophagus was found near Jacob's Well and taken away by Theodosius II?
short_answer: It likely was not Joseph's original sarcophagus, and strong conclusions based on later local identifications are doubtful.
expanded_answer: Joseph's original Egyptian sarcophagus would probably have been left in Egypt because the Israelites would have taken the mummy, not the heavy sarcophagus. In his view, later local identifications of patriarchal tombs are unreliable without stronger evidence than Byzantine or local tradition.

question: What is your opinion on identifying Jacob with "Yikabhar"?
short_answer: He lacked enough information about the name's origin, date, and findspot to make a firm identification.
expanded_answer: The seal-ring name might be related to Jacob, but that is far from enough to identify the biblical patriarch. More context is needed, including the name's origin, date, and findspot, so the identification remains doubtful without stronger evidence.

question: Did the Egyptians ever undertake expeditions like the Phoenicians?
short_answer: Yes; Egyptian Red Sea expeditions to Punt are a clear example.
expanded_answer: Egypt sent regular Red Sea trading expeditions to Punt for gold, malachite, incense, spices, and other goods. Bronze tools were exchanged for raw materials, and he suggested this cycle may have ended around Ramesses III after Punt learned to smelt copper for itself.

question: Why were the Sea Peoples on the move, and why target Egypt?
short_answer: Their movement is tied to food pressure and Late Bronze Age instability; Egypt was a rich but risky target because it was the region's breadbasket.
expanded_answer: The Medinet Habu inscription attributes the Sea Peoples' movement to a food crisis, with people coming "for their bellies." Egypt's grain wealth offered the largest payoff, even though its defenses made the attempt especially risky.

question: Did Amenhotep III refuse a Babylonian king's request to send an Egyptian princess in marriage?
short_answer: Yes; the Amarna letters show Egypt generally did not reciprocate treaty wives.
expanded_answer: An Amarna letter preserves a foreign king's complaint that Egypt received treaty wives but did not send royal daughters in return. This fits a broader Egyptian diplomatic pattern, with Solomon's Egyptian wife named as a rare later exception during the severe weakness of Dynasty 21.

question: How would you refute James and van der Veen's theory identifying Zerah the Cushite with an official under Ramesses IV?
short_answer: He had not studied the exact proposal closely enough to evaluate it; he regarded van der Veen's broader views as highly idiosyncratic and fringe.
expanded_answer: He could not directly refute an identification he had not studied. Ramesses IV quickly lost Egyptian hegemony in the Levant and Kush, while he regarded van der Veen's wider Egyptological views as far outside conventional scholarship.

question: If Genesis preserves oral history but the Avaris community was polytheistic, who preserved the tradition?
short_answer: The sons of Jacob could have preserved it, and Genesis does not portray the patriarchs as strongly monotheistic in the later sense.
expanded_answer: The patriarchal narratives are compatible with preservation by a community that had not yet developed later Israelite monotheism in full. Genesis itself contains signs of polytheistic context, vocabulary updating, and retrojection, so oral preservation and later written shaping can coexist.

question: Is there much more biblically related material still to be found among the Oxyrhynchus texts?
short_answer: Probably not much more biblical material; most of the major biblical finds were likely extracted early.
expanded_answer: Oxyrhynchus still contains enormous amounts of unpublished material, but the remaining bulk consists largely of receipts, legal documents, wills, and texts of more specialist interest. Its continuing value lies especially in comparative Koine Greek evidence, which already transformed biblical lexicons and interpretation.

question: How much Phoenician influence was there on Israel?
short_answer: Not much in early Israel, but more during the divided monarchy through trade, diplomacy, and royal contacts.
expanded_answer: The Phoenicians belonged to the Canaanite population of Lebanon and coastal cities such as Byblos, Tyre, and Sidon. Their influence on Israel was limited during Joshua and Judges but grew later through Solomon, Hiram of Tyre, northern-kingdom trade, cultural exchange, and royal marriages.

question: What is your favorite programming language?
short_answer: Python.
expanded_answer: He preferred Python because it is easy to program and debug. His earlier work with Perl, C, kernel engineering, and computers also proved useful for Egyptological chronology calculations.

question: Any thoughts on the identity of Cushan-Rishathaim?
short_answer: After a viewer supplied context, he connected Cushan-Rishathaim with Aram Naharim, Mitanni, and a Hurrian setting, though no external record identifies the individual.
expanded_answer: Aram Naharim points to the Mitanni and Hurrian sphere, which fits the period of Judges. No external record identifies Cushan-Rishathaim himself, and Judges is organized theologically rather than in strict chronological order.

question: Did the sons of Jacob identify their god with a generic high god like El until Yahweh identified himself to Moses?
short_answer: Yes; El or El Shaddai language fits the period before the Mosaic revelation of the divine name.
expanded_answer: In this interpretation, Exodus 3 indicates that Israel did not know God by the name Yahweh before Moses. Ramesses recognizes other Canaanite gods but not Yahweh, which fits an Avaris community that knew El or El Shaddai instead.

question: Did ancient Israel practice chattel slavery in a way similar to U.S. chattel slavery?
short_answer: No; ancient Israelite slavery differed significantly from U.S. chattel slavery, though it was still slavery.
expanded_answer: Ancient slaves could earn income, own other slaves, and in Israel an Israelite slave had to be released in the seventh year unless choosing permanent bond service. Slavery was still bad, especially under a bad master, but it was not equated with modern U.S. chattel slavery.

question: Could the famine in Ruth roughly correlate with the famines of the Late Bronze Age collapse?
short_answer: Possibly, because the Late Bronze collapse was a long regional crisis rather than a single-year event.
expanded_answer: He rejected the idea that 1177 BC marked a single neat collapse date. In his account, the crisis began earlier and lasted for centuries, which could carry into the Judges and Ruth setting and place Ruth's famine within the same long disruption.

question: Would Falk debate Petrovich again?
short_answer: He indicated no interest in another three-way debate under the proposed arrangement.
expanded_answer: He would not repeat the proposed three-way format, doubted Petrovich would agree, and thought their earlier exchanges made another debate unlikely.

question: Magic: The Gathering or Dungeons & Dragons?
short_answer: Dungeons & Dragons; he played third edition and enjoyed being dungeon master, but never got into Magic: The Gathering.
expanded_answer: He played third-edition Dungeons & Dragons and enjoyed running games as dungeon master, including setting up the situations and rules. Magic: The Gathering did not draw the same interest.

question: How should Gobekli Tepe affect our understanding of later Egyptian and Canaanite culture?
short_answer: Very little directly; if there was influence, it was more agricultural than religious.
expanded_answer: Gobekli Tepe predates Egyptian and Canaanite culture by thousands of years, so it offers little direct help in explaining them. He identified agriculture as the only possible influence, especially the domestication and spread of grains such as chickpeas and barley, rather than a religious inheritance.

question: Which Candace of Ethiopia did the eunuch of Acts 8 serve under?
short_answer: Amanitore seems the likeliest candidate, though the Candace chronology is confusing and thinly documented.
expanded_answer: The succession is difficult to reconstruct because several queens reigned close together and the chronology is thin. He accepted Amanitore as the likeliest candidate while stressing that little biographical evidence survives for the Acts 8 timeframe.

question: Where did the modern "curse of the pharaohs" myth come from?
short_answer: It largely came from a British newspaper reaction to Howard Carter's exclusive arrangement, though some tomb warnings do exist.
expanded_answer: The modern myth grew from newspaper resentment after Howard Carter gave the *Times* exclusive access to Tutankhamun tomb coverage. Some Egyptian tomb inscriptions warn of punishment for improper entry, but those are different from the modern popular curse story and were uncommon.

question: Hieroglyphics versus cuneiform: which appears first in the archaeological record?
short_answer: They appear very close together in time, within roughly a century, and the evidence does not settle the question cleanly.
expanded_answer: Early Egyptian hieroglyphic evidence and early Sumerian/proto-cuneiform evidence fall in the same broad window, roughly 3100 to 3300 BC. The evidence does not establish which appeared first.

question: What is the grammatical function of the prefixed `lamed`?
short_answer: It is the dative preposition, usually carrying a `to` or `for` sense.
expanded_answer: Semitic prepositions in Hebrew are often single letters attached to the front of a noun. In this case the prefixed `lamed` marks a dative construction, indicating motion toward something, relation to a place, or purpose for something.

question: Could the Torah have been written in Amorite and later updated into Hebrew?
short_answer: Yes, that is quite possible given how close Amorite and Hebrew appear to be.
expanded_answer: The possibility is strong because Amorite appears extremely close to Hebrew in grammar, spelling, and syntax. If an Amorite text used an alphabetic script, later updating it into Hebrew would not require a large linguistic leap, and the newly discussed tablets open interesting questions about Torah textual development.

question: What was the most interesting piece of political palace intrigue in Egyptian history?
short_answer: The harem conspiracy against Ramesses III was the most interesting example.
expanded_answer: The harem conspiracy involved secondary wives and court officials trying to remove both Ramesses III and his named successor, Ramesses IV, so Pentawere could take the throne. Examination of Ramesses III's mummy indicates that the assassination succeeded, but the successor survived and the conspirators were later condemned in court proceedings.

question: Is the mention of iron in Job evidence for an Iron Age date?
short_answer: Smelted iron points that way, though the broader ethnic and cultural setting in Job is even stronger evidence.
expanded_answer: Ordinary meteoritic iron, which predates the Iron Age, is distinguished from the reference to iron being taken from rock and smelted. The stronger evidence is Job's cultural setting, especially the picture of Aram, Sabeans, and Chaldeans after the breakup of the Late Bronze Age order.

question: What did ancient Egyptians call themselves?
short_answer: They generally called themselves `remetch` or class-based terms, not `Kemet` as a self-name in the modern popular sense.
expanded_answer: Egyptians normally referred to themselves as "the people" and sometimes by class, with an upper stratum called something like the "pat" people. The popular claim that they called themselves Kemet as a regular ethnic self-name is rejected because that term is rare in Egyptian documents and more national labels appear later under wider foreign contact.

question: What does he think of the Bible Project?
short_answer: The Bible Project has a useful big-picture aim, but it sometimes leans on outdated scholarship.
expanded_answer: The Bible Project's purpose is broad, digestible book-by-book summary rather than detailed background work, and that general summary approach is mostly fine. The main criticism was that it sometimes uses dated scholarship, with the plague-against-Egyptian-gods idea in Exodus given as an example.

question: What are the benefits of learning Latin, is it useful for Bible study, and are there study tips?
short_answer: Latin helps indirectly by teaching grammar that later supports Greek and Hebrew study, though he could not offer personal study tips.
expanded_answer: Latin teaches categories such as dative, genitive, accusative, and nominative, which English speakers often have to learn from scratch before studying Greek or Hebrew. It also opens access to a large body of Western writing. Because he never learned Latin, he could not offer personal study tips; its main Bible-study payoff comes when students approach the biblical languages.

question: Is he familiar with Old Testament scholar Elmer Martin's thoughts?
short_answer: Dr. Falk knew only a little background about Martin and had not read enough of his work to comment on his theology.
expanded_answer: Martin had worked at a Mennonite college, but his work rarely appears in the Exodus literature Dr. Falk studies. He had not explored Martin's theology or writings and declined to evaluate them.

question: Why did God not choose an empty land as the promised land?
short_answer: Exodus 23:29 says an empty land would become desolate and overrun with animals and thickets before Israel could occupy it.
expanded_answer: Exodus 23 says God would not drive the inhabitants out all at once because the land would become desolate and dangerous animals would multiply. An empty land would require Israel to clear thorns, thickets, and wildlife before occupying it, making the practical burden too great.

question: In Deuteronomy 10:27, does Moses convince God, and is this how prayer works?
short_answer: The question could not be answered because Deuteronomy 10 has only 22 verses.
expanded_answer: The malformed reference prevented a direct answer rather than inviting a guess at the intended passage. Since Deuteronomy 10 has only 22 verses, the referenced text could not be located; the questioner was asked to provide the correct reference before an answer could be given.

question: How did the Pharisees interpret the Bible wrongly in Matthew 23:13, and what was the right interpretation?
short_answer: They treated law-keeping as salvific, while the law exposes unrighteousness and points to trust in God through Christ.
expanded_answer: Matthew 23 alludes to a Second Temple Jewish idea that entrance into the kingdom could come through strict law observance and temple practice. In his reading, the Pharisees missed that the law functions as a schoolmaster, exposing unrighteousness and pointing people to trust God through Christ rather than trusting the law to save.

question: Why did God pick Egypt as the place for Joseph, Mary, and Jesus to flee in Matthew 2:13?
short_answer: Egypt had established Jewish communities, was outside Herod's reach, had protected roads, and offered work for Joseph.
expanded_answer: Egypt was a natural refuge because it had established Torah-observant Jewish communities in places such as Alexandria, Pelusium, Tell el-Yehudiya, and Elephantine. Once outside Judea, the family was beyond Herod's practical power, and Roman Egypt also had protected travel routes and public building work where Joseph's skills could support the family.

question: Why did God bring up Job to Satan in Job 1?
short_answer: The text does not give God's reason, but it shows a larger drama under God's control that Job could not fully understand.
expanded_answer: Job never gives the specific reason God allowed Job to become Satan's target, and that omission is part of the book's point. Job is righteous and does not deserve the suffering, but God's later questioning shows that Job is not in a position to understand all the cosmic dimensions of the drama.

question: Does the Old Testament clearly distinguish between veneration and worship?
short_answer: No; that distinction develops much later in church history rather than in the Old Testament.
expanded_answer: The Old Testament does not provide the later theological distinction between worship as praise and glory and veneration as respect without worship. The clearer development of that distinction belongs in the church era, especially around the rise of icons and related controversies centuries later.

question: What is the best way to share the gospel with children, and can children understand sin, heaven, and hell?
short_answer: Children can understand at an age-appropriate level, and should be given the biblical story and realistic building blocks for the gospel.
expanded_answer: Children around six or seven can begin to understand sin, heaven, and hell, though a four-year-old may not yet have the same cognitive framework. His advice was to teach the biblical story truthfully, with realistic rather than fantasy-like presentation, so children gain the background pieces needed to understand and respond to the gospel.

question: Is there an age of accountability, and does it vary from person to person?
short_answer: Scripture gives no fixed age; accountability depends on what a person has been given and what they can understand, with grace covering those who cannot.
expanded_answer: The Bible gives no fixed age of accountability, and the wilderness generation's age twenty cutoff does not establish one. Accountability is framed in terms of grace and responsibility: those who cannot understand are covered by grace, while those given more understanding are more accountable.

question: What is his favorite sitcom?
short_answer: He does not watch sitcoms, so he has no favorite.
expanded_answer: This was the second part of the Matthew 23:13 super chat, but it was answered after the age-of-accountability discussion. He does not watch sitcoms and could not name a favorite.

question: What does he think of Eliakim typological arguments for the papacy?
short_answer: The Isaiah 22 and Matthew 16 connection is dubious, and the keys refer to the gospel rather than a papal storehouse of merits.
expanded_answer: The argument connects Isaiah 22's key of David to Matthew 16's keys of the kingdom, but that connection reads too much into the texts. Matthew's keys concern the preaching of the gospel under Christ's authority, not an exclusive Petrine storehouse of good works or papal authority.

question: Does an Aramaic original undercut the Petros/Petra distinction in Matthew 16?
short_answer: Exegesis should follow the inspired Greek text received in Matthew, not a hypothetical Aramaic reconstruction.
expanded_answer: The saying may have been spoken in Aramaic, but interpretation must be based on Matthew's received Greek wording rather than a reconstructed underlying Aramaic text. In that context, the keys are the gospel and the authority of Christ, with serious responsibility for those who preach it.

question: What was the average age for marriage in ancient Near Eastern culture, especially among Israelites?
short_answer: Women often married around 15 to 19, men varied more and often married later, and there is no precise average.
expanded_answer: First marriages were usually arranged by families and reflected survival, fertility, wealth, and future security rather than modern romance. Women might marry in the later teenage years, while men varied widely depending on wealth, inheritance, military obligations, and life circumstances, so any average remains approximate.

question: What are good resources, commentaries, or articles on Job?
short_answer: He could not recall the older resources he had read, but recommended the NICOT and possibly Hermeneia commentaries as starting points.
expanded_answer: He could not recall the sources from a graduate course on Job taken decades earlier. He recommended the NICOT volume as a starting point because the series is strong in Old Testament work, and possibly Hermeneia for well-done liberal scholarship. Neither was presented as part of a remembered personal bibliography.

question: If parents enable the rebellious drunkard in Deuteronomy 21:18-21, is there a punishment for them?
short_answer: The law places the burden on the parents to bring the adult son forward, and the text does not specify a legal penalty for bad parenting beyond communal shame and pressure.
expanded_answer: The passage concerns an adult son whose gluttony and drunkenness threaten a community living close to subsistence, not a small child. Because the parents are the ones required to seize and bring him to the elders, the text puts responsibility on them, but it does not prescribe a formal penalty for enabling beyond shame, public pressure, and likely communal consequences.

question: Could the Hebrew word for leech in Proverbs 30:15 refer to a vampire because of a later Arabic cognate?
short_answer: No; the proverb uses the leech image for someone who preys on the needy, and reading the later Arabic vampire sense back into Hebrew would be an etymological fallacy.
expanded_answer: Proverbs 30 compares an exploitative person to a literal leech that drains others, especially the afflicted and needy. Later Arabic use of a cognate for a vampire may make sense as a development from the leech image, but projecting that later meaning back into Proverbs would misuse etymology.

question: Does the story of the Eloquent Peasant show materialistic thinking in Egyptian culture?
short_answer: It is less a critique of materialism than a story about status, wisdom, and not overlooking an outsider with real skill.
expanded_answer: The story belongs to a context without money in the modern sense and should not be read as a straightforward modern critique of materialism. It is framed more as a story about a socially marginal but wise and skilled figure whose worth should not be missed in a status-conscious society.

question: How similar is Coptic to ancient Egyptian?
short_answer: Coptic is essentially the last phase of Egyptian, mostly late Egyptian with some Greek vocabulary and a Greek-based script.
expanded_answer: Coptic is described as about ninety percent late Egyptian and ten percent Greek vocabulary, written with the Greek alphabet plus additional letters for Egyptian sounds. Because its grammar and syntax remain Egyptian, he recommended teaching it after late Egyptian and having instructors who understand Egyptian rather than Greek alone.

question: If classical theology says God is dispassionate, how should biblical language about God's emotions be understood?
short_answer: In this reading, God's emotions are positional responses rather than changes of state, and such language should not automatically be treated as anthropomorphism.
expanded_answer: Classical theology often treats emotion as a change of state, which creates problems for divine simplicity. In this reading, biblical language describes God's unchanging position toward things: God is always against sin and always loves the image of God in people, so anger or love need not imply internal change.

question: How did Egyptian warfare develop from the early to late kingdoms in weapons, tactics, and goals?
short_answer: Weapons and tactics developed from stone maces and simple bows to bronze arms, siege equipment, chariots, composite bows, iron, and Greek-style weapons; changing military goals were not discussed.
expanded_answer: Early warfare used stone maces, simple bows, reed arrows, and flint-edged weapons. Bronze arms, spears, javelins, and siege equipment became more important in the Middle Kingdom, while the Second Intermediate Period brought chariots and composite bows. Late and Ptolemaic warfare added iron, Greek-style arms, and elephants as mobile archery platforms. The response focused on weapons and tactics without explaining how military goals changed.

question: Why is there no documented evidence of Yahweh before the Bronze Age collapse?
short_answer: Preservation and the ambiguity of the divine name are issues, and Israel as a nation and Israelite Yahweh worship belong to the Exodus and later context.
expanded_answer: Yahweh is difficult to identify in fragmentary texts because the same form can relate to the verb "to be," unlike more distinctive divine names. The lack concerns Israelite evidence rather than pre-collapse religion in general: standing stones, animal offerings, and texts from Ugarit attest other religious activity, but there was no cohesive Israel before the Exodus in this account. Moses brought Yahweh worship to the people, while earlier worship in Midian remains plausible but needs more evidence.

question: Was there a title he wanted instead of *The Ark of the Covenant in Its Egyptian Context*?
short_answer: The working title was *Before the Ark of the Covenant: Exploring the Egyptian Context of Israelite Ritual Furniture*, though he thought the editors' title was better for marketing.
expanded_answer: The original proposal title was longer and more descriptive, while the editors chose a stronger market-facing title. He also pushed back on other editorial issues, especially keeping dates in the book because the Egyptian material is tied to reigns and chronology.

question: What is his favorite poetic passage in the Bible, and why?
short_answer: Psalm 1 is compact Hebrew poetry with contrast, figurative language, and advice about meditating on Scripture.
expanded_answer: Psalm 1 is a compact example of Israelite poetry, with couplets, contrast between righteous and wicked, figurative language, and the tree-by-water image. He especially liked its connection between meditation on Scripture and fruitfulness in season rather than immediate payoff.

question: What is the oldest Psalm in the Bible?
short_answer: Psalm 90 is probably the oldest, traditionally and textually attributed to Moses.
expanded_answer: Psalm 90 is identified because it is introduced as a prayer of Moses and is traditionally, as well as textually, associated with him. He acknowledged that some question Mosaic authorship, but still treated it as probably the oldest psalm in the Psalter.

question: What is his favorite evidence for the Trinity?
short_answer: Isaiah 44:6 supports two persons called Yahweh, Acts 5 supports the Holy Spirit as person and God, and God's inherent goodness adds a philosophical argument.
expanded_answer: No single passage gives the whole doctrine, but Isaiah 44:6 shows, in this reading, two distinct persons called Yahweh speaking in unity. Acts 5 identifies lying to the Holy Spirit with lying to God, and the philosophical argument is that divine goodness is more coherent if there are interpersonal relations within the one God before creation.

question: Why is there a large disproportion of secular liberal or mainline Protestant scholars in biblical academia and fewer evangelical scholars?
short_answer: In his view, evangelical scholars are numerous but have less control of major institutions, presses, journals, and conference resources, so their voice is less amplified.
expanded_answer: He argued that evangelical scholars are often outside the most prestigious schools, presses, journals, and conference structures. Liberal or mainline institutions have larger platforms, travel funding, and publication control, so their scholarship can appear much more dominant.

question: What did ancient Israelite kings dress like, what did royal garments look like, and did they wear crowns?
short_answer: They wore robes, sandals, and a turban or headcloth with an ornate headband crown, with rosette-patterned fabrics also attested.
expanded_answer: The royal crown is described as a headband-like ornament, likely gold for kings, worn over a turban or cloth rather than a modern pointed crown. Based on depictions such as Jehu on the Black Obelisk, he pictured robes from neck to feet, sandals, and decorated fabrics, with rosette or flower patterns appearing on Israelite clothing.

question: Was Joseph's colorful cloth common or something very special?
short_answer: Colorful tunics were common among Levantine Asiatics, but Joseph's particular pattern would have been distinctive.
expanded_answer: Colorful tunics are attested for Levantine Asiatics, including in scenes such as Beni Hasan, so the presence of a colorful garment was not unique to Joseph. What would distinguish Joseph's garment was the particular woven pattern, since handmade fabrics could carry family or individually recognizable designs.

question: Did ancient Egyptians have coffee?
short_answer: No; coffee requires high elevations, and Egyptians did not drink hot drinks until the Islamic period.
expanded_answer: Ancient Egypt did not grow coffee because coffee requires high elevations that Egypt lacks. Coffee drinking in Egypt is connected to the Islamic period, when alcohol restrictions created a stronger role for coffee, and ancient Egyptians drank beer rather than hot drinks.

question: In 2 Chronicles 35, what does Pharaoh Necho mean when he tells Josiah that God is on his side?
short_answer: Necho likely claimed an oracle from a deity, though Chronicles may frame it as God. In this reading, Josiah wrongly ignored the warning.
expanded_answer: Necho was a polytheist, but Egyptians could still speak of "God" in the singular when describing an oracle. Necho was on his way to Carchemish to aid Assyria against Babylon and warned Josiah not to interfere. In this reading, Josiah acted without proper consultation and ignored a warning that Chronicles presents as divinely significant.

question: Why have evangelicals or non-liberals not worked from within institutions and journals to influence academia?
short_answer: In his experience, some have tried, but institutional culture, tenure pressure, career penalties, and entrenched momentum make internal change very difficult.
expanded_answer: He described academic departments as cultures with strong hierarchies where openly Christian scholars may face penalties in tenure, promotion, scheduling, committee assignments, or publication. Years of avoiding conflict before tenure can become habitual, and in his experience attempts to change major institutions from within have yielded poor returns.

question: Has the battle of Gog in Ezekiel 38-39 already taken place, is it yet to come, or is it symbolic?
short_answer: In his reading, it has not happened and concerns the final rebellion against God; it may depict a symbolic rebellion or a real future battle.
expanded_answer: In this reading, Ezekiel 38-39 is apocalyptic literature about mankind's final rebellion against God, so it should not be identified with current wars or past events. Whether it depicts a literal battle or symbolizes a final rebellion cannot yet be known because apocalyptic literature reveals itself through later recontextualization.

question: Did ancient Egyptians likely consider frogs to be a type of fish?
short_answer: They did not consider frogs fish, though they could view tadpoles that way and associated frogs with magical transformation.
expanded_answer: The relevant Egyptian text is poetic rather than a biological classification. Egyptians did not consider mature frogs to be fish, but tadpoles could be treated as fish-like, and the transformation from tadpole to frog helped explain the frog's association with magic and the goddess Heqet.

question: If Yahweh is connected to the Hebrew verb "to be," why does the form differ from `hayah`?
short_answer: Yahweh reflects a secondary tense of the verb "to be," possibly older or Amorite-related, later reserved for the divine name.
expanded_answer: Hebrew appears to preserve two forms or tenses of the verb "to be," one of which became reserved for the divine name. The Yahweh form may have originated as an older or Amorite-related secondary tense that later fell out of ordinary Classical Hebrew use, while its connection to `hayah` remains widely recognized.

question: Is there support for the conquest of Canaan involving Exodus Israelites joining local Hapiru groups?
short_answer: There is not much evidence for that; it is conceivable but remains speculative.
expanded_answer: The closest biblical analogue would be groups such as the Gibeonites joining Israel, but they are not Hapiru. Since Hapiru are usually outcasts or mercenaries in the Amarna-period evidence, the idea is conceivable but there is no real evidence for Exodus Israelites joining local Hapiru groups in the conquest.

question: Could Akhenaten's monotheism have been inspired by Israelites in Egypt?
short_answer: No, because Akhenaten is too early for the Exodus chronology and his Atenism was not true monotheism.
expanded_answer: Akhenaten belongs in the 1340s BC while the Exodus, in his chronology, is around the 1260s, leaving roughly eighty to ninety years between them. Atenism was better described as monolatrous pantheism than true monotheism, and Israelites in Egypt before Moses were not yet Yahweh-worshiping monotheists.

question: Was Revelation coded for its time to evade Nero, and how much of it is prophetic?
short_answer: A strictly Nero-preterist reading is not persuasive; Revelation's imagery is heavily Old Testament, and 666 may allude to Solomon as a type for a fast-rising ruler.
expanded_answer: Nero could function as a type of antichrist, but this reading does not treat Revelation mainly as a coded text about Nero because the book is dated decades after his death. Revelation is saturated with Old Testament symbolism, and 666 appears with Solomon's gold in 1 Kings 10:14 and 2 Chronicles 9:13, suggesting a symbolic pattern of rapid royal ascent and power.

question: Why do sources say Egypt had anywhere from 30 to 33 dynasties?
short_answer: The differences come from how later periods and foreign rulers are counted beyond Manetho's original scheme.
expanded_answer: Manetho's standard numbering ended with Dynasty 30 and did not assign official dynasty numbers to the two Persian periods or the Ptolemies. Modern counts vary according to which of those foreign periods they add, producing totals of 30, 31, or 33.

question: If the Exodus was in 1265, how can the 430-year or 215-year chronology fit Jacob meeting a Hyksos king and Abraham in the time of Hammurabi?
short_answer: The 430 years likely include time in Egypt and Canaan, with the effective Egyptian sojourn closer to roughly 300-350 years, which can still fit Jacob in the Hyksos period and Abraham near Hammurabi.
