expanded_answer: He had not watched the video and offered no judgment on it. The week had been unusually busy, and finishing the popcorn review had taken all his available production time.

question: What do you do all day now that the channel is full time?
short_answer: Full-time work includes writing scripts and books, editing videos and shorts, preparing podcasts and thumbnails, collecting questions, and doing wider creative ministry work.
expanded_answer: Full-time channel work is a mix of writing, production, administration, and creative work. The day includes Bible reading and prayer, scripting Monday videos, working on books and proposals, editing audio and video, preparing shorts, turning live streams into podcasts, making thumbnails, and collecting questions. The move to full time mainly bought time to write and fact-check more carefully, improving the quality of the channel's educational and cultural-engagement work.

question: Is Dr. Falk's fiction science fiction?
short_answer: Yes. He writes science fiction and was seeking a literary agent for his next work.
expanded_answer: Science fiction gives him room to explore large ideas and "what if" questions. At the time of the stream, he was looking for a literary agent for his next work.

question: Would Dr. Falk make a manga someday?
short_answer: Probably not, because manga would take too much work and he prefers novels for exploring large ideas.
expanded_answer: Manga and comic-book art take too much time, especially when the writer also creates the art. He had completed about twenty pages of an earlier comic, but novels suit his preference for developing large ideas over a longer work.

question: Where can viewers read a sample of Dr. Falk's fiction?
short_answer: Pages 4-11 of *The Ark of the Covenant in Its Egyptian Context* contain a short historical-fiction sample.
expanded_answer: A small piece of historical fiction appears near the beginning of *The Ark of the Covenant in Its Egyptian Context*, on pages 4-11. This sample is historical fiction rather than the science fiction he usually writes.

question: Would Dr. Falk do a live reading of his fiction?
short_answer: He generally avoids live readings and prefers a narrator other than the author.
expanded_answer: Hearing authors read their own work breaks the imaginative experience for him. He prefers a narrator who comes to the work fresh and may find the right emphasis more naturally than its author.

question: Does a recent critical article correctly identify Moses as a late, non-Egyptian name?
short_answer: He regards Moses as Egyptian in origin, though he would need to read the exact article closely before giving a full response.
expanded_answer: Moses fits Egyptian etymology better than Hebrew, whether derived from an Egyptian word connected with water or from the Egyptian root meaning "to be born." Israelites were pastoralists, so a name explained as being drawn from water would be less natural as an Israelite invention. Without the article in front of him, he limits his conclusion to saying that the name is not late and that its Egyptian origin remains defensible.

question: Is there a preferred way to send many Super Chat questions without spamming the stream?
short_answer: No special method is required; Super Chats buy visibility, and the channel did not consider these questions spam.
expanded_answer: YouTube describes a Super Chat as buying greater visibility, while the streamer still decides whether to answer it. Multiple relevant Super Chats were welcome and were not treated as spam.

question: Why was a Super Chat question rejected?
short_answer: It was inappropriate; sexually explicit or otherwise unsuitable questions may be declined.
expanded_answer: The channel's moderator filters sexually explicit and other inappropriate material to keep the discussion suitable for its audience. Subscriber-only chat had also reduced porn bots and inappropriate messages. Paying for visibility does not override those standards.

question: Will the viewer like the upcoming popcorn review?
short_answer: Maybe; the reaction depends on the viewer and the episode.
expanded_answer: He could not predict whether the viewer would like the upcoming popcorn review. It might appeal to some viewers and miss with others, so he made no firm promise about the episode.

question: Are books like Enoch, Maccabees, Sirach, and Wisdom Scripture, and why do churches disagree about them?
short_answer: In his view, they are not Scripture, though they are worth reading because they illuminate the cultural world of the New Testament.
expanded_answer: He does not regard these books as Scripture and would not build doctrine on them. He still strongly recommends reading them because they belong to the cultural world of the New Testament and help readers understand its background. Protestant, Catholic, Ethiopian, and Eastern Orthodox approaches developed differently through their respective histories.

question: Is the angel of Yahweh the Son, and how do we know?
short_answer: Some passages suggest the angel of Yahweh may be divine, but the identification has to be argued from context rather than assumed.
expanded_answer: "We do not know" is the general answer because not every angel-of-Yahweh passage gives the same clarity. Some appearances may be christophanies, especially when the figure is identified with the Redeemer or Lord of hosts, while other appearances are better described more generally as theophanies. In unclear passages, such as some appearances to Abraham, identifying the person of the Trinity becomes speculative because the text does not tell us.

question: When you say students need three years of Greek and two of Hebrew, do you mean years or semesters?
short_answer: Years are meant, while many programs only offer shorter sequences.
expanded_answer: The intended standard is actual academic years: six semesters of Greek and four semesters of Hebrew. The usual sequencing is first-year Greek, then Hebrew and second-year Greek together, then second-year Hebrew and advanced Greek together. Two introductory ancient languages should not be taken at the same time, though advanced language years can overlap.

question: What is a textual apparatus and how do you use it?
short_answer: It is the scholarly note system below a critical text that records manuscript variants and helps readers evaluate readings.
expanded_answer: An apparatus is the coded section at the bottom of a critical text, such as the Greek New Testament or BHS, that lists variant readings and the manuscripts that support them. The main printed text reflects the editors' best judgment, while the apparatus shows other readings, their textual families, and sometimes their date or distribution. To use it, readers learn the key in the introduction, follow the footnotes, and evaluate what evidence stands behind a reading.

question: What biblical book besides Numbers would you write a commentary on?
short_answer: He would choose Exodus because of its Egyptian cultural references and the need for a commentary that handles them well.
expanded_answer: He would choose Exodus without hesitation because it contains many Egyptian cultural references that need careful treatment. Numbers also needs better commentaries, while an Exodus commentary that integrates the Egyptian material could make a distinct contribution. He would undertake the project only with a publishing contract.

question: Are the popular distinctions among eros, phileo, and agape valid, did C. S. Lewis originate them, and what sources address this?
short_answer: No. The distinctions do not hold for first-century Greek, C. S. Lewis repeated them rather than inventing them, and D. A. Carson's *Exegetical Fallacies* is recommended.
expanded_answer: The popular sermon distinction among eros, phileo, and agape does not hold for first-century Greek. It entered commentaries in the nineteenth century but had disappeared from serious commentaries about a century before this stream. C. S. Lewis repeated the distinction rather than originating it. D. A. Carson's *Exegetical Fallacies* is recommended for this and similar word-study errors caused by reading modern associations back into ancient Greek.

question: Does the Schneider article say Moses is an Egyptian name but from an Iron Age Egyptian loanword?
short_answer: He rejects that chronology because the relevant Egyptian forms and sound shifts are earlier than Iron Age I-II.
expanded_answer: The Egyptian names and phonological developments in question reach back into the Late Bronze Age, including the 18th and 19th Dynasties. In his view, Schneider moved away from earlier Egyptian explanations under pressure from the biblical-studies consensus. His specific objection is that Schneider dates the relevant sound shift too late.

question: Do you believe Moses wrote Job, who wrote it, and what do you think about the Rapture?
short_answer: He rejects Mosaic authorship, regards Job as anonymous and later than Moses, and reads Rapture texts as summary judgment rather than a pre-tribulation removal of believers.
expanded_answer: He rejects Mosaic authorship because Moses belongs to the Late Bronze Age while Job reflects an Iron Age setting, including references that fit the Arameans and the kingdom of Aram. The book is anonymous and may even have originated in Aramaic before entering Hebrew Scripture. He also rejects a pre-tribulation removal of the saints and reads the relevant passages as summary judgment of the reprobate.

question: Is the John 20 folded-napkin tradition historically accurate?
short_answer: No reliable folded-napkin custom is identified; John 20 distinguishes linen wrappings from a separate face cloth.
expanded_answer: John 20 describes linen wrappings and a face cloth lying separately, but it does not present the folded or rolled cloth as a symbolic custom. Establishing such a custom would require evidence from rabbinic or similar sources, and no such source is identified in the answer.

question: Why is there no trace of a separate face wrapping in the image on the Shroud of Turin?
short_answer: Shroud defenders say the face cloth lay over the shroud, but he finds that explanation weak.
expanded_answer: Shroud defenders commonly argue that a separate face cloth was placed over the larger shroud. In his view, that explanation is doubtful because John 20 refers to multiple wrappings and first-century burial practice involved wrapping and binding the body rather than leaving a single loose cloth over it. He also regards the Shroud's three-dimensional texture mapping as a major problem.

question: Were there hippos in Mesopotamia, and who might Nimrod have been?
short_answer: Mesopotamia had hippos, but he has no firm hypothesis about Nimrod's identity.
expanded_answer: Mesopotamia once had hippos, lions, bears, hyenas, crocodiles, scorpions, and poisonous snakes, though many larger animals were later driven extinct. He offers no firm Nimrod hypothesis because he has not done the necessary work in Mesopotamian literature. In his reading, the Bible does not villainize Nimrod as strongly as later interpretations do; it mainly presents him as a hunter and founder of cities.

question: How should we handle accusations of being false teachers when explaining views that differ from popular American Christianity?
short_answer: Distinguish essential doctrines from secondary issues, then require accusers to justify treating a disputed secondary view as necessary for salvation.
expanded_answer: In his definition, a false teacher denies an essential of the faith, such as salvation by grace through faith, Christ's deity, the Trinity, the fall, Christ's sinless life and resurrection, the atonement, or the second coming. Disputes over the Rapture, the cultic language of Genesis 1, or the clan-age interpretation concern secondary issues. Anyone making the accusation should explain why that disputed position belongs among the essentials of the historic Christian faith.

question: Why would the unjust be taken when Jesus comes like a thief in the night?
short_answer: The Noah comparison and the parables of the weeds and dragnet place the removal of the wicked before the gathering of the righteous.
expanded_answer: Matthew 24 compares the coming of the Son of Man with the flood, which swept away the wicked while Noah remained preserved. The thief image also makes the person or property taken the object of loss. Jesus' parables reinforce that order: the weeds are gathered for burning before the wheat enters the barn, and the dragnet has the angels remove the wicked from among the righteous. In this reading, the person "taken" is removed in summary judgment.

question: What did you sell as vendors at a Renaissance fair?
short_answer: They sold art jewelry and related convention-style items, with some overlap into science-fiction convention work.
expanded_answer: Their vendor work involved art jewelry made through their own casting and lapidary work, with unique pieces they produced themselves. The work overlapped Renaissance fairs, science-fiction conventions, and intergem-style shows, and included compliments from established science-fiction artists. The period is remembered as fun and formative, even if it was not the right long-term path.

question: What is Athanasian Trinitarianism?
short_answer: In his account, it holds that God has eternally existed as Father, Son, and Spirit, unlike semi-Arian and social Trinitarian models.
expanded_answer: In his account, semi-Arianism treats the generation of the Son and Spirit as an event before time, while social Trinitarianism makes Jesus a human whom the Father made divine. Athanasian Trinitarianism instead holds that God has always existed as three persons and that there was never a time when the Son was not God. Christian understanding of the Trinity developed historically as the church reflected on what Scripture had revealed.

question: What is the biblical stance on violence and defense?
short_answer: Scripture allows defensive or sanctioned violence in some cases, while distinguishing it from murder or senseless violence.
expanded_answer: Ecclesiastes' language about a time for war and a time for peace is used to distinguish defensive or sanctioned violence from murder. "You shall not murder" is not the same as an absolute ban on all killing, and self-defense or defense of life and property is treated as morally different from senseless violence or killing the innocent. This is a broad overview rather than a full just-war treatment.

question: When Jesus says not to test the Lord your God in Matthew 4:7, is he talking about the Father or himself?
short_answer: The Father, the Son, and the Triune God can all be included because "Lord" stands for Yahweh.
expanded_answer: In this reading, "Lord" in the quotation stands for Yahweh. Because Jesus is Yahweh of hosts and the Redeemer, Satan's test can be understood as testing the Father, the Son, and the Triune God rather than only one divine person.

question: Do Jews take a literal approach to the toledot when calculating the current year, as Josephus seems to?
short_answer: Some do and some do not; Jewish writings are not consistent, and some skip genealogical elements for religious or teaching reasons.
expanded_answer: Jewish writers are inconsistent on this question. Some take the toledot literally, but others already recognize by the first century that the genealogies are not always being used in a strictly literal chronological way. Josephus should not be treated as the totality of Jewish scholarship because other Jewish writings handle the genealogical material differently.

question: What does Luke 8:46 mean by power coming from Jesus?
short_answer: In the healing context, Jesus knows healing and cleansing have occurred when the woman touches him.
expanded_answer: The woman's twelve-year hemorrhage made her ritually unclean, and uncleanness was communicable. She risked severe consequences by entering the crowd and touching others, yet she touched Jesus in desperation and was healed. "Power had gone out" may mean that Jesus knew someone had touched him and received healing and cleansing, reversing the usual spread of uncleanness.

question: Why is Pharaoh's daughter at the river in Exodus 2 if elite women had private bathing spaces?
short_answer: She was still the daughter of a vizier rather than of a reigning pharaoh, and river bathing was normal across social classes.
expanded_answer: At the time of the Exodus 2 incident, she was probably the daughter of the vizier of Lower Egypt, not yet the daughter of a reigning Pharaoh. Administrative palaces at Avaris would not have had every royal amenity, and bathing at rivers or lagoons was common even for higher-status people outside the royal family. Priestly and royal contexts could have special bathing facilities, but that does not mean a vizier's daughter would never bathe at the river.

question: How do we become more holy, and what are your thoughts on furries?
short_answer: Holiness grows through Scripture, prayer, spiritual disciplines, confession, and focus on Christ; wholesome anthropomorphic characters should be distinguished from sexualized forms.
expanded_answer: Holiness grows through studying Scripture, prayer, meditation on God's word, confession, and keeping one's attention on Christ. A person may sin less while becoming more aware of the depth of that sin. On furries, ordinary anthropomorphic animal characters in works such as classic Disney or C. S. Lewis are distinguished from sexualized forms that he regards as sinful.

question: How could Solomon, the wisest man, fall as low as 1 Kings 11 describes?
short_answer: Solomon's many foreign wives turned his heart toward other gods.
expanded_answer: First Kings 11 identifies Solomon's love for many foreign women as the cause of his fall. His wives turned his heart toward their gods despite what he knew, fulfilling the warning that Israel's kings should not multiply wives, horses, or gold. His loyalties became divided between God and his wives.

question: What Greek verb does the Septuagint use for Solomon's love of his foreign wives?
short_answer: It uses agapao, which shows that the verb does not always describe uniquely pure or divine love.
expanded_answer: The Septuagint uses agapao in 1 Kings 11:2 for Solomon's destructive love of his foreign wives. That usage undercuts the popular sermon claim that agape and its related verb always refer to a uniquely pure form of love.

question: What leads Tom Holland to connect Yahweh's origins with Canaanite bull gods?
short_answer: He rejects a simple derivation of Yahweh from Canaanite bull deities and sees little evidence for the theory.
expanded_answer: He connects the claim with a northern Canaanite-origin theory that treats Yahweh as an extension of Baal or Hadad-type cults. In his view, this theory has almost no warrant, while the Kenite hypothesis at least proposes a Midianite or Edomite origin. He considers the northern theory attractive mainly to scholars who already hold that Israel emerged from native Canaanite culture.

question: Does John 6:15 dispel the rebellion narrative?
short_answer: John 6 shows Jesus refusing the kind of kingship people wanted to force on him.
expanded_answer: John 6:15 says that when the people wanted to seize Jesus and make him king by force, Jesus withdrew by himself. That action directly undercuts the idea that Jesus intended to lead a political or military rebellion. There is more than enough evidence that Jesus was not trying to take the world or the government by force.

question: How do the Gospel accounts fit together on Peter's second denial?
short_answer: The accounts can be harmonized by treating the courtyard and fire scene as overlapping narrative perspectives.
expanded_answer: The texts should not be read as if they specify only one fire, one accuser, or one static location. A cold Jerusalem night could have several fires, people could be moving around, and the Gospels give snapshots rather than every detail of the scene. The best harmonization is therefore a broader courtyard situation with multiple accusers and overlapping movements around the gateway and fires.

question: Have you talked to Zack Miller about your misgivings?
short_answer: He told Miller the behavior was not cool but avoids prolonged exchanges with people who test his boundaries.
expanded_answer: He had hinted at the problem and had directly told Miller that the behavior was not cool. Because he dislikes dealing with people who test his boundaries, he chose not to pursue a long confrontation.

question: Do you have advice for good commentaries on Isaiah while dealing with the Hebrew Roots movement?
short_answer: He recommends the NICOT Isaiah commentary, finds structural value in the Word Biblical Commentary, and also recommends Tremper Longman's Old Testament commentary guide.
expanded_answer: He rates the NICOT Isaiah commentary highly. The Word Biblical Commentary is weaker on details but useful for understanding Isaiah's structure. For broader recommendations, he points to Tremper Longman's Old Testament guide and D. A. Carson's New Testament guide. He describes Hebrew Roots advocates as stubborn Judaizers.

question: What is your opinion on deconstruction content by Alisa Childers and Tim Barnett?
short_answer: He had not watched the specific video, so he gave no full judgment; he remained hesitant about Childers as an apologist.
expanded_answer: He had not watched the video and did not evaluate it directly. Some of Alisa Childers's statements had struck him as inaccurate or poorly suited to apologetics, which made him hesitant about her work. His assessment remained provisional because it concerned his general impressions rather than this video.

question: In 2 Peter 2:4-10, are Noah and Lot rescued?
short_answer: Yes, but their rescue comes through judgment on the wicked, not through a Left Behind-style Rapture scenario.
expanded_answer: Noah and Lot are indeed rescued in 2 Peter 2, but their rescue works through judgment on others: Noah is preserved in the ark while the world is flooded, and Lot is led out before Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed. That is not a pre-tribulation removal scenario. For him, the passage supports rescue through judgment, with the wicked removed or punished, not a Left Behind-style rapture of believers.

question: How many wives count as many?
short_answer: The humorous answer is that one wife is enough, with the point tied back to the danger of Solomon's many wives.
expanded_answer: From his own marital experience, one wife is enough and more would be trouble. In context, the joke points back to Solomon's many wives and the dangers described in 1 Kings 11. The serious point behind the humor is that multiplying wives creates divided loyalties and spiritual danger.

question: What is the Christian view of intercourse, marriage, purity, and relationships, and how can flawed Christians improve their marriages?
short_answer: Husbands should love their wives as Christ loved the church, sacrificing selfish desires for their spouse's good.
expanded_answer: Husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church, seeking the spouse's good and sacrificing selfish desires. Both spouses are fallen and selfish, and neither will practice this perfectly. Christ can heal the separation that sin creates between husband and wife, while marriage itself can expose sin and foster holiness.

question: What are your thoughts on marrying young, around ages 18 to 24?
short_answer: It can be acceptable; marrying young may help with having children, while marrying later may help people know their goals and find a like-minded spouse.
expanded_answer: Marrying between 18 and 24 can be acceptable and may have advantages, especially for having children. Marrying later can make it easier to know one's goals and find a like-minded spouse. There is no strict rule for marrying young or late, so the answer weighs fertility and the possibility of children against the advantages that can come with greater age.

question: What are some misconceptions about demon possession, spiritual warfare, and liberation theology?
short_answer: The question was too broad to cover all three topics, so he chose liberation theology and condemned its use of Christian language to support Marxist political violence.
expanded_answer: Demon possession, spiritual warfare, and liberation theology would each require a separate answer. He chose liberation theology and defined it as using Christian language to support Marxist revolutionary politics and armed conflict. He condemned cases in which aid or ministry resources were diverted into funding violence.

question: How do I handle referencing and giving credit when I do not know what sources already exist?
short_answer: Read broadly, learn the scholarship, and cite earlier work once similar arguments are discovered.
expanded_answer: Scholarship requires knowing what earlier writers have already said. Wide background reading reveals existing sources, arguments, and prior discussions, which lets a researcher credit them appropriately. Without that reading, accidental plagiarism is easy because most research consists of learning the documents and published scholarship before adding a smaller original contribution.

question: If aliens exist, would that contradict the Christian faith?
short_answer: No. Scripture tells us what happened in this world, not everything that may exist elsewhere.
expanded_answer: Alien life would not automatically contradict Christianity because Scripture tells us what happened on this world, not necessarily everything that may exist among the stars. Such life could raise interesting questions about the image of God, communication, sin, and redemption, but those questions are not contradictions by themselves. Science fiction is also useful for exploring those hypotheticals.

question: What kinds of names should be used in a story set in Old Kingdom Egypt?
short_answer: Names should fit the period and culture instead of merely sounding Egyptian.
expanded_answer: He recommends Ranke's Egyptian name reference works, especially the volume covering Old Kingdom names. The catalogues organize names by historical period and can show when a name first appears in the record, including Ramesses-type names from much later periods. Historical fiction should use period-appropriate names found in Egyptian sources.

question: What could students at Tel Shimron find that would help support understanding of the Hebrew scriptures?
short_answer: Good archaeology starts with careful method, and written finds such as ostraca, seals, or seal impressions would be especially valuable.
expanded_answer: The first contribution is doing proper archaeology with good method, staying in the assigned square and learning from supervisors. Finds might include oil lamps, seals, seal impressions, altars, or other artifacts, but written material is the most valuable. Ostraca, papyri, seals, and seal impressions are especially valuable because texts give direct insight into cities, context, and the world behind the Hebrew Scriptures.

question: How would you introduce the gospel, Jesus, and the New Testament to someone raised with nothing?
short_answer: Begin with the Old Testament story of sin and death so the need for Christ and the gospel makes sense.
expanded_answer: Begin with the story leading to the gospel: creation, the garden, the fall, sin, death, Sinai, Israel's repeated failure, exile, and the continuing weight of sin. Once the person understands that problem, introduce Jesus as the one who pays for sin in full through the cross. The need for a Savior makes sense after the problem of sin and death is clear.

question: What defines early, late, and sub-period labels in ages like Bronze and Iron?
short_answer: Broad ages and their subdivisions are material-culture labels, with dates that vary by region and scholar.
expanded_answer: Major ages are named for prominent technologies or material culture, such as stone, bronze, or iron, and their dates differ by region. Scholars divide long periods into early, middle, late, numbered, and lettered phases, often in rough one- or two-century blocks. Pottery and other artifacts define those phases in an archaeological stratum, so the labels provide relative material-culture dates rather than an inflexible calendar.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What is your opinion on the Gosford glyphs?
short_answer: They are a modern hoax, not legitimate Egyptian inscriptions.
expanded_answer: The Australian glyphs are modern, badly executed Egyptian-looking marks with a mix of hieroglyphs and non-hieroglyphs. Specialists have treated them as a hoax, not legitimate inscriptions from an Egyptian source.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Did lower-class Egyptians, farmers, and slaves have tombs?
short_answer: Ordinary poor Egyptians generally did not have elaborate tombs like elites.
expanded_answer: Lower-class Egyptians were usually buried in simple pit or pan-grave-like burials in the desert. The body might be placed in a hole with a few grave goods and covered with sand, without cut tombs, decoration, or elite funerary display.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What happened to Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4:29-33?
short_answer: The historical evidence is limited, so several explanations remain possible.
expanded_answer: Nebuchadnezzar's last days are historically obscure: Babylonian evidence preserves his long reign and later imprisonment by Amel-Marduk, but not a clear medical account. Possible explanations include a real illness, conflation with traditions about Nabonidus, or a literary blending of Babylonian royal traditions, with the evidence still limited.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: In Genesis 3:19, is "bread" an anachronism because Adam would not have known bread in the garden?
short_answer: The wording can use later ordinary language without requiring Adam to have known later food technology.
expanded_answer: The Hebrew term often glossed "bread" has a broader lexical range and can mean food generally. Because English translations can make the term sound more specific than the Hebrew requires, the verse need not imply later bread-making technology.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What are your thoughts on Logos University?
short_answer: Accreditation concerns make the institution a poor recommendation.
expanded_answer: The concern is especially with accreditation language. State religious exemption and membership claims are distinguished from recognized academic accreditation, one cited accreditor is called an accreditation mill, and questionable credentialing should make prospective students avoid the school.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What books would you suggest for arguments against Mormonism?
short_answer: The field changes constantly, so recommended starting points include strong Joseph Smith biographies from both friendly and critical sides rather than one polemical source.
expanded_answer: Recommended reading includes both critical and sympathetic biographies of Joseph Smith, specifically Fawn Brodie's *No Man Knows My History* and Richard Lyman Bushman's *Rough Stone Rolling*, to get outside and inside perspectives. For theology and apologetics, he mentions the Mormonism chapter in older editions of Walter Martin's *Kingdom of the Cults* but warns that later editions and polemical approaches need caution; engagement should be done in love, not as a combat sport.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Was John 8:1-11 a real event or a later addition?
short_answer: The passage is text-critically later, while the event itself could still be historical.
expanded_answer: The passage is the pericope adulterae, and scholars are broadly agreed it was not original to John's Gospel, noting its limited manuscript distribution in Byzantine witnesses and Codex Bezae. The story could preserve an oral tradition or real event, but it does not appear to be original Johannine Scripture.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Would you consider doing a popcorn review of The Prince of Egypt?
short_answer: No; legal and copyright risks make it impractical.
expanded_answer: No, for legal and copyright-risk reasons. A review using the film would likely run into YouTube content detection and litigation risk from rights holders, so the channel avoids reviews that could consume time in legal disputes.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What are some sources on the Ten Commandments?
short_answer: Commentaries and peer-reviewed articles supplied the research; Christians live out the Decalogue through love of God and neighbor, with Sabbath uniquely fulfilled in Christ.
expanded_answer: The Ten Commandments work grew out of research on Israelite monotheism and relied on commentaries and peer-reviewed articles, including database access from academic training. The Decalogue is treated as treaty and covenant material, and Christians live it out under the law of love: not as a means of salvation, but as obedience that reflects love for God and neighbor, with Sabbath uniquely fulfilled in Christ.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: How could Jacob fight a divine man, understood as Christ, and prevail?
short_answer: Jacob could not overpower God in a normal sense; the scene is a theophany with God allowing the encounter.
expanded_answer: Jacob was wrestling a theophany, a temporary embodied manifestation rather than the fullness of deity. Jacob's "prevailing" is not overpowering God but enduring the encounter, while the hip injury shows God remained in control; the reason for the fight and the daybreak detail are not fully explained in the text.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Why so much money for an Assassin's Creed Origins review?
short_answer: A proper review would take many hours and would turn leisure into work.
expanded_answer: An archaeology-focused game review would require roughly 20 to 40 hours and would displace other work. Games related to archaeology or Egypt stop being relaxing because specialized training makes them feel like professional work, so the project would need to be worth that time.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: In John 5:23, does "just as" mean "in the same way" or "likewise," and what made Hur, father of Uri, powerful?
short_answer: The Greek term can carry those senses with a consequential nuance, and Hur was likely powerful as a Judahite clan or tribal leader.
expanded_answer: More biblical context would help for Hur, but he was probably a clan or tribal leader within Judah, a powerful tribe with many men. For John 5:23, the relevant term is *kathos*, which can mean "just as," "in the same way," or "likewise," while also carrying a consequence/result nuance in the verse.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: How can someone take three years of Greek and two of Hebrew if universities only offer two semesters?
short_answer: Serious language training often requires stacking courses, independent work, or programs beyond the minimum sequence.
expanded_answer: Two semesters gives only beginning Greek or Hebrew, enough to be dangerous but not enough for serious exegesis. Greek normally needs foundation, exegesis, and application years, while Hebrew usually needs foundation and exegesis; universities may offer only the foundation sequence, so seminaries, dialect courses, related languages, or another institution may be needed.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What was the environment and climate like in Israel when the Jews entered the land?
short_answer: Ancient Israel was wetter and more humid; geological change and modern swamp drainage have made the region drier and hotter.
expanded_answer: Ancient Israel differed from today in both geology and environment, including earthquake-shaped changes around Galilee. A large north-south swamp, later drained in the twentieth century, affected travel, humidity, storms, and flooding, so modern Israel is drier and hotter in ways that obscure some ancient conditions.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What ancient nations practiced circumcision, and why?
short_answer: Circumcision is attested among Egyptians and Israelites and discussed as a cultural and religious marker.
expanded_answer: The two ancient nations clearly known for circumcision are Egypt and Israel. Israel practiced it as the sign of the Abrahamic covenant, while Egyptian evidence includes Old Kingdom tomb scenes and inscriptions, though the Egyptian reason is not known and may have included sanitation or other cultural motives.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Were people who deconstruct sincere in their initial profession of faith, and if salvation requires perseverance, how can anyone have assurance?
short_answer: Their initial sincerity should generally be granted; assurance rests in God's promise to keep those who choose to remain on the path.
expanded_answer: Deconstruction stories should get the benefit of the doubt on sincerity, while still distinguishing very different reasons people leave: never believing, following a shallow emotional faith, rejecting rules, becoming weary of God or church life, or pursuing other desires. Sincerity does not make every reason legitimate, and mature faith was rarely represented in his experience. Assurance rests in the promise that God keeps those who remain on the path; people are not forced to stay if they choose to leave.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What offerings will Christians make in the Third Temple, who will be high priest, and was the Shekinah glory in the Second Temple?
short_answer: Christians would have no obligatory offerings; an Aaronic Levite would serve as high priest, and the Second Temple could contain the Shekinah without its being continuously visible.
expanded_answer: The Shekinah glory was not always visibly manifest, but the Second Temple could be understood as containing sacred presence, with the torn veil at the crucifixion marking that presence going out into the world. For a future temple, the high priest would have to be a Levite from Aaron's family, likely a Messianic Jew in an eschatological scenario, and Christians would not have obligatory sacrifices, though some permissible offerings such as thanksgiving could remain.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Is the abomination of desolation a person or an act?
short_answer: It is both: an act that defiles the temple and a person who embodies that defiling abomination.
expanded_answer: The act is a sacrifice or temple action that defiles sacred space and requires sacrifices to stop until the temple is rededicated and cleansed. Some texts also speak of a person standing where he should not be, so the person becomes the personification of the abomination that makes the place desolate.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What was divorce and remarriage like in ancient Israel?
short_answer: Early Israel allowed polygyny and male-issued divorce; Second Temple Judaism made polygyny less common, and Christian practice moved toward monogamy and eventually some female-initiated divorce.
expanded_answer: The changes are divided into broad periods: early Israel, Second Temple Judaism, and the Christian era. Early Israel allowed polygyny and male-issued divorce; the Second Temple period made multiple wives less common while retaining male divorce initiative; the Christian era moved toward one man and one woman and, eventually in some contexts, rare cases of women initiating divorce, while remarriage remained debated.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: How do we know when Solomon's temple was built, do we have synchronisms, and why did Siamun's dynasty send Solomon a treaty wife?
short_answer: The temple is dated through 1 Kings 6:1 and Assyrian synchronisms, and Siamun's weakened dynasty needed alliances.
expanded_answer: 1 Kings 6:1 places the temple in Solomon's fourth regnal year, commonly dated to 966/967 BC because Assyrian synchronisms for the divided monarchy let scholars date Solomon's reign closely. Siamun's Twenty-First Dynasty was falling apart, depended heavily on Libyan mercenaries, had lost effective control in several regions, and needed treaty wives to shore up alliances.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What is a concubine, how did the idea change over time, and what ancient countries did not have harems?
short_answer: A concubine is a lower-status slave used for procreation, and ancient Near Eastern harems were widespread.
expanded_answer: A concubine is a slave set apart for procreation, without the status or rights of a wife unless a particular culture granted rights after childbirth. The basic idea did not change much, and ancient Near Eastern countries generally had harems tied to treaty households, wife exchange, and sometimes surrogate-like arrangements in fertility crises.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Were there STDs in the ancient Near East?
short_answer: Yes, but nutrition was probably a larger cause of infertility than STDs.
expanded_answer: STDs existed in the ancient Near East, though not necessarily with the same profile people might expect. In the context of infertility, a barley-heavy and vitamin-poor diet probably contributed more than STDs, while some of the worst Old World STD problems came later from the New World.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Were there male concubines?
short_answer: No, because the social function of concubinage did not create the same category for men.
expanded_answer: There were no male concubines because the institution served a demand for female treaty partners, household sexual access, and offspring production. Even female rulers such as Hatshepsut could receive female treaty wives or concubines, but those women were not necessarily used for that purpose.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: How fluid was the title of Great Queen, and could a Great Queen be replaced?
short_answer: Royal titles could shift with status and court politics, but the details depend on period and context.
expanded_answer: The title could be quite fluid because a Great Queen designated the male heir's mother and also performed temple rituals with the king. A queen who did not produce a male heir could be replaced, though not always; some retained the title despite minor queens producing sons, while other kings demoted or replaced Great Queens for succession or court reasons.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Aside from the Hyksos and the Seleucids, when did Egypt have non-Egyptian rulers?
short_answer: The Seleucids never ruled Egypt. The transcript does not preserve a full list of non-Egyptian rulers.
expanded_answer: The answer begins by correcting the premise that the Seleucids ruled Egypt. The stream then moves into other follow-ups without giving an expanded list of foreign or foreign-origin rulers.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Can you speak some ancient Egyptian, and how did you learn Egyptian?
short_answer: A few short Egyptian phrases are given, and Egyptian was learned through four years of school.
expanded_answer: A couple of short Egyptian phrases are spoken on stream, with the warning that they may be butchered. Egyptian was learned the hard way: by going to school and studying it for four years.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Is it selfish to invest in your own spiritual development if that means you cannot make other financial contributions?
short_answer: It can be noble to invest in ministry preparation, but obligations and sacrifices still matter.
expanded_answer: Voluntary giving is distinguished from unavoidable obligations such as taxes, and investing in spiritual growth in order to serve the body is not selfish. Preparation can require real sacrifice, using the move for PhD work as an example, so someone should understand the cost rather than romanticize it.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What are your thoughts on communion and the Eucharist?
short_answer: The preferred view is in-communion, and some traditions overread the text.
expanded_answer: John 6 is read as not directly equated with the Lord's Supper, because its immediate context concerns receiving Christ's words and spiritual life. The preferred view is an in-communion understanding, where the gathered body of believers practices the rite together, and many sacramental readings import later medieval or superstitious categories into the text.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: When did you become a Christian?
short_answer: He became a Christian in August 1977, when he was seven years old.
expanded_answer: He became a Christian in August 1977 at age seven, praying in the back seat of a 1967 Chevy on the way home from evening church. He did not tell his parents for years because he did not think it was important to announce it.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What is your freakiest paranormal experience?
short_answer: The main example is a West Elm store experience, especially seeing a shadow figure in the stock room.
expanded_answer: The strangest experience was at a West Elm location in Vancouver, where he saw a dark shadow-like figure walk across the stock room while the lights were on. He also mentions other reported incidents there, including objects coming off shelves, a reported small-girl apparition, and a doll found under shelving.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Why would Abimelech take Sarah in Genesis 20 when she was old?

The traditional option is that Abimelech took Sarah as a treaty wife to cement relations with Abraham, but the answer doubts a simple attractiveness explanation and suggests that Abraham and Sarah traditions may conflate a family line or clan, with a younger "Sarah" figure being associated with the older matriarchal name.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Do you have a literary agent?
short_answer: No, and he is looking for one.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Did Jephthah sacrifice his daughter in Judges 11?
short_answer: The text points toward an actual sacrifice and is not easy to reinterpret away.
expanded_answer: The pastor's alternative explanation is wrong because Judges 11:31 uses language for a burnt offering, an offering burned to ash. He calls Jephthah a bad judge who was ignorant of the law and says he could have used the redemption price for a rash oath instead of carrying out the sacrifice.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: May you draw Joseph's Egyptian name in hieroglyphs?

Because the visual drawing is not preserved in the TXT transcript, the safest transcript-grounded summary is that he responded visually and the text transcript does not preserve a complete explanation.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Where are your intro songs from, and what are they based on?

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Does writing lyrics count as composing, or do you need to write notes too?
short_answer: Writing only lyrics makes someone a lyricist; composition is the notes.
expanded_answer: Lyric writing is distinct from composition: lyrics alone make someone a lyricist, which is a valid role, while composition concerns the musical notes. A composer can also write lyrics, but if someone only writes words and not music, he would call that lyric writing rather than composing.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Do you inventory your book library?

expanded_answer: Past attempts included entering many books into a database, but the size of the library made complete cataloging overwhelming. Electronic books are kept in broad subject categories, and some professional books are sorted by author, but fully categorizing tens of thousands of books would take too much time.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?

expanded_answer: Current projects include a proposal for an Exodus book and a novel that is part of why he wants a literary agent. The broader work is framed as cultural engagement through intellectual and artistic media, including drawings, paintings, jewelry, animation, video games, novels, and music.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Does the folded cloth in John 20:7 indicate that the master will return?
short_answer: That symbolism is a later Messianic seder association, not something original to the first-century Jewish seder.
expanded_answer: After the questioner clarifies that they mean the tradition of folding a cloth to indicate the master's return, the answer connects it to later Messianic seder practice involving the hidden unleavened bread. The return-of-Christ symbolism was grafted onto the seder and was not original to the first-century Jewish practice.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: How do you translate "Ittai": "Yahweh is with me" or "friend"?
short_answer: The term cannot be translated securely without the Hebrew context and a biblical example.
expanded_answer: The context is not clear enough to translate the term confidently. Because it is a language question, a biblical example and the original Hebrew context are needed before narrowing the translation.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Why is the livestream so late?
short_answer: The time fits the show's circumstances and late-night audience better than an earlier slot.
expanded_answer: The 8 p.m. start originally worked around his work schedule, and later experiments with an earlier time hurt both viewer numbers and super chats. The show's esoteric question-and-answer format also performs better late at night, when some viewers are working overnight or looking for that kind of programming.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Do you believe the Trojan War was a real event, and would you do a video on it?
short_answer: A historical core is likely, but no video is planned.
expanded_answer: Most scholars now accept some Trojan War as historical, but no specific video is planned. Anatolian archaeology is outside the channel's main expertise, so it is not something he expects to address soon, though he leaves open that it could happen someday.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What made Egypt, Tyre, and Sidon enemies of Israel in the sixth century BC?
short_answer: Their treaty alliances brought foreign worship into Israel, so prophetic judgment focused on idolatrous influence rather than direct military hostility.
expanded_answer: The issue was mainly religious influence rather than direct military threat. Political alliances and treaty wives from places such as Tyre and Sidon brought foreign religion into Israel and turned kings' hearts toward other gods, so the prophetic judgment addressed idolatrous influence more than simple hostility.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: How should we interpret large numbers in the book of Numbers if Israelites did not always use numbers literally?
short_answer: Numbers have to be read in their ancient literary and administrative context.
expanded_answer: There are several proposals for the census figures, including clan, hero, genre, and literal readings, but the demographics make a strictly literal reading difficult. He leans toward a clan interpretation because the word often translated "thousand" can also refer to a clan, and he sees the wilderness censuses as showing that God preserved clan integrity despite judgment and death.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: How should Christians apply 1 Corinthians 6:1-8 today?
short_answer: The passage does not forbid every lawsuit but warns believers against scandalous disputes and fraud.
expanded_answer: Paul is addressing petty lawsuits among members of the same Corinthian congregation, not every possible legal action. Small internal disputes should be settled by wise church arbitration if possible, but serious fraud, predation, abuse, and large-scale swindling should be exposed to proper legal authorities rather than hidden inside the church.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Is the command for wives to submit to husbands universal or only for women who chose their spouse?
short_answer: The command is part of Christian marriage ethics, while abuse and coercion are contrary to that ethic.
expanded_answer: The command is universal, not limited to women who personally chose their spouses. It is paired with the universal command for husbands to submit to Christ and give themselves to their wives, so the answer frames it within mutual Christian obligations rather than unilateral privilege.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: When should a wife submit to her husband if both spouses are trying to follow God and disagree?
short_answer: Submission is not blind obedience and should be understood within mutual faithfulness, wisdom, and non-abusive marriage.
expanded_answer: Circumstances matter, so the principle should not be turned into a blanket rule. Sometimes the integrity of the marriage requires the husband to defer to the wife, such as when he is financially irresponsible; abuse is not submission but a violation of the marriage covenant, and no spouse should be required to endure it.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Would you take a cryptocurrency sponsor or an unrelated video-game sponsor?
short_answer: No; sponsors that could shape answers or fall outside the channel's mission are rejected.
expanded_answer: Cryptocurrency sponsorships and video-game sponsorships unrelated to the ancient Near East or the Bible would be refused. The concern is that sponsors could expect favorable answers or redirect the channel away from its mission, while the channel's answers need to remain truthful and independent.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Does God plan every detail of our lives, including calamities like cancer?
short_answer: No. Knowing what people will choose differs from planning or desiring every calamity.
expanded_answer: Scripture supports contingent knowledge rather than God arbitrating every detail, using David's choice not to go where he would have been captured as an example. God may know what people will choose without planning or desiring every evil, and some calamities arise from chance or human behavior, such as cancers linked to smoking.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Could the book of Esther be a story loosely based on a real event?
short_answer: Yes, though it could also be more closely based on a real event; the evidence is limited.
expanded_answer: Esther could be loosely based on a real event, but it could also be based more closely on one. The difficulty is that records from the relevant Persian court period are sparse, so the identities of the queens and the court background remain somewhat opaque.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Does Genesis 30:27 show that divination was permitted before Sinai, and does the practice point to an ancient origin for the composition?
short_answer: Divination was permitted before Sinai and later abolished; the practice supports an ancient setting for the narrative, not necessarily for its composition.
expanded_answer: Divination was among practices permitted in the patriarchal period and later forbidden at Sinai, alongside certain pillars and altar forms. Laban's claim and Joseph's divination cup fit that earlier religious setting. The practice therefore supports an ancient origin for the narrative, though not necessarily for the composition, which he dates to the thirteenth century.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: Why does God answer the way he does when asked his name in Genesis 32:29 and Judges 13?
short_answer: The reason is uncertain. Possible explanations involve idolatry, name magic, and God's refusal to be manipulated.
expanded_answer: Genesis 32 does not state why God withholds his name. In Judges 13, one possible explanation is that Samson's paganized parents might have added Yahweh to their pantheon. The answer also connects the withheld name with resistance to name magic and manipulation: Yahweh remains sovereign and refuses to be controlled through divine names.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: What does channel membership give?
short_answer: Membership gives access to member-only videos, polls, updates, and other tier benefits.
expanded_answer: Listeners should use the join tab for the exact tier descriptions, because different levels have different benefits. In general, members receive access to special content such as occasional member videos on Bible and archaeology issues, plus polls and member-only updates.

short_answer: The source is unknown and cannot be recommended or evaluated.

On the Ron Wyatt point, intentionally promoting those claimed discoveries is treated as deceiving the flock and helping a wolf, while calling it a sin in a technical sense is less clear.

episode_title: An Evening with David Falk, Whatcha Expecting?
question: If historians identify ancient Judaism as originating in henotheism, how do monotheists justify their monotheism?
short_answer: The question is unclear, but Israelite religion does show a movement from henotheism or polytheism toward monotheism.
expanded_answer: The theological framing of the question is not fully clear, but ancient Israelite religion probably originated with henotheistic or even polytheistic patterns. Monotheism eventually dominated Israelite religion, especially after the Babylonian exile helped push polytheism out of the system.
