expanded_answer: Job reflects Aramaic and Hurrian-influenced cultural settings, likely after the fall of Mitanni and during the period of the divided Aram states. Because those details fit Syria or Aram better than Solomon's Jerusalem, the composition is dated after Solomon rather than to Solomon himself.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Could Job simply be a novel meant to give wisdom?
short_answer: "Novel" is an anachronistic category, and Job is better treated as wisdom literature.
expanded_answer: Calling Job a novel is problematic because that genre category is anachronistic for ancient literature. Job is meant to impart wisdom, but it belongs within ancient wisdom literature influenced by Mesopotamian and Aramean contexts rather than modern fiction.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Is Job one of the older books of the Old Testament?
short_answer: That idea is a late scholarly myth, and Job is more plausibly dated to the Iron Age.
expanded_answer: The claim that Job is among the oldest Old Testament books circulated in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, but later contextual study points elsewhere. Chaldeans, Arameans, and the post-Mitanni setting are markers that fit the Iron Age, probably Iron II, though not with precision.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: If theosis was the expected hope in Egypt after death, what made Pharaoh special as a potential god?
short_answer: Pharaohs had the power of life and death and were viewed as godlike in a way that changed over time.
expanded_answer: Egyptian views of pharaoh's divinity changed over time, but for much of Egyptian history pharaohs were humans who became gods after death. Their special role was royal and mediatorial: they assisted Osiris in the people's apotheosis and, unlike ordinary people, joined Re on the solar boat rather than working in Osiris's fields. A follow-up frames pyramids as resurrection machines, not ancient power plants or grain-storage silos.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Is Heli in Luke 3:23 best understood as Mary's father?
short_answer: Yes, treating Luke as the maternal line while Matthew gives the legal line through Joseph.
expanded_answer: Matthew's genealogy is treated as the legal Davidic line through Joseph, while Luke's genealogy is treated as the genetic line through Mary. On that basis, Heli is probably Mary's father, with both lines still Davidic though diverging at different points.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Does fear always mean respect in some sense?
short_answer: Yes, but fear is only one kind of respect; not all respect is fear.
expanded_answer: Fear can involve respecting something because it can do harm, while another kind of respect is honor without fear. A person can respect fire because it is dangerous without honoring it, and can honor a person or position without being afraid.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Should Amun-her-khepeshef's death-date calculation use 1288 minus 25, or does Ramesses II's family chronology change it?
short_answer: The relevant calculation is 1288 minus about 25, and the proposed 40th-year issue does not seem to fit the chronology.
expanded_answer: In the middle-low chronology, Ramesses II comes to the throne in 1288, so Amun-her-khepeshef's death around the 25th regnal year gives roughly 1263, allowing some uncertainty in the prince's age. Seti I did not reign 40 years, so the proposed father's-40th-year calculation would need more context.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Who are Resheph and Astarte?
short_answer: They are Canaanite deities: Astarte related to Ishtar and Resheph as a war god.
expanded_answer: Astarte is the Canaanite form of Ishtar and probably connected with Venus, though her mythology is not explored in detail here. Resheph, by contrast, is identified confidently as a vicious Canaanite war deity, roughly comparable to other war gods.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Is HALOT's two-volume physical set worth getting?
short_answer: HALOT is worth having for serious Hebrew work, though Holladay's concise lexicon is enough for many beginners.
expanded_answer: The physical versus electronic format is a matter of preference, but anyone doing substantial scholarly work in the Hebrew Old Testament will eventually need HALOT. Holladay's concise Hebrew and Aramaic lexicon is a much cheaper resource for someone still learning Hebrew and covers most early needs.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: If Miriam is an Egyptian name, why did later Jews take up the name?
short_answer: It means "beloved" and has no theophoric element, so it could be adopted into Israelite culture.
expanded_answer: Miriam is an Egyptian name meaning "beloved," but because it is not theophoric it did not carry an Egyptian divine name that would prevent adoption. It simply became part of Israelite naming culture, and most later users likely did not examine its origin.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: What does Dr. Falk mean when he says Eastern Orthodox critics misunderstand sola Scriptura?
short_answer: They often confuse sola Scriptura with nuda Scriptura.
expanded_answer: Many Eastern Orthodox critics treat sola Scriptura as if it excludes councils, church history, and theological debate, which is nuda Scriptura rather than sola Scriptura. Sola Scriptura means Scripture is the final authority, not the only consulted authority, and some Eastern Orthodox practice something close to it while denying the label.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: How does divorce in the area of abandonment work when there is no certificate of divorce?
short_answer: That situation is messy; modern no-fault divorce removes one problem, but ancient abandonment left women in a harsh position.
expanded_answer: Abandonment without a certificate left a wife in limbo in ancient Israel, though the surrounding community could become involved because marriage carried communal and contractual obligations. Village leaders might pressure or punish the abandoning husband, and the New Testament is also harsh toward someone who abandons family obligations.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: What kinds of spirit creatures are there, and how do they relate to angels, demons, and divine council beings?
short_answer: The categories are diverse and include more than just angels, demons, unclean spirits, and council members.
expanded_answer: Categories include principalities, powers, watchers, primordial deities, and shades, with a warning that demonology can become arbitrary or sensationalized. Scripture and associated ancient literature imply a wide diversity of spiritual beings beyond the familiar categories.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Is Lawson Younger's Ancient Conquest Accounts a good place to read about what happened to the northern tribes of Israel?
short_answer: Yes, especially for tracing the ten northern tribes in Assyrian sources.
expanded_answer: Lawson Younger's work is a good starting point for the fate of the northern tribes after Assyrian conquest and exile. Younger follows Assyrian documents showing Israelites joining the military, taking up trades, and continuing to appear in Assyrian records.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Are there any Gospel Coalition recommended commentaries that Dr. Falk takes issue with?
short_answer: No specific listed commentary bothers him, but commentaries as a genre can be repetitive and surface-level.
expanded_answer: Conservative and liberal commentaries can both be useful, and the Gospel Coalition list is treated as a good starting point. The larger criticism is that many commentaries lean heavily on earlier commentaries, so they often repeat inherited views rather than producing groundbreaking work.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Has Dr. Falk ever considered a discipleship ministry?
short_answer: The current channel already functions partly that way, though it is described mainly as an educational ministry.
expanded_answer: Many forms of ministry have been considered, including pastoral, missionary, pulpit, and discipleship work, but the channel is where they believe God has called them. The channel is framed as training younger Christians to read, think, and stand on Scripture, while still remaining open to non-Christian viewers.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: In Luke 23:43, where should the comma go in Jesus' statement to the thief on the cross?
short_answer: The comma most likely belongs after "you," so "today" begins the promise.
expanded_answer: Either punctuation is possible because the Greek text itself does not settle the matter, but the preferred reading is "Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise." Reasons include Jesus' repeated use of "truly I tell you" as a verbal hook and the fronting of "today" for emphasis on the immediacy of salvation.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Who was Darius the Mede in Daniel 5:31, and is he the same Darius as Daniel 9:1?
short_answer: Darius the Mede is identified with Cyrus the Great, while Daniel 9:1 is taken as Darius II.
expanded_answer: Following Donald Wiseman, Darius the Mede in Daniel 5 is identified with Cyrus the Great under a Median regnal identity in a dual Medo-Persian kingdom. Daniel 9:1 is distinguished as Darius II, with "son" allowing a broader descendant sense in Hebrew.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: In Luke 11:1, what would Jesus teach his disciples about prayer that was different from how Jews normally prayed?
short_answer: Formal prayer was not a normal, consistently taught practice for many Jews at the time.
expanded_answer: First-temple communication with God centered on offerings and sacrifices, while synagogue prayer developed during exile and was not uniformly retained after the temple was rebuilt. Jesus' disciples ask for instruction because prayer was seeing a revival, especially among Pharisaic and holiness-oriented circles, but practice and posture still varied widely.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Does Eve being created within the garden suggest a special relationship to the inner world of the garden?
short_answer: Possibly, especially if Eden is understood as a temple setting, but the conclusion remains tentative.
expanded_answer: The idea is possible because Adam is brought into the garden from outside, while Eve appears to be created inside the sacred space. If Eden is a temple setting and Adam and Eve serve priestly roles for humanity, that could imply a special relationship, though the argument would need closer reading.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: What does Dr. Falk think about reported evidence of an Assyrian camp that supports the Bible?
short_answer: He had heard only a little about it, so it sounded provocative if true but required more reading.
expanded_answer: He had heard only a little about the reported Assyrian camp and needed more information before judging it. If true, it would be provocative, but Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem is already unusually well documented in biblical and Assyrian sources; the main new value might be evidence about the camp's size. The Assyrian account discussed says Hezekiah was trapped "like a bird in a cage" and then ends without the expected victory or tribute boast, which is treated as highly unusual.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Where do evil spirits or demons originate in the Bible?
short_answer: They are part of the ancient Near Eastern worldview, and the Bible assumes that broader context.
expanded_answer: The Bible does not introduce evil spirits from scratch because such beings already belonged to the ancient Near Eastern worldview. In this explanation, their ontology belongs within creation and the ancient assumption that creation needs continuing spiritual maintenance rather than running on its own.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Is there a lore reason for demons, and did God create them?
short_answer: Spirit beings are part of creation, but the biblical texts are high-context and do not spell everything out.
expanded_answer: Spirit beings are part of creation, either created to support creation or arising as part of creation's cataclysmic reality, and some faithfully maintain creation while others rebel. This background is connected to chaos monsters, primordial gods, the divine council, and Psalm 82, while stressing that biblical writers assume much of this context rather than explaining it directly.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Is that spirit-being background related to Psalm 82?
short_answer: Psalm 82 refers to the divine-council background but applies it to human judges.
expanded_answer: Psalm 82 invokes the assumed mythological background of God's council and lesser elohim, but the psalm quickly applies that imagery to earthly judgment. The contrast is between beings called gods or sons of the Most High and human judges who will die like men.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: How should someone discuss Preston Sprinkle's arguments with an affirming Christian friend?
short_answer: The discussion needs care, love, and attention to how it is handled.
expanded_answer: Handle the topic carefully and in love, especially because the subject is sensitive and difficult to discuss publicly. The practical counsel is to speak the truth in love, care for the person, and then let the conversation play out without turning it into a reckless confrontation.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Were the Nephilim UFOs, aliens, fallen angels, sons of Cain, or ordinary giants?
short_answer: None of those options; they are human men of renown born from an illegitimate cultic union.
expanded_answer: In this interpretation, Genesis 6 speaks of humans throughout: sons of God, daughters of Adam, and men of renown. This reading treats "daughters of Adam" as cultic language tied to ancestor worship, so the problem is an unequal religious union between a legitimate priesthood and an illegitimate priestesshood, not demigods or extraterrestrial beings. It also treats Numbers 13's Nephilim and grasshopper language as part of a defamatory report, so that passage does not establish that the Nephilim were giants.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Are the daughters of Adam a contrast to the sons of God?
short_answer: Yes in a way, contrasting priestly identity with ancestor-oriented worship.
expanded_answer: "Sons of God" is read as priestly identity and "daughters of Adam" as cultic language connected to ancestor worship, so the contrast is between a legitimate priesthood and an illegitimate priestesshood. The union is framed as religiously unequal and socially destructive, producing the Nephilim as human men of renown rather than demigods.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Where can someone read more about Dr. Falk's interpretation of the Nephilim?
short_answer: It has not been published yet.
expanded_answer: That specific interpretation had not been published, so there was nowhere to read more about it. He had many ideas awaiting publication and little time to write them up.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Did the Nephilim survive after the flood?
short_answer: Later cases could occur because similar vow-breaking practices continued, not because a spirit race survived.
expanded_answer: The Nephilim could appear after the flood because people could still break the relevant cultic vows, just as before. They no longer exist because the religious practices that produced them no longer exist.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: What is the relationship between the image at the top of the Re-Harakhti stela and the Zoroastrian Faravahar?
short_answer: No direct relationship is established; earlier Egyptian winged-disc symbolism could have influenced the Faravahar.
expanded_answer: Re-Harakhti is a solar disc with the solar serpent, not the same winged figure. Egyptian winged-disc symbolism is much older and may have influenced the later Faravahar imagery. If it did, the influence would run from Egypt to Zoroastrianism.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Is it true that cultic prostitution did not exist in the world during Leviticus?
short_answer: No; cultic prostitution existed long before Leviticus, including in Mesopotamia.
expanded_answer: Cultic prostitution was an old practice, nearly as old as temples, and was already present in Mesopotamia before Leviticus. It was often separated from the main temple building and functioned as a fundraising practice connected to temple activity.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Might the Indo-Aryan Mitanni elite have had the Vedas?
short_answer: It is possible, but the Mitanni left no writing that would let us know.
expanded_answer: The possibility cannot be ruled out, but the Mitanni left almost no internal literature, royal documents, inscriptions, or usable synchronisms. Because their capital cannot be fully excavated and the surviving evidence is so sparse, we simply do not know what texts or traditions the elite had.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Were Ham or his sons deified as gods under other names in ancient Egypt?
short_answer: Not to current knowledge; Egyptian records do not mention them that way.
expanded_answer: Egyptian records do not mention Ham or his sons as deified figures under other names. Since Egypt was already an established population long before the historical periods with records, a preserved Egyptian record of that kind would not be expected anyway.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: What does Dr. Falk think of Patrick D. Miller's work on Israelite religion?
short_answer: He had not read Miller's work and usually consulted Richard Hess on early Israelite religion.
expanded_answer: He could not evaluate Miller because he had not read his work. Richard Hess was his usual reference for early Israelite religion. After hearing that Michael Heiser recommended Miller, he made a note to look into it.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: What does Dr. Falk think about the cultural-memory view of the Exodus?
short_answer: He rejects that view in favor of a historical Exodus.
expanded_answer: He rejects the cultural-memory view and argues for a historical late Exodus in the nineteenth dynasty under Ramesses II, including a real crossing of the Reed Sea, a real wilderness wandering in Sinai, and a real conquest of Canaan.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: In Egypt and Turkey, is it permitted to talk openly about Jesus Christ in public?
short_answer: Not in Turkey, while Egypt is more nuanced and depends on setting and initiation.
expanded_answer: Turkey has strict limits on initiating public religious talk, and one could end up in jail. Egypt, in his description, has formal tolerance in law but dangerous social realities, so a public street-preaching approach in a major square could provoke mob violence even if prosecution is not the main risk.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Is salvation conditional, and are repentance or baptism caveats to salvation?
short_answer: Salvation has conditions, repentance is not a work, and baptism is not a condition in the same way.
expanded_answer: The thief on the cross is evidence that baptism is not required for salvation. Repentance is framed as agreeing with God that sin is evil and turning away from it; salvation is compared to an amnesty whose recipient must not reject the amnesty by choosing sin against God.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: What does epiousion mean in Matthew 6:11?
short_answer: The word is controversial, with several possible meanings in the Lord's Prayer.
expanded_answer: Epiousion is a controversial hapax whose meaning is not known from other usage. "Daily" is an assumed contextual rendering, while other possibilities include subsistence, coming-day, provisioned, or rationed bread, so interpreters are making informed guesses from the Lord's Prayer context.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: How likely is it that Joseph met Mary at Zechariah's home on the way to Bethlehem rather than leaving with her from Nazareth?
short_answer: The text does not say that, and the Luke timeline makes it possible but unlikely.
expanded_answer: Luke says Mary visited Zechariah and Elizabeth in the Judean hill country for about three months, then returned home to Nazareth. By the time of the census, Joseph goes from Nazareth to Bethlehem with Mary, so Joseph meeting her at Zechariah's home is possible but not stated and does not seem likely from the immediate timeline.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Is there a correlation between human sacrifice associated with bulls in Minoan, Canaanite, and Carthaginian contexts?
short_answer: Carthage and Canaan are connected through Phoenician origins, but a Minoan connection is not really established.
expanded_answer: Carthage and Canaan have a plausible connection because Carthage was founded by Phoenicians from the northern Canaanite region. A comparable Minoan relationship is not established: Minoan civilization appears to follow a separate trajectory despite later Egyptian contacts, Baal predates the Sea Peoples, and the Minoan evidence sounds like human sacrifice rather than cannibalism.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Did the cult of Yahweh come from Canaan or the Kenites?
short_answer: In his view, the Kenite or Midianite-Edomite hypothesis fits the biblical texts better, though both proposals lack positive evidence.
expanded_answer: The Kenite hypothesis is probably better described as a Midianite-Edomite hypothesis and, in his view, fits the biblical texts more strongly. The northern Levant or Ugaritic-style proposal relies on similar language around Baal and the Ancient of Days, with some versions identifying Yahweh with El instead. Neither proposal has a smoking-gun inscription, so the question remains speculative and he does not treat his preference as certain.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: How old are the roots of Genesis 1:3?
short_answer: The oral roots are hard to date and could be thousands of years old, but any estimate is speculative.
expanded_answer: If the question concerns oral roots, the answer is very hard to pin down because oral history is difficult to date. Some traditions with which Genesis interacts are thousands of years old, and the speculation could stretch far earlier in light of ancient Near Eastern ritual cultures and early agriculture, but methods such as measuring oral drift are uncertain and cannot give a confident date.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Since the Ark of the Covenant is called God's footstool, could the cherubim have formed an actual throne?
short_answer: An empty miniature throne is possible, but the text does not tell us.
expanded_answer: An empty miniature throne is possible in principle, but the ark text only says the cherubim faced each other with wings over the mercy seat. Because ancient throne designs normally have paired figures side by side facing forward, the ark's facing cherubim make an actual throne-style design unlikely.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Why is Egypt's Fourteenth Dynasty not considered Hyksos?
short_answer: The Fourteenth Dynasty was Semitic but did not rule Egypt the way the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty did.
expanded_answer: The Fourteenth Dynasty is described as Semitic wandering warlords or gangs in the Delta rather than a real ruling dynasty. By contrast, the Fifteenth Dynasty established rule from Avaris and controlled major parts of Egypt, so the Hyksos label fits the Fifteenth Dynasty's foreign rulership but not the anarchic Fourteenth.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Who were the Shasu?
short_answer: They were an Edom-based nomadic tribal group, not merely a generic word for nomads.
expanded_answer: The Shasu are identified as migratory herdsmen based out of Edom who ranged through Sinai and as far as Egypt. "Shasu" is an ethnonym with specific dress, culture, diet, and migratory practices, not just a broad term for any nomads.

episode_title: Is Dr. Falk The Biblical David?
question: Do the Shasu have a connection to the proto-Israelites?
short_answer: Not as far as can be seen, apart from perhaps a small connection to Moses.
expanded_answer: No real connection is made between the Shasu and the proto-Israelites, apart from a possible limited link through Moses. The proto-Israelites are identified as Amorites moving from northern Mesopotamia through Syria into the Levant and Egypt, while the Shasu have a different ethnic origin in Edom.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Does the shift from Moabites to Midianites in Numbers 25 support the documentary hypothesis?
short_answer: No; the passage can be explained without defaulting to source-critical reconstruction.
expanded_answer: The question assumes a documentary-hypothesis reading, but Numbers 25 can be explained within the narrative setting. By this point the wilderness generation has largely died, so Zipporah is likely already dead, and Moses' later marriage in Numbers 12 would have ended the earlier marriage alliance with the Midianites.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: How can 2 Thessalonians 1:9 and Revelation 14:10 be reconciled on whether hell is in God's presence?
short_answer: They use different Greek expressions: separation from God's face or direct presence does not exclude remaining in the sight of the Lamb and angels.
expanded_answer: Second Thessalonians describes being away from the Lord's face, while Revelation says the condemned are in the sight of the Lamb and holy angels. In this reading, the Eastern Orthodox essence-energy distinction allows the condemned to be separated from God's essence or direct presence while remaining within reach of divine energies and judgment.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What is the history of the clan interpretation of biblical ages?
short_answer: The interpretation goes back to nineteenth-century German scholarship and developed through comparative Semitic work.
expanded_answer: Friedrich Gardiner is named as the 1870s source for connecting biblical ages with clans. Clan readings had fallen out of view as European clan structures disappeared, and their recovery is linked to late nineteenth-century comparative work, especially renewed attention to Semitic languages and social structures.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Who is the most underrated biblical figure?
short_answer: Barak is an underrated figure, while the producer suggests Jael.
expanded_answer: Barak's request that Deborah accompany him can be read as prudence rather than cowardice: he wanted the prophet to share the risk and show confidence in the message. He accepts that a woman will receive the glory, and Hebrews 11 names him among figures of faith. These details support reading him as a good judge who was not driven by personal fame.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Who is the most overrated biblical figure?
short_answer: Samson is overrated because he repeatedly violates his Nazirite vow and behaves badly.
expanded_answer: Samson is often lionized in Sunday school, but the narrative repeatedly presents him as impure and destructive. He touches a lion's corpse, takes honey from it and gives it to his parents, drinks at a wedding, pursues sexual relationships, and violates his Nazirite vow. He also robs people after losing a bet and ties foxes' tails together before setting them on fire and sending them into fields. In this view, these acts make him a poor choice for a hero.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Why were Achan's children stoned with him in Joshua 7?
short_answer: They were probably complicit because the hidden goods were in the family tent, and the episode also involves corporate judgment.
expanded_answer: The family probably knew because the stolen goods were hidden in a shared tent. Joshua 7 is also framed in clan terms: Achan is identified by generations within a clan structure, so the episode reflects corporate clan justice, not only modern individual culpability.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Did ancient people ever get tired of being brutal to one another?
short_answer: The absence of centralized justice made clan protection and retaliation the practical system.
expanded_answer: Ancient clan societies lacked police, magistrates, and courts, so retaliation and clan protection were how justice and survival worked. Describing that system is not endorsing it; modern legal systems are better, but the ancient context had no comparable authority.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: In a clan, who breaks the tie when a decision is not unanimous?
short_answer: The clan chief or leader ultimately speaks for the clan.
expanded_answer: Most real authority rested with the clan chief, who spoke for the clan. A tribal chief could call clan leaders together, but if a clan refused something like going to war, pressure could be applied while compulsion remained limited.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Are there limits on preaching from Job's friends, such as using Eliphaz's words for declaring and decreeing?
short_answer: Yes; Job's friends are misrepresenting God, so proof-texting them is dangerous.
expanded_answer: Job 22 presents Eliphaz accusing Job of pride and hidden sin, which the book later condemns as bad speech about God. Because Eliphaz is one of Job's mistaken friends, his words should not be lifted as doctrine without accounting for their narrative role.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Is Job a rebuttal to salvation by works?
short_answer: No; Job is instead a book about the limits of human understanding in the face of suffering.
expanded_answer: Job is not mainly a book for the suffering person but for the comfortable person who assumes prosperity is secure. Its point is that righteous people can lose everything without being at fault, so human explanations for suffering are limited and often wrong.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Is there biblical warrant for saying people see Jesus before death, and could those who never heard receive a chance to accept or reject him after death?
short_answer: Scripture does not say people see Jesus before death; a post-death choice is left open only as a possibility for those who never had one in life.
expanded_answer: People who were presented with the choice in this life are not promised another chance after death. The transcript leaves open, without guaranteeing, the possibility that someone who never had an opportunity to hear could receive one choice after death, based on God's mercy and the text's silence about that case.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: If our sins were paid for, are we really forgiven?
short_answer: Yes, if the forgiveness is accepted.
expanded_answer: Jeremiah 31 contrasts the old covenant's cumulative family debt, pictured as fathers eating sour grapes while their children's teeth suffer, with the new covenant's individual responsibility: the person who eats the grapes pays. Christ's mercy adds the option of having him pay that personal debt. Forgiveness therefore means the debt is paid in full for someone who accepts it; a person who refuses remains responsible.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: How tall were Egyptian birthing bricks?
short_answer: They were about four inches high, enough to create clearance during delivery.
expanded_answer: A pair of bricks, each about four to six inches high and roughly eighteen inches long, supported one foot apiece. The mother stood on them so gravity could help and the midwife had room to catch the child.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Does forgiveness simply constitute a transfer of debt?
short_answer: Forgiveness is indeed a transfer of debt, and that is the point.
expanded_answer: Forgiveness is compared with financial debt: the obligation is transferred and dealt with rather than ignored. *Tetelestai* basically means "complete" or "finished," and its use on financial documents supports the paid-in-full analogy. A fuller demonstration would require examining the relevant papyri.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Why didn't Satan also take Job's wife if the objective was to maximize suffering?
short_answer: The brief answer is partly humorous: leaving her may have maximized Job's suffering.
expanded_answer: The response is brief and partly humorous: Satan may have left Job's wife precisely because that made Job suffer more. The transcript does not develop a longer doctrinal argument for the question.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: At what rate were ivory clappers used during childbirth?
short_answer: We do not know exactly, but probably near a natural breathing rhythm.
expanded_answer: The clappers were likely used to keep a laboring woman's breathing in time. A rough estimate is 10-12 beats per minute, while the exact rate is not known from the evidence.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: How should Christians understand being chosen in Christ?
short_answer: Scripture presents both chosenness and free will, but how they fit together is difficult.
expanded_answer: The ship analogy treats passengers as free aboard the vessel while unable to set its destination. Chosenness is compared to God's providential shaping of a person's life while still allowing real human agency within that direction.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Why do some Christians treat inspiration as dictation or words zapped into a writer's head?
short_answer: Many Christians have not thought through inspiration carefully enough.
expanded_answer: Automatic-writing models of inspiration are rejected, with Heiser's contrast between Christian inspiration and passive channeling used as an example. Biblical writers used their own language, education, and experience, while God providentially shaped those factors.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What does "pillar of salt" mean in Genesis 19:26?
short_answer: The exact meaning is uncertain; mythic, literal, and euphemistic readings are possible.
expanded_answer: The text itself only says Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt. Possible readings include connection to salt formations near the Dead Sea, mythic retellings, becoming part of the environment, or a euphemistic description, but the context is too limited for certainty.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Did Moses bring plagues on his own cousin?
short_answer: Yes.
expanded_answer: The transcript gives only a brief confirmation for this super chat. The implication that Moses brought plagues on a relative is accepted without developing the answer beyond that short acknowledgement.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What did royal nurses do?
short_answer: They handled daily care for royal children and could also begin instruction.
expanded_answer: Royal nurses fed, cleaned, clothed, and bathed royal children. They could also begin basic education by teaching language, reading, or literature, so their role was broader than simple childcare.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Were Thutmose II and Hatshepsut related?
short_answer: Yes; they were half siblings.
expanded_answer: Both were children of Thutmose I but had different mothers, making them half brother and half sister. This is given as a short historical clarification.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Is divine council theology Iron Age or Bronze Age theology?
short_answer: It is generally Iron Age, though there are rare Late Bronze examples.
expanded_answer: The distinction is between general pantheons or divine assemblies and a fuller divine-council model with a head god taking counsel from subordinates. That fuller form is mainly Iron Age, while scattered Late Bronze evidence exists and needs careful definition.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Do Ugaritic texts show a divine council in the Late Bronze Age?
short_answer: They do, but such examples are comparatively rare and not equally common across Egypt and Mesopotamia.
expanded_answer: Ugaritic evidence can show a divine council, but it should not be treated as common across the whole Late Bronze world. Egypt and Mesopotamia have pantheons and assemblies, but not always a head god taking counsel from subordinates in the same sense, so the definition of divine council matters.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What does Dr. Falk mean by saying Joseph's brothers may have been drunk in Genesis 37?
short_answer: The text's bad report leaves several possibilities, and drunkenness is only one possible reconstruction.
expanded_answer: Joseph's bad report could refer to neglecting the sheep, eating them, getting drunk, or other misconduct, and Joseph may even have exaggerated. The key point is that the report created deep conflict, but the text does not specify exactly what the brothers were doing.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Did Dr. Falk's neighbors panic over gunshot-like sounds in his apartment?
short_answer: No; city noise makes people less likely to react.
expanded_answer: No one reacted because his noisy city environment makes people develop a thick skin toward disturbances. The sound may have been a capacitor failure, but either way it did not appear to alarm the neighbors.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What time frame comes after the Mitanni Empire but before the united kingdom?
short_answer: Mitanni is placed roughly from 1550 to 1260 BC, and Aram is later than Abraham.
expanded_answer: Mitanni is dated to about 1550-1260 BC, after Abraham and ending around the time of the Exodus. After Mitanni, there is roughly a century of fragmented city-states before Aram forms, with earlier Syria occupied by Hurrian groups rather than an Aramean kingdom.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Were Judges, Samuel, and Kings all written after the exile, or compiled from earlier documents?
short_answer: Kings clearly uses sources, and compilation and later editing are plausible.
expanded_answer: Kings explicitly names source materials such as royal chronicles and likely reached its edited form during or after the exile. Samuel may have a similar editorial history, while Judges is harder to place because it lacks the same obvious Persian loanword signals and may preserve older source documents.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Were Samuel and Kings originally one book later broken into four?
short_answer: No; although Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles were each split in two, Samuel and Kings were not one book together.
expanded_answer: Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles were each once single books before being split into two, but Samuel and Kings are not treated as one original combined work. Reasons include a compositional break and the unwieldy size such a combined scroll would have had, while allowing that a later editor may have smoothed the transition.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Will travelers need a visa for Egypt?
short_answer: Yes, and Egypt uses an online visa process.
expanded_answer: The practical tour guidance is to use the official Egyptian visa site rather than look-alike services and to present the resulting document at entry. This reflects the livestream answer, not a current travel advisory.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Where is the best place for a family to buy cheap furniture?
short_answer: A few quality pieces are better than relying on cheap or mid-range furniture.
expanded_answer: Inexpensive and mid-range furniture can fall apart quickly. The advice is to prioritize durable central pieces such as a couch, coffee table, or dining table, while finding cheaper options for less important items like some chairs.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Do some U.S. areas have better thrift stores than others?
short_answer: Yes, especially places with large transient populations.
expanded_answer: Rochester, Minnesota, is an example where students, patients, medical workers, and other temporary residents created strong thrift-store inventory. Wealthy-area garage sales can also be good but are inconsistent and require effort.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Can Dr. Falk recommend books or articles refuting theistic evolution?
short_answer: A Crossway book made a major splash, though it is not endorsed because he has not read it.
expanded_answer: A 2017 Crossway volume was promoted as a major critique of theistic evolution, but he had not read it and did not endorse either side. Michael Denton's work is also mentioned for broader critiques of evolution, with its value and criticisms acknowledged. His main interpretive objection is to concordist readings in any camp, including theistic evolution, young-earth creationism, and old-earth approaches.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Why do people get worked up about the Tetragrammaton in Exodus 3:14?
short_answer: The name comes from God's own self-identification to Moses, while later reverential avoidance developed much later.
expanded_answer: Much of the concern comes from religious tradition around the four-letter divine name Yahweh, including groups that insist on particular pronunciations and Jewish traditions of avoiding pronunciation. Those later traditions are distinguished from the Exodus context, where God identifies himself to Moses.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Is avoiding the Tetragrammaton an example of Pharisees adding rules on top of rules?
short_answer: Yes; the avoidance is linked to layered Second Temple traditions about holiness.
expanded_answer: In this account, Phariseeism began as a second-century BC holiness movement that added protective rules around the law. Yahweh gave way to Adonai and later Hashem; the added rules eventually obscured God's name and, in this interpretation, drifted from the commandment's intent.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Why do some translations render Matthew 28:19 as baptizing "into" the name rather than "in" the name?
short_answer: "Into" can be more literal, but English style often explains why many translations choose "in."
expanded_answer: "Into the name" better reflects the Greek construction, but it sounds awkward in English. English translations often choose "in the name" for readability, while the singular "name" still matters for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit formulation.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Did Bryant Wood conflate Middle Bronze III and Late Bronze Jericho?
short_answer: Yes, especially around the surviving mudbrick and wall evidence.
expanded_answer: Wood conflates Middle Bronze II, Middle Bronze III, and Late Bronze I material by treating the cyclopean wall as Rahab's wall. The evidence is said to point to a distinct Late Bronze I wall and Late Bronze II occupation, so the surviving wall evidence cannot simply be collapsed into Wood's reconstruction.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What language did Yeshua ben Sira speak?
short_answer: Greek, and probably Hebrew and Aramaic, given second-temple Jerusalem context.
expanded_answer: Ben Sira is located in second-century BC Jerusalem under Seleucid influence. In that setting, Aramaic is expected as the day-to-day language, Greek because of the Hellenistic political setting, and Hebrew because Ben Sira was a Jewish sage.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Why does Dr. Falk think Hebrew came from Amorite instead of Canaanite?
short_answer: Israelite ancestry, Avaris, and close Amorite-Hebrew linguistic evidence point that direction.
expanded_answer: The Israelites' ancestors came from Amorite-speaking territory, lived among Amorite-speaking Semites at Avaris, and remained isolated there long enough for the dialect to develop. Amorite-Akkadian material is also cited as showing many forms close to Hebrew.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What language was Sirach originally written in?
short_answer: Uncertain; Apocrypha studies are not his field.
expanded_answer: The earliest texts mentioned are Greek, but those appear to be translations. He leaves an earlier Hebrew or Aramaic form open because Apocrypha studies are outside his specialty.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Did Hebrew come from Amorite, or did both come from something else?
short_answer: Hebrew likely developed from Amorite, while both ultimately belong to West Semitic.
expanded_answer: Both ultimately belong to West Semitic, but the historical evidence makes Hebrew look like a branch from Amorite. The judgment is tentative and would be revised if new evidence pointed elsewhere.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Does Isaiah's apparent silence about the Exodus show that a northern tradition preceded the Exodus story?
short_answer: No; Isaiah speaks of the Exodus through both direct and indirect references.
expanded_answer: Isaiah 62:8 uses strong-arm language associated with the Exodus. Isaiah 10 compares Assyria's oppression and God's response with Egypt, the sea, and the wilderness period, while Isaiah 11:16 explicitly compares the remnant's return with Israel's departure from Egypt. These passages undercut the claim that Isaiah preserves a tradition preceding the Exodus story.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What is Dr. Falk's take on claims that biblical landmarks like Noah's Ark or Moses' rock have been found?
short_answer: Such claims are bad archaeology, especially claims tied to Ron Wyatt.
expanded_answer: The Noah's Ark, split rock, and similar landmark claims are in the wrong places, conflict with biblical geography, or rest on weak evidence. Ron Wyatt-style claims are especially damaging because they invite ridicule by presenting poor or fabricated archaeology as evidence.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What is the best archaeological evidence for the Exodus?
short_answer: The case cannot be reduced to one artifact because archaeology works by assembling many pieces of evidence.
expanded_answer: Archaeology reconstructs history by combining evidence rather than finding one decisive object. The examples given include Avaris's abandonment in mid-Dynasty 19, the death of Ramesses II's firstborn, the appearance of Israelite settlements near the end of the thirteenth century BC, the Merneptah Stela, and route place-names associated with the reigns of Seti I and Ramesses II. The proposed case rests on that cumulative pattern.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What is Dr. Falk's view of the documentary hypothesis?
short_answer: It is unnecessary, misleading, and often less useful than literary readings.
expanded_answer: In this view, belief in the documentary hypothesis does not determine salvation, but the method often blinds readers to the text's artistry. Apparent contradictions can function as literary contrast or supplemental information, and hypothetical source divisions should not outrank reading the received text as literature.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Is the documentary hypothesis still the general academic consensus?
short_answer: It remains common in North America, while Europe and Israel more often favor supplementary approaches.
expanded_answer: In his assessment, the documentary hypothesis remains the general consensus in North American academic theology but no longer in Europe or Israel, where versions of the supplementary hypothesis are more prevalent and range from liberal to conservative.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What is the difference between the supplementary hypothesis and essential Mosaic authorship?
short_answer: It depends on the version; conservative supplementary views can retain Mosaic core documents, unlike more liberal versions.
expanded_answer: Liberal forms of the supplementary hypothesis can resemble the documentary hypothesis, but conservative forms may hold that Moses wrote core documents later arranged by Joshua and scribes. Later editors may have added transitions, smoothed language, and updated diction, so supplementing is not necessarily opposed to essential Mosaic authorship.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Could Moses have written core documents if Hebrew was not yet a written language?
short_answer: Yes; alphabetic writing existed, Egypt was literate, and Hebrew is presented as colloquial Amorite that could be written alphabetically.
expanded_answer: Moses came from a literate Egyptian setting and could plausibly have been trained to write Egyptian, Akkadian, and the local Amorite language. On the view presented in the transcript, Hebrew was colloquial Amorite written in an alphabetic script, so the claim that written Hebrew did not yet exist does not rule out Mosaic documents.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Would Moses have created Hebrew?
short_answer: No; Hebrew developed from Amorite over centuries before the Exodus.
expanded_answer: Hebrew was not invented by Moses but developed from Amorite in the isolated community at Avaris over two or three centuries. The comparison is linguistic divergence, where a separated population keeps changing its language until a related but distinct dialect emerges.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: How did ancient Near Eastern civilizations understand disease and mental illness, and what resources are useful?
short_answer: Ancient medical texts and specialized resources on ancient Near Eastern medicine are the best starting points.
expanded_answer: Egyptian and Mesopotamian medical texts, including publications on the Edwin Smith Papyrus and ancient Mesopotamian medicine, are relevant resources. Disease could be explained religiously, such as through Sekhmet, while physicians also treated illness practically with medicines, spells, and procedures; mental illness could be attributed to demons or simply treated as sickness depending on who was diagnosing it.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: How popular was Sirach among Jews and Gentiles outside Egypt and Palestine?
short_answer: It circulated, but as a minority text rather than a major cultural force.
expanded_answer: Sirach and other Apocrypha circulated in the ancient Mediterranean world, but their influence is treated as often overstated. Works such as Plato and Aristotle are described as much more widely read, with the caveat that this is a general answer rather than detailed Sirach specialty work.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: How was math done in the ancient Near East, and did early kingdoms know geometry or algebra?
short_answer: Mesopotamia had strong mathematical tools including sexagesimal calculation and trigonometry-like work.
expanded_answer: Mesopotamia had geometry, trigonometry-like angle work, and a base-60 system that made divisions and angle calculations useful. Egypt had fractions, including Eye of Horus fraction symbolism, but the evidence supports geometry, trigonometry, and fractions rather than algebra with variables.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Does Dr. Falk view Sirach as equal to Tanakh Scripture?
short_answer: No, not even close; Tanakh is distinct from apocryphal books.
expanded_answer: Tanakh means Torah, Prophets, and Writings, which corresponds to the canonical Old Testament. Sirach is treated as Apocrypha: useful as wisdom literature, but not Scripture and not a source from which doctrine should be drawn.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Was recent news about Sirach prompting the stream's many Sirach questions?
short_answer: No recent Sirach news was identified.
expanded_answer: He had not heard of anything in the recent news about Sirach and did not know why so many questions about it were appearing in the stream.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Who or what is Abaddon in Proverbs 15:11 and Revelation 9:11?
short_answer: The Hebrew and Greek references treat Abaddon as a debated term connected with destruction.
expanded_answer: In Proverbs 15:11, Abaddon is a Hebrew word for destruction or ruin and may function near-synonymously with Sheol, perhaps specifying the punitive side of the grave. In Revelation 9, the term is tied to the abyss and the king over the tormenting locusts; both the Hebrew Abaddon and Greek Apollyon mean destruction, but the angel's exact identity is unknown.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Were Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon bad judges in Judges 12:8-15?
short_answer: Yes, or at least they should be read negatively because the book is arranged didactically from better to worse.
expanded_answer: Because Judges is arranged didactically from better to worse, judges placed in the downward sequence should be read negatively even when the text gives little detail. Since Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon fall between Jephthah and Samson, they are treated as worse than Jephthah but better than Samson.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What is Dr. Falk's favorite Bible verse?
short_answer: No single favorite verse is identified.
expanded_answer: Individual passages resonate at different times, but repeated reading keeps drawing his attention to the whole text rather than one stable favorite.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Can Dr. Falk give an overview of the seven spirits of God?
short_answer: The identity of the seven spirits is hotly debated and not known with certainty.
expanded_answer: Isaiah 11:2, Zechariah 4:10, and Revelation 4:5 are surveyed as possible background. The seven spirits might be read as attributes, but completeness is treated as more likely: seven is an idiomatic number of fullness, so the phrase may represent God's complete knowledge or the fullness of the spirit realm, while interpreters still disagree.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Were Israelites originally from Canaan or from Ur?
short_answer: It depends on the definition, but technically Israel originates at Sinai.
expanded_answer: Abraham originates in Ur, Isaac and Jacob are present in Canaan, and the descendants of Jacob live in Egypt. The Israelites become a nation when God brings them out of Egypt and forms them at Sinai, including the mixed multitude.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What is the true meaning of Revelation 6:12-14?
short_answer: It is the sixth seal's prelude to the great day of the Lord, depicting cosmic darkness and cataclysmic judgment.
expanded_answer: The sun and moon are both read as going black: "blood" is interpreted as battlefield-black rather than ruby-red. Falling stars are compared with a meteor shower, while the earthquake, displaced mountains and islands, and panicked people portray a cataclysm immediately before the day of the Lord. He offers this as the best reading available from this side of the prophetic events.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Is there concern that most biblical studies programs, journals, and tenure positions are mostly non-Christian?
short_answer: The dynamic is real in a way that does not happen the same way with other religions.
expanded_answer: This happens especially in Western Christian studies because the West is increasingly post-Christian and secular institutions can be staffed by non-Christian scholars. By contrast, fields centered in Buddhist or Hindu regions tend more often to be occupied by people who belong to those traditions.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: What are Dr. Falk's thoughts on Logos software, and is it worth it?
short_answer: No Logos subscription is used, so its value cannot be judged here.
expanded_answer: No Logos subscription is used, so no evaluation is offered on whether it is worth the cost. His own software use has centered on BibleWorks and, previously, other tools mainly for commentary access, so Logos' value is left to users who actually use it.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: How can someone contact Dr. Falk for a panel discussion on the historicity of Jesus?
short_answer: The historicity of Jesus is outside his specialty; for relevant topics, short Twitter or Facebook messages are preferred.
expanded_answer: The historicity of Jesus is outside his main specialty, which is Egyptology, Exodus, and the ancient Near East. For relevant topics, short direct messages on Twitter or Facebook are more likely to get a response than long emails.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: How should someone understand free will and blessings when a friend refuses to report lethal working conditions while waiting for God to change things?
short_answer: The friend should not ignore danger and should report unsafe conditions.
expanded_answer: God's provision may include ordinary means such as reporting unsafe work and finding another job. Responsible trust means acting rather than staying silent when dangerous conditions could get someone hurt or killed.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Are missing YouTube cards and a poorly loading Egypt and the Bible website known issues?
short_answer: Missing cards are a known issue, and the website problem may involve HTTP rather than HTTPS.
expanded_answer: Missing YouTube cards are a known issue because cards can be forgotten during the final upload step. On the website, the site is not configured for HTTPS and may only load over HTTP, while the site is not maintained as actively except for Groundhog-related updates.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: How should someone explain to family why they do not want to attend Biola to study theology?
short_answer: Start by finding out why the family is pressuring them toward Biola.
expanded_answer: Family pressure may come from cost, distance, familiarity, or parents paying the bill. Rather than simply attacking the school, the advice is to identify the family's concerns and work with those constraints to find a theology education that is not a waste of time.

episode_title: The Credible Falk Always Checks The Sources
question: Super Nintendo or Sega Genesis?
short_answer: Super Nintendo, based on personal experience, while acknowledging limited Sega experience.
expanded_answer: The preference is personal: Super Nintendo was familiar from working in a home entertainment department and playing Street Fighter after shifts. Genesis experience was limited, and commenters are invited to correct the technical comparison, but the personal answer leans Super Nintendo.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: How can someone stop going several days at a time without reading the Bible?
short_answer: A steady habit helps: make Bible reading a priority and choose an attentive setting, such as morning or table reading, rather than reading in bed.
expanded_answer: The problem is common, even for Bible scholars, because stopping is easy and restarting is harder. Bible reading needs a deliberate daily place, such as breakfast, and should be done attentively while sitting upright at a table or desk. Reading in bed is discouraged because fatigue makes it easy to stop paying attention or fall asleep.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: How can Numbers 25 move from a Moabite woman to a Midianite woman if that is not evidence of a P source, and were the Midianites Moses's kin and originally Yahweh worshippers?
short_answer: Moab and Midian are already allies in Numbers 22; Moses was related to Midian by marriage, and Midianite worship of Yahweh remains uncertain.
expanded_answer: Numbers 22 already presents Moab and Midian conspiring against Israel, so the woman in Numbers 25 belongs to the same allied strategy rather than an unexplained source switch. Whether the Midianites worshipped Yahweh is uncertain; some may have done so. Moses was related to Midian by marriage, and this reading takes the Cushite marriage in Numbers 12 to mean that his earlier marital bond to Zipporah was no longer controlling.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Was the Late Bronze I destruction cited by Petrovic only a minor, partial destruction?
short_answer: Yes. It affected only a small part of the lower city and does not support identifying it with Joshua's destruction.
expanded_answer: The destruction was limited to a small part of the lower city rather than the upper city or the entire site. Thutmose III claimed it, and a Thutmose III scarab was found in the destruction layer. For those reasons, he rejects dating it after Amenhotep II or identifying it with Joshua's destruction.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: What ancient law codes help explain Abraham and Sarah's treatment of property, Hagar, and Ishmael?
short_answer: Mesopotamian law codes illuminate the legal background Abraham and Sarah appear to be using.
expanded_answer: Kitchen and Lawrence's _Treaty, Law and Covenant_ supplies examples from Eshnunna, Hammurabi, and Lipit-Ishtar. The laws cover identifying a seller in property transactions, limits on returning a runaway slave who expected abuse, how a mistress could respond when a slave woman who bore children claimed equality, and inheritance rules requiring a father to declare a slave woman's child as his child. Abraham and Sarah appear aware of these rules and sometimes use legal wording in ways that defeat the law's spirit.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Who enforced clan rules for sojourners when there were no courts?
short_answer: There often was no central enforcement, so covenantal and social expectations had to be maintained by the parties themselves.
expanded_answer: In the patriarchal setting there are no local courts in Canaan, Aram, or Syria to enforce these rules, so Abraham and Sarah effectively have to apply covenantal expectations to themselves. Ancient treaty and covenant structures still matter, including covenant scenes involving Abraham, Abimelech, and Yahweh, because the parties understand obligations even without a state court system.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Is it true that "Lucifer" was not treated as the devil's personal name until much later Christian interpretation?
short_answer: Yes; the later name usage comes from the Vulgate and subsequent reading tradition.
expanded_answer: "Lucifer" is not a Hebrew or Greek term in the biblical text, but a Latin translation choice for language meaning something like a bright morning star in Isaiah 14:12. Jerome was trying to render the meaning into Latin, and the term later became associated with the devil because of the passage where it appeared. On that basis, nobody before the Vulgate period would have thought "Lucifer" was the devil's personal name.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: How do Christians reconcile monarchial monotheism?
short_answer: Christianity distinguishes one ontologically independent God from created lesser spiritual beings.
expanded_answer: Monarchial monotheism means one ontologically independent God who is first cause, all-knowing, all-good, and all-powerful, while also affirming created beings beneath him. Angels and other spiritual beings are greater than humans but still vastly less than God, so their existence does not threaten Christian monotheism. This hierarchy comes from Christianity's Judaic background.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Were the gods of other nations real deities or only spirits?
short_answer: National idols can function like masks through which real spirits act, but that does not make them true gods.
expanded_answer: Deuteronomy alludes to spiritual powers connected with nations, while Scripture can also describe the nations as worshiping nothing. Idols are proxy bodies or masks that spirits may use, but the mask itself is empty and not every idol has a spirit behind it. Most idols are empty most of the time, and pagan worship changes enough that a single static explanation is too simple.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: What would he recommend to a non-believer who has never seriously opened a Bible?
short_answer: Begin with the person's background and hesitation, then choose an accessible resource that addresses the obstacle.
expanded_answer: The reason someone has never opened the Bible matters. If the obstacle is doubt about the Gospels, Peter J. Williams's _Can We Trust the Gospels?_ is an accessible entry point; if the need is biblical context, John Walton's books are hard to beat. _The Screwtape Letters_ is another accessible option, though it still does not provide enough biblical context by itself. A bare New Testament can also be difficult for someone without Christian background, and he did not offer a simple all-purpose Bible primer that fills the gap.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Who is Peter J. Williams?
short_answer: Peter J. Williams is the warden of Tyndale House, a Cambridge research center focused on evangelical biblical scholarship.
expanded_answer: Tyndale House is a research center on the Cambridge University campus whose staff work on Bible translation and biblical research. Williams leads it as warden and helped organize David's scholarship to Liverpool. The Cambridge research center and Tyndale House publishing were once connected but later became separate organizations.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: What are his thoughts on an Enoch passage that seems inspired even though Enoch is not Scripture?
short_answer: A passage can be inspiring without making the whole book inspired or canonical.
expanded_answer: Inspiration is not judged passage by passage that way. First Enoch is Second Temple pseudepigrapha, Second Enoch is later, and pseudepigraphal attribution disqualifies the text from being inspired Scripture in his view. A reader may find a passage inspiring without treating the work as divinely inspired or canonical.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Does Jude's quotation of Enoch mean that Enoch is inspired Scripture?
short_answer: No. Biblical authors can quote non-inspired works without making those works canonical.
expanded_answer: Jude's use of Enoch does not make Enoch inspired. Biblical writers also quote non-inspired sources: Paul quotes Greek philosophers, the Old Testament refers to Jasher, and Psalm 104 interacts with the hymn to the Aten. An inspired text can use outside material to support its point without conferring inspiration on the source.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: If incest was rare in ancient Egypt, why do cases such as Hatshepsut and Thutmose II or Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun appear?
short_answer: Incest was rare; the Hatshepsut and Thutmose II case is explained as a succession-crisis measure, while Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun are not separately addressed.
expanded_answer: He explains the Hatshepsut and Thutmose II pairing through Thutmose I's succession problem: an aging king with only one vulnerable son might marry that heir to a sister or half-sister in an attempt to combine what was thought to be "strong royal blood." He calls this sympathetic magic rather than sound biology. Thutmose II produced no son with Hatshepsut but did father Thutmose III through a minor queen. He does not separately explain the Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun example.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Would Joseph's strong moral character in Genesis 39-41 go against an exaggeration interpretation of Genesis 37?
short_answer: Not necessarily; exaggeration or "puffery" differs from lying, and Genesis 37 could still fit Joseph's character.
expanded_answer: Exaggeration differs from deliberate falsehood, and advertising "puffery" supplies an analogy for claims that contain truth but are heightened. In that framework, Joseph could exaggerate in Genesis 37 while still having strong moral character if the report generalized behavior he had genuinely seen from his brothers. Numbers 13 is a related comparison where exaggeration may cross the line into an unreliable report.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: If the Arameans came after Abraham, why does Deuteronomy 26:5 call Abraham a wandering Aramean?
short_answer: This is a retrojection, using later vocabulary for an earlier figure.
expanded_answer: Retrojection applies later terms to earlier people or places, and Deuteronomy 26:5 uses the later Aramean label for Abraham's region after the Mitanni empire had collapsed. Other biblical examples include Philistines, the land of Rameses, and Pharaoh. Such wording does not by itself create a historical problem.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: What did the paper's peer reviewers not like?
short_answer: They wanted more dendrochronology, a comparison with competing software, and a less abrasive, more collegial tone.
expanded_answer: The journal and some reviewers were heavily invested in dendrochronology, while his work focuses on historical chronologies using epigraphy, king lists, synchronisms, and other historical sources. In his argument, dendrochronology works poorly in the ancient Near East because of carbon-sink and tree-ring problems. They also required a comparison with the leading competing software, which forced him to answer what he described as an earlier hit piece, and criticized the paper's tone as abrasive and insufficiently collegial.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Could AI interpret and do ancient chronology without dedicated chronology software?
short_answer: Probably not; ancient Near Eastern chronology is too complex and ambiguous for AI to replace the software work.
expanded_answer: Ancient chronology has many interlocking uncertainties, including ambiguous reign lengths, synchronisms, historical sources, and data types that software must handle explicitly. That complexity makes AI an unlikely practical replacement for dedicated chronology tools.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Would the Egypt tour work for someone who is not a native English speaker?
short_answer: Yes, especially if a companion can translate; limited English is not treated as a disqualifier.
expanded_answer: The tour itself will be in English, but a companion could translate and the Egyptian guide may also be multilingual. Limited English is not a major obstacle because much of the tour involves seeing the sites directly, with the Egyptian material explained along the way. A non-native English speaker could still get a lot out of the trip.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: What five to ten biblical books most need solid commentaries for teaching Christ and Old Testament influence on the New Testament?
short_answer: The list starts with the Pentateuch, Isaiah, selected Gospels, Romans, and Hebrews, then grows to Psalms, Kings, Numbers, and Chronicles.
expanded_answer: The recommended core is the Pentateuch, Isaiah, selected Gospels such as John, Mark, or Luke, Romans, and Hebrews, with Psalms added if the list can grow. Kings is also useful, while he considers Numbers and Chronicles badly underserved. Commentaries often skim genealogies or fail to explain Egyptian background in Exodus, leaving readers without the contextual help they need.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: What is a good ratio for commentary length to the length of the biblical book being commented on?
short_answer: A commentary should be much longer than the original text because it should explain many sections and provide information readers cannot get by themselves.
expanded_answer: A commentary should be much longer than the biblical book because it is supposed to comment on as many sections as possible, not merely restate the text. A useful commentary explains background, context, and interpretive details that readers would not normally know on their own. Many commentaries are too thin where readers most need explanation.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Should a good commentary pass the "thumb test" for substantial thickness?
short_answer: Yes, as a rough indicator of adequate coverage, though a thick commentary can still be concise.
expanded_answer: A useful commentary should generally be longer than the underlying biblical text and comment on many of its passages. The "thumb test" is a rough sign that a volume has enough room to do that work, but substantial length and concise writing can coexist. Thickness alone is not the standard; the commentary still needs to provide information readers could not obtain for themselves.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: What should someone stay away from when looking for commentaries?
short_answer: Avoid commentaries that cover too much, are too old, come as indiscriminate sets, or are written outside the author's expertise.
expanded_answer: Whole-Bible, whole-Old-Testament, and whole-New-Testament commentaries are usually too broad to be useful. Commentaries more than about fifty years old are often out of date, readers should pick the best commentary for each book rather than buying whole sets, and authors who range far outside their expertise may produce weak work.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Did Kenneth Kitchen have any commentaries?
short_answer: No, Kitchen did not write commentaries, and James Hoffmeier also declined to write them.
expanded_answer: Kenneth Kitchen never wrote commentaries, and neither did James Hoffmeier, though publishers had asked Hoffmeier. Kitchen's work style and research-university context made commentaries a poor fit, while Hoffmeier's seminary teaching and Egyptology background would have made an Exodus commentary valuable. He regards Hoffmeier's refusal as a lost opportunity and Kitchen's as more understandable.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Is Tanis in Numbers 13:22 a retrojection?
short_answer: In this reading, the Tanis or Zoan reference is a scribal gloss rather than a retrojection.
expanded_answer: Tanis is Zoan in the passage. A retrojection uses later vocabulary for an earlier setting, whereas he reads the clause about Hebron being built seven years before Zoan as a later explanatory addition. He considers the detail historically wrong because Hebron is much earlier, which illustrates the risk of treating a scribal gloss as original text.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: What are his thoughts on the Alex O'Connor and Dinesh D'Souza debate, and how would he answer the debated question?
short_answer: The question was too broad to debate meaningfully, and D'Souza was a poor match because he is not a biblical scholar; he would not answer it in that form.
expanded_answer: "Is the Bible true?" is too broad to discuss meaningfully, much less settle. Alex O'Connor was prepared; in his judgment, Dinesh D'Souza was a political commentator without relevant biblical education who gave evasive and poorly informed answers. He concludes that the debate did more harm than good and would not answer its question in that form.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Why was Dinesh D'Souza asked to participate in the debate?
short_answer: Because he is famous and marketable, not because he has relevant biblical expertise.
expanded_answer: The choice is attributed to celebrity value: D'Souza is a recognizable political pundit whose name can attract an audience. That marketability did not make him qualified for a debate requiring biblical scholarship, which contributed to the mismatch with a better-prepared opponent.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: When is he going to debate Andrew Tate?
short_answer: He joked that Tate would first have to accept a cage match, then said he would not hold a serious debate with someone who lacks relevant expertise.
expanded_answer: The cage-match answer is a joke. He then links Tate to the D'Souza mismatch and says he would not debate either man because neither has the required subject knowledge. No substantive debate topic with Tate is proposed.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: Would he collaborate with Jimmy Akin?
short_answer: Yes. He likes Akin and would collaborate with him, while not endorsing every apologetics tactic Akin uses.
expanded_answer: Akin has used David's material on seraphim and credited him. In David's view, Akin's _Mysterious World_ material is some of the strongest content on the internet. He regards Akin as a brother in Christ and would collaborate without hesitation, although he does not endorse every apologetics tactic Akin uses.

episode_title: Have Nothing to Do with Those Spirally Galaxies
question: How far back does the veneration of saints go, and does it originate in Jewish tradition?
