question: Since God split Israel, were the northern tribes still expected to go to Jerusalem?
short_answer: Yes. Jerusalem remained the prescribed place for Yahweh worship.
expanded_answer: The split did not change the prescribed place of worship. The northern tribes were still expected to go to Jerusalem, because worshiping God had to be done God's way even when political judgment divided the kingdom.

question: Does God allow recently deceased loved ones to visit one last time?
short_answer: In his view, it is possible but rare, and not for the reprobate.
expanded_answer: Hebrews says people die once and then face judgment, so he answered cautiously. In his view, God could permit a temporary visit for someone not facing condemnation, but such a visit would be rare and would not apply to an unbeliever facing judgment.

question: Does a Christian need to instantly forgive people who wrong them and waive all consequences?
short_answer: No. Christians must forgive, but repentance, timing, and consequences all matter.
expanded_answer: Christians do need to forgive, but not necessarily instantly, especially in severe or ongoing harm. If there is no repentance, there is no basis for forgiveness in the full relational sense, and forgiveness does not erase consequences. Anger can also function as protection in an active harmful situation.

question: Was the New Kingdom Egyptian calendar the same as the modern calendar?
short_answer: Not quite. It had 365 days but did not yet account for the quarter day.
expanded_answer: The New Kingdom calendar had 365 days and drifted through the solar cycle because it did not account for the additional quarter day. That correction came later, around the early Ptolemaic period, and the difference accumulates significantly over time.

question: Could the tribes in 1 Kings 12:16 simply "peace out" from Rehoboam like that?
short_answer: Yes. The monarchy depended on clan assent, manpower, taxation, and labor.
expanded_answer: Israel was a clan or tribal society, so the king ruled with the assent and support of the clans. If the clans withdrew their fighting men, taxes, and corvee labor, the king effectively lost the kingdom. Solomon tried unsuccessfully to weaken that tribal structure, leaving the monarchy vulnerable to such a withdrawal.

question: Doesn't Shechem predate Jeroboam in 1 Kings 12:25?
short_answer: Yes. The text means Jeroboam built Shechem up, not that he founded it from nothing.
expanded_answer: Hebrew does not express "build up" in the same way English does, so "built Shechem" can mean adding to or fortifying an existing city. In this reading, Jeroboam added to Shechem with structures such as walls or a palace, and no ancient reader would have taken him as the city's original founder.

question: Why does 1 Kings 12:28 say "gods" when Jeroboam made two golden calves?
short_answer: The calves were part of an aberrant Yahweh temple program that replaced cherubim with bull imagery.
expanded_answer: Jeroboam was not initially setting up full idolatry but a competing, illegitimate Yahweh shrine. The two calves functioned like paired sacred-space imagery, substituting for cherubim, while the Judahite writer linked them with the golden calf tradition to show the northern kingdom's path toward idolatry.

question: Why did the demons in Matthew 8 beg Jesus to send them into pigs?
short_answer: They wanted to avoid the abyss, and the pigs' destruction also ended an impure local industry.
expanded_answer: The demons wanted another body rather than being sent to the abyss. Jesus permitted it because Jewish pig-herding for Roman customers produced ritually impure money, so the episode both freed the man and destroyed a compromised cottage industry.

question: Who are your favorite and least favorite people in the Bible apart from Jesus?
short_answer: His favorite was Moses; his least favorites included Ananias, Sapphira, Simon Magus, and Judas.
expanded_answer: His favorite was Moses because he is an Exodus scholar. For least favorite, he named figures such as Ananias and Sapphira, Simon Magus, and Judas Iscariot, with particular frustration at what he called the stupid greed of Ananias and Sapphira.

question: Is Judas in hell?
short_answer: Yes. Judas is the son of perdition and is in hell.
expanded_answer: Judas is in hell because he is the son of perdition. The transcript gives no further explanation.

question: Have you seen Ear to Hear's biblical archaeology video, and are its Egyptian claims suspicious?
short_answer: He had not seen it, but many apologists and Old Testament scholars make weak claims about Egypt.
expanded_answer: He had not watched the video, but was not surprised by questionable claims because Egyptology is a difficult primary-source discipline. Real competence requires extensive language, history, iconography, and artifact study, and even good Bible scholars often mishandle Egyptian material when they do not vet it with Egyptologists.

question: How should the very long ages in the Old Testament be understood?
short_answer: Many of them may reflect clan ages or collective lineage duration rather than only individual lifespans in the modern sense.
expanded_answer: In this interpretation, the progenitor receives credit for the lifespan of the clan. Clans are born, live, reproduce, and die, so some figures who live for hundreds of years represent the duration of a group under one ancestral name rather than only an individual's biological age. The pattern also appears beyond Genesis, including in Exodus 6.

question: Is there a paper or book on the clan-age interpretation?
short_answer: He planned to write on it, and named Clinton Bailey plus an older Friedrich Gardiner article as helpful.
expanded_answer: He hoped to write a paper on the topic for an ETS journal. He said Clinton Bailey's work on clan identity shaped his view and also named an older Friedrich Gardiner article from the 1880s that touched on the subject.

question: Does subtracting Isaac's age from Abraham's age give Isaac's actual age?
short_answer: It appears close, though the clan-age calculation is more complicated than a simple subtraction.
expanded_answer: He said the relationship appears to work roughly that way but cautioned that the clan-age interpretation is not quite so simple. He planned to explain the details in a future paper.

question: Why should someone believe the Hebraic founding story if their own people have a different founding myth?
short_answer: Another culture's origin story does not discredit Israel's; each tradition must be evaluated, and this objection is more cultural than logical.
expanded_answer: Another civilization's origin story does not automatically discredit Israel's because the traditions are not necessarily mutually exclusive; each must be judged for veracity. He contrasted remote, self-glorifying, or highly supernatural national stories with Israel's comparatively sober slavery-and-deliverance account, whose human events remain intelligible even apart from the divine claim. He characterized the objection as a cultural and emotional apologetic rather than a logical argument. Effective engagement therefore requires presenting the Christian account in terms that address the listener's cultural assumptions instead of relying only on abstract logic.

question: Is all of the Old Testament intended as a human history book?
short_answer: No. Parts of it are doing other kinds of literary and theological work rather than functioning as straightforward human historiography.
expanded_answer: The Old Testament is not all intended as a human history book, though that does not mean it contains no history. It is a book on religion with much historical material, but parts of it, especially the beginning of Genesis, are better described as mytho-history. That means a combination of history and mythology used to reach religious understanding, not simple event-by-event historiography.

question: After finishing James P. Allen's Middle Egyptian book, what should someone study next?
short_answer: He recommended remedial work with Collier and Manley, then Gardiner as a reference grammar, with Hoch as a possible bridge.
expanded_answer: He criticized Allen's pedagogy, especially its early emphasis on adjectival sentences. He recommended working through Collier and Manley to get back on track, then using Gardiner's Egyptian grammar as a reference. James Hoch's book could serve as an intermediate resource for material missing from Gardiner.

question: Is the Egyptian adjectival sentence the same thing as the stative in other languages?
short_answer: No. The stative is its own thing in Egyptian, while the adjectival construction is a different, niche clause type.
expanded_answer: Egyptian also has a stative, but the adjectival construction here is a separate circumstantial clause that primarily uses an adjective as a verb. He criticized placing such niche grammar near the beginning of an introductory textbook.

question: What do you want out of *Dune Part Three*?
short_answer: He wanted a redo of Part Two because its compressed timeline and missing developments left Part Three with a difficult setup.
expanded_answer: He thought Part Two compressed the first book's multi-year story into only a few months and removed or weakened crucial elements such as the time skip and Alia's role. In his view, that setup made it difficult for Part Three to reach the `Dune Messiah` material properly because major character and plot developments had not been allowed to mature.

question: What are your thoughts on North American cryptids and supernatural creatures?
short_answer: They are a guilty pleasure, but he does not believe in them.
expanded_answer: He enjoys documentaries about North American cryptids as entertainment and calls them junk food, but he does not believe in Bigfoot, Mothman, lizard men, or chupacabra. For him, the subject is fun viewing rather than credible supernatural evidence.

question: Why did Pharaoh not simply have Moses, Aaron, or the Israelites killed earlier?
short_answer: Egyptian legal and religious constraints mattered, and unjust execution could threaten Pharaoh's standing with both law and the gods.
expanded_answer: Pharaoh still needed legal cause. Without insurrection or a direct offense against Pharaoh, there was no proper ground for arrest or execution, and Moses was an adopted member of the royal family. Egyptian jurisprudence required an actual offense against Pharaoh, such as attempted assassination or stealing royal property. Killing without warrant would violate Maat and could have consequences in this life, including the gods withdrawing favor, so even powerful kings could be conservative about penalties.

question: Would killing someone unjustly make a person's heart heavier than the feather?
short_answer: Yes. Unjustified killing violated Maat and would weigh against the person in judgment.
expanded_answer: Killing without warrant upset the balance represented by Maat, so it counted negatively in the weighing of the heart. Egyptian kings were often more concerned about consequences in this life, such as the gods withdrawing favor or denying future victories.

question: What happens if your heart is lighter than the feather in Egyptian judgment?
short_answer: That was also a failure, because it meant the person did not do anything in life.
expanded_answer: In this account, the weighing of the heart required balance rather than simple sinlessness. A heart lighter than the feather meant the person had done nothing in life, so the judgment was still negative.

question: Did ancient Egypt have lawyers?
short_answer: No. Parties represented their own cases before magistrates.
expanded_answer: No. In Egyptian legal procedures, people represented their own cases. Egypt had magistrates, but not lawyers in the sense asked about.

question: Were there spells to mitigate the effects of violating Maat in this life?
short_answer: No. Spells applied to afterlife concerns, not fixing Maat violations in this life.
expanded_answer: There were no spells to mitigate violations of Maat in this life. Egyptian spells addressed afterlife dangers, while in this life the concern was that the gods could withdraw favor or deny future success if a king acted unjustly.

question: What was the role of prophetic communities like the one in 1 Samuel 19?
short_answer: They sought the word of the Lord and also trained or supported future prophets.
expanded_answer: These were prophetic communities, including what could be called schools of prophets or bands of prophets. Their primary role was to seek the word of the Lord and discern God's will for Israel; their secondary role was to raise up new prophets. Some members became prophets through aptitude or anointing, while others supported the prophetic work through ordinary community tasks.

question: What is the context of the Tower of Babel, and was the language confusion only regional?
short_answer: The event was tied to human refusal to spread out after the flood and likely involved a temporary, region-specific dispersal effect.
expanded_answer: Humanity had been commanded after the flood to spread out over the earth, but the Babel project concentrated people around a city and religious structure so they could make a name for themselves and secure their own future. The confusion of languages scattered them. In this reading, its effect was regional and temporary because the development of languages does not point to every language originating in one place.

question: Where would you rank Imhotep among the great inventors or creators of history?
short_answer: Very high, especially because of Imhotep's architectural, artistic, medical, and intellectual significance.
expanded_answer: He ranked Imhotep very highly because Djoser's funerary complex at Saqqara was both a technical and artistic achievement that later Old Kingdom kings repeatedly imitated. The complex includes distinctive columns, tile galleries, and a vast burial chamber, and its pyramid was the tallest building humanity had yet made, a record that lasted about 300 years. He also credited Imhotep with medical, literary, and priestly wisdom.

question: Why was Eleazar of Damascus Abraham's heir instead of Lot?
short_answer: Lot had already parted ways and had no practical inheritance claim, so the steward Eleazar was the natural heir before Isaac.
expanded_answer: Lot was not the better heir because he and Abraham had already parted ways after serious tension between their households and servants over grazing lands. Once Lot moved away, the relationship was effectively severed, and Lot was also a distant relative with no practical claim on Abraham's estate. Since Abraham had no child at that point, Eleazar of Damascus, as the steward of Abraham's house, would naturally stand next in the inheritance order.

question: Why do some people consider Christianity an interest rather than a belief system?
short_answer: He did not understand the question clearly and asked for it to be restated later.
expanded_answer: He answered only in a limited way because he found the wording confusing. Christianity is definitely a belief system, and the transcript gives no clear sense in which it could merely be treated as an interest. He asked the questioner to restate the question the next week.

question: Can Falk use Morse code with his amateur radio license?
short_answer: Yes. Canadian amateur operators may use international Morse code without a separate Morse certificate, though he is just learning it.
expanded_answer: The separate Morse certificate mainly matters for becoming an instructor. His license already allows Morse operation, and a later chat clarification specifies that he means the international Morse code standard.

question: Does someone need a license to transmit with a small Baofeng radio in the United States?
short_answer: Yes. Transmitting with even a small Baofeng requires a license, while buying one and listening without transmitting are allowed.
expanded_answer: A small Baofeng is treated as a ham radio for transmission purposes. Owning one and listening are allowed without the license, but transmitting with it in the United States requires one under the FCC rules described in the transcript.

question: Can a wind setdown keep a body of water split apart for several hours?
short_answer: Yes. Wind setdown events can last for several hours, with reports of much longer durations.
expanded_answer: Several hours is not a problem for a wind setdown. Documented cases have reportedly lasted far longer, including one described as four days, and sustained wind gives the water the momentum needed to remain held apart.

question: Is 2D theatrical animation dead?
short_answer: Yes. Traditional theatrical 2D animation has largely been replaced by computer-assisted 2D and 3D methods.
expanded_answer: Traditional theatrical 2D animation is treated as effectively dead because surviving 2D work has long been computer-assisted, while major studios moved toward 3D and cheaper production methods. The traditional skill is difficult and expensive, so it now survives mostly among art students rather than large theatrical productions.

question: Is there anything a student can do to make a professor accept traditional Gospel authorship?
short_answer: Not much. A student usually cannot force an entrenched professor to accept traditional Gospel authorship.
expanded_answer: Academic positions can become locked in even when a professor is challenged with contrary data. The practical expectation is that a resistant professor may simply stop discussing the issue rather than reconsider it, so one student's argument is unlikely to make the professor accept the traditional authorship position.

question: What languages has Producer Falk studied?
short_answer: Her listed languages were English, French, some German, some Egyptian, American Sign Language, and formerly proficient Spanish.
expanded_answer: The language inventory starts with English, then French, some German, some Egyptian, American Sign Language, and Spanish, where she says she used to be proficient. The list records languages she has done rather than current active study.

question: Why has Producer Falk not studied Latin?
short_answer: Trinity listed Latin, but they could not take a taught Latin class because no instructor was available.
expanded_answer: Latin appeared in Trinity's catalog, but for years they could not actually get into a graduate-level Latin class because the school never had an instructor. The example is used to show that graduate catalogs may list courses that are not really offered in practice.

question: Should a writer limit how much pain a character must endure?
short_answer: No, unless the suffering stops serving the story. Character pressure, fear, agony, and hard decisions can strengthen the narrative.
expanded_answer: Fictional characters can be put through severe pain and misery because conflict and pressure drive story development. The limit is narrative purpose: if the suffering does not move the story forward, it becomes gratuitous rather than useful.

question: Is the Holy Spirit at work when Christians write?
short_answer: Sometimes. It depends on the writing and purpose, and it is usually recognized from the later results.
expanded_answer: Whether the Spirit is at work depends on the kind and purpose of the writing. The Spirit may give insight or direct the writing, but the writer normally cannot know this in the moment; only the later results may reveal it.

question: Are handwritten letters obsolete?
short_answer: They are uncommon but not obsolete; Falk personally types letters when clarity matters.
expanded_answer: Handwritten correspondence is now rare, and he usually types because his handwriting is difficult to read. His mother still writes letters by hand, and Producer Falk once did so when Kenneth Kitchen required it. He nevertheless calls handwritten letters a skill worth learning, especially because nondigital communication can regain value when technology fails.

question: Is handwriting, including cursive, obsolete?
short_answer: No. Cursive supports speed, second-script literacy, access to older texts, and resilience when technology fails.
expanded_answer: Cursive is faster and gives readers practice with a second script, like the parallel scripts found in many languages. It preserves access to handwritten historical sources and still appears in current uses such as signs and some examinations. Removing it from education therefore loses useful literacy, while handwriting remains a nondigital fallback when communication systems fail.

question: Does Hebrew have more than one script?
short_answer: Yes. Hebrew has the modern square script, older Paleo-Hebrew, and cursive forms.
expanded_answer: Modern Hebrew is based on the Aramaic-derived square script, while older Paleo-Hebrew was an earlier alphabetic script. Hebrew also has cursive forms, used more in schools, informal correspondence, and some Israeli contexts than in formal signage.

question: Do early celebrations happen too often in Christian spaces, such as with recruitment numbers or new research?
short_answer: The question was unclear, but if it meant announcing research too early, then yes.
expanded_answer: The wording is unclear, but on the proposed reading, promising research can be announced too soon. The Mount Ebal curse amulet is the example of a claim presented as strong evidence that later, in his view, turned out to be nothing.

question: Does the Bible explain why the universe is so vast, and how does Falk frame the philosophical issue?
short_answer: No. The Bible recognizes cosmic vastness but does not explain why the universe is so vast, and even modern people struggle to grasp the scale.
expanded_answer: The Bible can speak of the heavens as stretched out, but it does not explain the reason for the universe's enormous size. The philosophical point is that if modern people struggle to comprehend cosmic scale, Bronze and Iron Age readers should not be expected to provide a detailed explanation of it.

question: Where should one draw the line between fringe archaeology claims and legitimate criticism of academic consensus?
short_answer: The line is evidence: fringe claims lack a sound basis, while legitimate majority or minority positions can challenge consensus with evidence.
expanded_answer: The question falsely narrows the field to fringe versus consensus, because many academic issues are really majority and minority positions rather than settled consensus. The dividing line is evidential: fringe claims usually lack training and sound evidence, while legitimate criticism can challenge either a majority view or a consensus when new evidence requires it.

question: What is happening in 1 Kings 13:4-5?
short_answer: Jeroboam is acting as priest, is rebuked through the prophet, and receives a sign when his hand withers and the altar breaks.
expanded_answer: Jeroboam, as king of northern Israel, is improperly taking on priestly duties by burning incense at the altar. When he orders the prophet seized, his hand withers and the altar breaks, which is read as God's rebuke and confirming sign against Jeroboam's act.

question: Why did the old prophet lie to the man of God in 1 Kings 13:18?
short_answer: The text does not give a motive, but the old prophet may have wanted the company of another true prophet; the episode warns against trusting a prophet merely because he claims authority.
expanded_answer: The text does not state the motive, but the suggested reason is that the old prophet wanted another true prophet's company, hospitality, and conversation. The larger warning is that real prophets are still men who can lie and sin, so God's word must outrank a prophet's claim of authority.

question: In 1 Kings 14:21, was Naamah the first wife of Solomon to bear a son?
short_answer: It appears likely under the forty-one-year reading. Rehoboam was probably one of Solomon's earliest sons, and Naamah may have been an early treaty wife from Ammon.
expanded_answer: Rehoboam's stated age of forty-one places his birth at the beginning of Solomon's reign, before the temple was built, so Naamah appears to have borne one of Solomon's earliest sons. Because she is called an Ammonitess, Falk suggests she may have been an early treaty wife and evidence of an early peace with Ammon. Later chat raised Septuagint variants that make Rehoboam younger, but he favored the forty-one-year reading while acknowledging that the textual question deserved more checking.

question: In 1 Kings 14:25, do we have the Egyptian side of Shishak's campaign?
short_answer: Yes in broad terms. Shishak's campaign is recorded in Egyptian sources, though not as a biblical-style account of Jerusalem's plunder.
expanded_answer: The campaign is recorded at the Bubastite Portal at Karnak. Falk reads the Egyptian route as bypassing Jerusalem and combines that with the biblical statement that Shishak took Jerusalem's treasures to infer that Jerusalem paid him off rather than being conquered. The Egyptian record therefore corroborates the broader campaign, not a biblical-style account of Jerusalem's plunder.

question: When dynasties changed in Egypt, how much would the average person have noticed?
short_answer: Usually very little. Ordinary farmers and craftsmen would normally notice only practical changes such as regnal-year dating unless warfare accompanied the transition.
expanded_answer: The average Egyptian farmer or craftsman usually would not notice a dynastic change unless war or disruption accompanied it. The practical change was scribal and administrative, especially regnal-year dating, and many early dynasty boundaries were later scholarly retrojections rather than categories ordinary people recognized.

question: Do females self-identify as Christians more than males, historically and today?
short_answer: It varies by culture: more women identified as Christians in some earlier periods, while his contemporary assessment was that the pattern has reversed in some contexts.
expanded_answer: The pattern is treated as culturally variable. Women identified as Christians more often in the first century and perhaps somewhat more in some medieval and Renaissance contexts; in his contemporary assessment, trends in some places have reversed under cultural pressures such as feminism and abortion politics.

question: Is there still a future for programmers and IT workers after the rise of AI?
short_answer: Yes. Technical work will remain necessary even if AI changes the field and weakens parts of the job market.
expanded_answer: AI may assist programming and change the job market, but it does not understand problems or know when code is appropriate. Some AI companies may fail and others survive, while technical workers will still be needed to adapt the technology, integrate mismatched systems, maintain infrastructure, and do practical work that management has long wished could be automated away.

question: Could the same AI recognition algorithm run on an Apple I replica?
short_answer: Only with enough memory; once the viewer said the replica had 1 KB, Falk could not say it would run.
expanded_answer: The PDP-11 example had 4 MB of memory, unusually large for that machine. Falk initially reasoned that the simple recognition algorithm could run on many old computers, but he withdrew confidence for a 1 KB Apple I replica. His broader point was that such algorithms can run on modest hardware only when it has sufficient resources.

question: Would there be a free King Tut coffin image on Wikipedia Commons instead of using AI?
short_answer: Not really. The public-domain images available there are Burton's black-and-white photos, not a finished modern color asset.
expanded_answer: The AI asset is described as based on public-domain Burton photographs. Those black-and-white images still had to be upscaled, colorized, and then manipulated in Photoshop, so Wikipedia Commons did not supply the finished color image needed for the project.

question: In 1 Kings 15:2 and 15:10, do Maacah, Abijam, and Asa imply the same mother and sibling relationship?
short_answer: Probably. The Masoretic reading is preferred, with Abijam and Asa likely treated as brothers with the same mother, though further textual work would be needed.
expanded_answer: The two verses name Maacah daughter of Abishalom in connection with both Abijam and Asa. The short reign and succession pattern make it likely that Abijam and Asa were brothers, while Septuagint variants and the lack of checked Dead Sea Scroll evidence keep the conclusion cautious.

question: Does 1 Kings 16:34 imply Joshua was still in common memory?
short_answer: Yes. Hiel's rebuilding of Jericho connects with Joshua's curse, and the event would have reminded people of Joshua's pronouncement.
expanded_answer: Hiel's rebuilding of Jericho directly invokes Joshua's curse after the city was placed under the ban. The deaths of Hiel's sons are connected with that curse, and Iron Age rebuilding or leveling at Jericho fits the kind of activity the text is describing.

question: What is the purpose of the wind, earthquake, fire, and gentle blowing in 1 Kings 19:11-13?
short_answer: In this reading, the passage rejects identifying God with dramatic natural forces and emphasizes God's presence in the still small voice.
expanded_answer: In this reading, the sequence denies that God should be identified with dramatic natural forces such as wind, earthquake, fire, lightning, or storm. The still small voice presents God as the one who meets Elijah in the quiet within and after them.

question: What does "God in the gaps" mean in the 1 Kings 19 discussion?
short_answer: It is the idea that people place God in gaps in human knowledge, but the passage is read as denying that and showing God meeting people in crisis.
expanded_answer: "God of the gaps" means assigning God to whatever humans do not yet understand. Falk reads 1 Kings 19 as rejecting identification of God with wind, earthquake, fire, or other natural forces while affirming that God meets people in personal gaps such as grief, crisis, and perceived absence. A gap in scientific knowledge does not itself prove direct divine action: learning a natural mechanism would not exclude ultimate divine responsibility, but ignorance alone is not evidence that God actively caused the event.

question: Would God like to speed up the end of the world?
short_answer: God does not desire any to be lost and will take as long as needed until the fullness of the Gentiles is complete.
expanded_answer: God is patient and will take as long as needed for those who are his to come home. This is connected with the fullness of the Gentiles: God is not concerned with speed in the way demons are, because demons want to delay that completion as long as possible.

question: Would Falk recommend a master's degree in informatics?
short_answer: Not usually. Informatics may fit specialized work like genetic sequencing, but a computer science master's is generally more versatile.
expanded_answer: Informatics is not usually recommended unless the person is aiming at a niche where it is specifically useful, such as genetic sequencing. For most technical careers, a broader computer science master's is preferred because it keeps more options open.

question: How do demons kick the can down the road?
short_answer: They subvert the gospel through false prophecies, new religious movements, secular ideologies, persecutions, and other roadblocks.
expanded_answer: Demonic delay is framed as any effort to keep people from the gospel and stretch history out before the fullness of the Gentiles is complete. Examples include false prophecy, new religious movements, secular ideologies, persecution, false messiahs, and other barriers that slow people from coming to Christ.

question: Did other ancient Near Eastern cultures think of their god as father over the nation?
short_answer: Yes, in a broad or casual sense. Other cultures had father-god language, including figures such as Amun-Ra, though not always in the same sense.
expanded_answer: Father-god language did exist in other cultures, though not necessarily as a creator-father relationship in the biblical sense. The examples range beyond the ancient Near East to comparative father-god language such as Odin and Zeus, with Amun-Ra described as father and king of the gods.

question: Does 1 Thessalonians 4:16 imply there is more than one archangel?
short_answer: No. The wording is singular and does not provide a basis for multiple archangels, though other texts would have to be considered separately.
expanded_answer: The relevant wording is singular, in a genitive construction treated as qualitative and definite in sense. It may imply a particular archangel, but this verse is not a good basis for arguing that there are multiple archangels.

question: Was Akhenaten monotheistic, henotheistic, or something else?
short_answer: Neither monotheist nor henotheist, but closer to a monolatrous pantheist based on Aten theology.
expanded_answer: Akhenaten was not a monotheist or a henotheist because Aten theology identifies everything with Aten: the sun, gods, people, objects, past, and future. It is monolatrous because only Aten is worshiped, but pantheistic because everything is treated as an expression of Aten.

question: Does Philippians imply Paul can hear what is happening with believers on earth after his death?
short_answer: No. Paul is talking about hearing reports through letters and the Roman postal system, not postmortem awareness.
expanded_answer: Paul is not describing awareness after death, but ordinary correspondence while absent. Roman roads and post are treated as efficient systems for circulating letters and reports, so Paul's expectation of hearing news from churches does not require postmortem perception.

question: How much Roman fan mail was thrown out unread?
short_answer: Some likely was, especially among popular figures such as gladiators who received large amounts of fan mail.
expanded_answer: Some incidents involved mail being discarded without being read, and gladiators are used as an example of celebrities who could receive large amounts of fan mail. The conclusion remains cautious: some of it probably was thrown out, but the transcript does not quantify how much.

question: How hard was the amateur radio exam compared to Egyptology?
short_answer: It was a different kind of hard, focused more on technology, math, components, and regulatory details.
expanded_answer: The exam was legitimately difficult but not the same kind of difficulty as Egyptology. It required technology knowledge, formulas, components, use cases such as dummy loads, and regulatory details, while the advanced exam leaned more on math and extra operating privileges.

question: What is the best way to answer a skeptic who says there is no evidence for biblical events like the Exodus or resurrection?
short_answer: Separate the claims. Falk treats resurrection support here as eyewitness testimony or anecdotal material, while the Exodus has extensive internal evidence; he would not spend time arguing with a skeptic whose mind is fixed.
expanded_answer: A blanket claim that the Bible has no evidence is too broad, but the resurrection and Exodus require different arguments. In this answer, resurrection support is chiefly testimony about a one-time event centered on Jesus, which he treats as anecdotal rather than evidential; the Exodus has extensive internal and historical support, including material even skeptical treatments acknowledge. His practical advice is not to spend time on someone committed to rejecting every evidential category, but to present the evidence to people who have not heard it.

question: What is the original interpretation of Genesis 3:16 in the ESV and NIV?
short_answer: The question is too vague to answer clearly, and the ESV and NIV are saying roughly the same thing at that point.
expanded_answer: The ESV and NIV renderings are read as broadly saying the same thing about pain in childbirth, desire for the husband, and the husband's rule. Hebrew nuances exist, but the question is too vague to answer without a more specific interpretive issue.

question: What training did the people behind the giant-pillars-under-the-pyramids claim have?
short_answer: Their relevant training was poor for the claim and is characterized as metaphysical or New Age rather than proper ground-penetrating-radar expertise.
expanded_answer: The technical basis of the claim is rejected, especially the idea of doing ground-penetrating radar from a plane or drone in that way. The people involved are not treated as specialists in that work, and their training is characterized as metaphysical or New Age rather than relevant archaeological or geophysical expertise.

question: When did Falk feel closest to being Indiana Jones in his career?
short_answer: The closest example was walking through the Valley of the Monkey to inspect the tomb of Ahmose-Nefertari, though it was dangerous and not something he would repeat.
expanded_answer: The closest experience was walking through the Valley of the Monkey to site-check the tomb of Ahmose-Nefertari, away from standard tourist paths. The danger came from heat, animals, rough terrain, illness, and no cell reception, so although the trip was worthwhile, he would not do it again.

question: In 1 Kings 19:15-18, was the command to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha a punishment?
short_answer: Yes. The sequence sounds like punishment because they are appointed to carry out judgment.
expanded_answer: The passage is read as a judgment sequence: Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha are appointed so that those who escape one sword meet another. Because the appointments are tied to death and cleanup after Israel's rebellion, it sounds like punishment.

question: What did Falk find in the Valley of the Monkey?
short_answer: The finds included Howard Carter's pottery sorting field, many potsherds, a flint blade, and a puzzling bright blue human femur fragment.
expanded_answer: The finds included Howard Carter's pottery sorting field with many potsherds still on the surface, plus a flint blade. A bright blue human femur ball joint from the fill of the tomb of Ahmose-Nefertari, likely from later burials, remained unexplained even after an osteologist saw the photograph.

question: In 1 Kings 22:10, did kings bring their thrones with them when traveling?
short_answer: Yes. Kings could use portable thrones or palanquin-like seats, distinct from heavier thrones of state.
expanded_answer: Kings had portable thrones, often palanquin-like kiosks carried on poles, which could be set down for audience or judgment. These differed from heavier thrones of state, which conveyed the authority of the state and were not meant to be moved around casually.

question: In 1 Kings 22:38, is the note about harlots bathing a lexical gloss?
short_answer: It looks like a scribal gloss rather than a lexical gloss because it adds an explanatory historical detail, not a term definition.
expanded_answer: The bathing note looks like an added scribal gloss because it is out of place and adds a historical explanation. A lexical gloss would explain a term, but this note adds narrative detail about the pool of Samaria, so it is treated as scribal rather than lexical.

question: Is Shinar really a good match for Sumer?
short_answer: Falk doubts it. The consonants and geography do not match well, though the issue remains debated and outside his specialty.
expanded_answer: Shinar and Sumer look closer in English than in the underlying consonants, especially because the N and M do not match well. The geography of Shinar seems more like Akkad, Babylon, and middle Mesopotamia than Sumer, while the answer acknowledges that the issue is debated and outside Falk's specialty.

question: What does Falk think of Martin Isles from IAG?
short_answer: He does not know because he has never heard of him.
expanded_answer: The transcript supports only that limited answer, not an assessment of Isles or IAG. Falk gives no evaluation because he has not heard of Martin Isles.

question: How does Falk view the sign of the cross as church tradition?
short_answer: He has no problem with it as a sign of respect, says it is not required, and says people may do it if it helps them feel closer to Christ.
expanded_answer: Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans, and Lutherans may use the gesture, and he has no objection to it as an act of respect. He does not make it mandatory, but says people may do it if it helps them feel closer to Christ.

question: Is the six-cubit height for Goliath in 1 Samuel 17:4 a scribal error?
short_answer: The evidence currently leans toward four cubits and a span, as in the Septuagint and Dead Sea Scrolls, rather than the Masoretic six cubits.
expanded_answer: The evidence currently leans toward four cubits and a span rather than six cubits and a span. The contrast is roughly six-foot-four versus nine-foot-four, and the Septuagint and Dead Sea Scrolls are given more weight here than the Masoretic reading.

question: How does Falk assess Matthean priority versus Markan priority?
short_answer: He leans toward Markan priority, while noting he does not have a strong stake in the debate.
expanded_answer: The debate concerns which Gospel served as the template for the others. Most scholars currently favor Markan priority, and Falk tends that direction too, but he does not have a strong stake in the issue.

question: Why is `fatness` translated as `anointing`?
short_answer: The link is oil: anointing uses oil, and oil is understood as a kind of fat.
expanded_answer: The connection is through anointing oil, especially olive oil. Because oil behaves like a fat and can solidify into a greasy substance when cold, fatness, olive oil, and anointing are linked etymologically.

question: Could Aten theology have been influenced by Brahman in Hinduism?
short_answer: Falk thinks that is unlikely because the evidence for Egypt-India contact is too thin and late to support a clear line of influence.
expanded_answer: The earliest Egypt-India interaction evidence is placed roughly around Tutankhamun's time, but Hindu inscriptions in Egypt are much later, in the Roman period. Atenism is instead treated as developing within Egyptian religious transformations, including ideas of manifestation, rather than from Hindu influence.

question: Does Jesus receiving sour wine in John 19:28-30 mean he completed the Passover cup?
short_answer: No. The hyssop and sour wine are read as evoking the Passover blood on the lintels rather than the fourth Passover cup.
expanded_answer: The crucial symbol is not simply wine, but wine on hyssop. In this reading, the hyssop points to Passover blood applied to the lintels, so Jesus is shown as the Passover sacrifice whose work is finished, not as completing the fourth Passover cup.

question: Would Falk recommend a master's degree in data science, AI, or cybersecurity?
short_answer: Cybersecurity is best learned on the job, and he would lean more toward a general computer science master's than a narrow specialization.
expanded_answer: Cybersecurity programs are described as often poor, and cybersecurity is usually better learned through work. Between narrower specializations and a broader path, Falk would generally choose a computer science master's unless there is a specific reason for data science or AI.

question: Could `Kasdim` be an ancient reference to the Kassites rather than later Chaldea?
short_answer: `Kasdim` is connected with Chaldea and Kassites, but the archaeological appearance of the Chaldeans is relatively late.
expanded_answer: Chaldea is described as a translation of `Kasdim`, while Kassites and Chaldeans are connected but distinguished in the record. Kassites are earlier, around the mid to late second millennium, while Chaldeans appear later, especially in northern Mesopotamian contexts around 1100 BC.

question: Are the Stations of the Cross legitimate locations?
short_answer: No. They are artistic depictions, and their claimed locations reflect the onomastica problem of later pilgrimage traditions.
expanded_answer: The stations are artistic depictions, but their claimed locations are not historically reliable. This is connected with the onomastica problem, where later pilgrimage traditions and holy-site lists conveniently locate events near roads or tourist routes, often without archaeological support.

question: Who does Falk think the woman in the Song of Solomon is, if not the Queen of Sheba?
short_answer: He does not know and does not want to speculate, but he rejects the Queen of Sheba identification because she would have been another man's wife.
expanded_answer: The transcript does not provide enough basis for Falk to identify the woman, and he does not want to speculate. He specifically rejects the Queen of Sheba because, in his view, she was the wife of the king of Saba, making that identification morally and politically implausible.

question: Should the Didache have been part of the biblical canon?
short_answer: No. It lacks apostolic authority, has no known author, dates too late, and is better understood as an early church operations manual.
expanded_answer: The Didache fails the tests of canonicity because it lacks apostolic authority, has no known author, and is too late for apostolic authorship. It is still useful as an early church operations manual for practical church situations, but not Scripture.

question: Was the Didache written around AD 60?
short_answer: No. Falk places it roughly in AD 90-140, probably around AD 120.
expanded_answer: AD 60 is too early in his view because the Didache presumes organized churches and itinerant preachers and fits stylistically with writers such as Ignatius, Polycarp, and Papias. At AD 60, the Jerusalem temple still stood, apostles remained active there, and the Christian diaspora presumed by the document had not yet developed.

question: Was the Titus Kennedy lambasting recorded?
short_answer: No. It was not recorded, though he discusses it in a separate "spilling of the tea" episode.
expanded_answer: The event itself was not recorded, though he discussed it in a separate "spilling of the tea" episode. The criticism summarized in this transcript concerned a misuse of Thutmose III prisoner counts, but the answer to the recording question is simply no.

question: How do we know the Didache was written in the second century AD?
short_answer: Its style, assumptions about organized churches and traveling preachers, and comparison with early Christian writers place it around the late first to early second century, likely near 120 AD.
expanded_answer: The Didache fits stylistically near writers such as Ignatius, Polycarp, and Papias, and it presumes organized churches and traveling preachers. A 60 AD date is rejected because the Jerusalem temple still stood, the apostles were still active, and the Christian diaspora was not yet developed enough; the suggested range is roughly 90-140 AD, with about 120 as a likely center.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Is Ruth 1:1 describing a common famine or a Late Bronze Age climate-change famine?
short_answer: It was probably a common cyclical famine, though its date could place it near the tail end of collapse-era climate stress.
expanded_answer: In this chronology, Ruth falls around 1100 BC, in the Iron Age period of the judges. That date could overlap the tail end of the wider collapse-era climate disruption, but the famine's movement through Canaan and Moab better resembles the region's recurring rain-driven famines.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: If Aram Naharaim in Judges 3 is clearly Mitanni, how do late Exodus proponents justify placing the context after Mitanni fell?
short_answer: The objection conflates Naharaim with Aram Naharaim; in this reading, Aram Naharaim refers to a post-Mitanni Aramean state.
expanded_answer: Naharaim and Aram Naharaim refer to different political settings in this reading. The Aram element points to later Aramean states after Mitanni's collapse, so Judges 3 does not force an early Exodus setting.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Could late daters also appeal to redactors even if they do not need to?
short_answer: They could, but late daters do not need that move here because the text can be read without invoking redaction.
expanded_answer: Late daters could invoke redaction criticism, but this passage already fits their chronology through the Aram Naharaim distinction. Appealing to redactors would therefore be unnecessary.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Does the Judges 3 narrative have to be after 1183 BC because of regional control before then?
short_answer: Yes, the post-Mitanni Aramean-state context points to a post-1200 BC setting.
expanded_answer: The political background points after 1183 BC because the relevant post-Mitanni and Aramean successor states do not fit earlier regional control. This supports reading Judges 3 as something other than the Mitanni Empire at its height.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: How could Israel attack Ashtaroth and Og beyond the Yarmouk without encroaching on Ammonite territory in Deuteronomy 2:37?
short_answer: The exception is self-defense: Israel requested peaceful passage, but Sihon crossed the boundary and attacked Israel in the wilderness.
expanded_answer: A show of force at one's own border, as in the comparison with Edom, would not itself justify invasion. Sihon left his territory and attacked Israel in the wilderness, so Israel could enter the land to eliminate an active threat without making a voluntary encroachment.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Do young-earth creationists think the Tower of Babel region was the only inhabited place on earth before Babel?
short_answer: It depends on the kind of young-earth creationist, but many American young-earth views do assume that.
expanded_answer: Young-earth views are not uniform. Continental young-earth creationists may not require Babel to be the only inhabited region, while many American versions tend to compress population geography more tightly around that event.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Are factors of significant numbers, such as factors of 40, also numerologically significant?
short_answer: Not really. Biblical numerology tends to use significant numbers, their multiples, and sometimes defectives, not ordinary factors.
expanded_answer: Ordinary factors of a symbolic number do not automatically become symbolic. Biblical numerology more often uses numbers such as 7, 12, and 40, along with their multiples and defectives, meaning forms one below the full number.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Is Jericho mentioned in the Amarna letters?
short_answer: Sort of. Jericho is not named in the main Amarna archive, but an Amarna-period letter was found at Jericho itself.
expanded_answer: Jericho does not appear as a named place in the main corpus found at Amarna. An Akhenaten-period letter was discovered at Jericho itself, although it is too badly worn to read fully.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What makes the tablet found at Jericho an Amarna letter?
short_answer: It is Akkadian cuneiform diplomatic correspondence from the Amarna period.
expanded_answer: The tablet is an Akkadian cuneiform letter, the medium used for Late Bronze Age diplomatic correspondence. Its date in Akhenaten's reign places it in the Amarna period.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Is the Akkadian in the Amarna letter from Jericho poor?
short_answer: No. The Akkadian is recognizable, but the unfired clay tablet is badly worn.
expanded_answer: The tablet is hard to read because its unfired clay weathered in Jericho's wetter environment. Letters found at dry Amarna survived in better condition.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: If Zadok was high priest under David and Solomon, how could his great-grandson Azariah serve during Solomon's reign?
short_answer: In this reading, the phrase about service in Solomon's temple is a scribal gloss that ended up in the wrong place.
expanded_answer: The line about service in Solomon's temple appears to be an explanatory gloss attached at the wrong point in the genealogy. That displacement creates the chronological difficulty involving Zadok and Azariah.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: How many years off was the scribe in that gloss?
short_answer: The exact error is unknown for Azariah, while the Hebron-Zoan gloss is off by roughly a thousand years.
expanded_answer: The Azariah case cannot be quantified with confidence because the gloss may have been misplaced or otherwise confused. By contrast, the Hebron and Zoan example is a clearer chronological mismatch of about a thousand years.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Could scribal glosses be removed from critical texts?
short_answer: No; they remain part of the received text, but critical editions and translations often mark or segregate them.
expanded_answer: Critical texts preserve these readings as part of the received tradition. Editors and translators may use parentheses or another marker to identify a likely gloss while keeping it in the text.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Are Targums simply Syriac or Aramaic translations of the Bible?
short_answer: No. Targums are extensively glossed, commentarial renderings, although many surviving examples are Syriac or Aramaic.
expanded_answer: Targums expand biblical text with enough explanatory glossing to function as commentaries. Many surviving examples are Syriac or Aramaic, but their language is separate from the commentarial form that makes them Targums.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Didn't the author of the gloss know that Zadok, not Azariah, was contemporary with Solomon?
short_answer: Not necessarily. The gloss may have been confused, misplaced, or corrupted during copying.
expanded_answer: The gloss writer or copyist may not have had the chronology straight, or the note may have been intended for a nearby name and then shifted. A small placement problem in a genealogy can produce the apparent contradiction without requiring the whole passage to be rewritten.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What would have been the most luxurious fruit in the time of Moses?
short_answer: Pomegranates were notable, but dates were the premier sweet luxury fruit of the Ramesside period.
expanded_answer: Pomegranates were one high-status fruit, but dates were the stronger answer. Dates were the candy of the Bronze Age, a sugary luxury that became prominent in Egypt and contributed to tooth decay and new dental treatments.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Could date juice be called honey?
short_answer: No. Date juice was not called honey; Egyptians had actual honey and did not confuse the two.
expanded_answer: Egyptians had both date juice and real honey, and they did not use the same name for the two sweet substances.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Would it be healthy for every city today to have at least ten righteous people?
short_answer: Yes. Any city is better off with more righteous people, though ten would still be a very low number.
expanded_answer: Abraham's exchange over Sodom frames the answer: more righteous people are always beneficial for a city. Ten would still be a very small remnant rather than a healthy target for a modern city.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Have you read Nigro's recent book dating Jericho's LB2B destruction to about 1270 BC under Ramesses II?
short_answer: No. He had not read it, and he did not think the evidence favored that reconstruction.
expanded_answer: He had not yet bought or read the book, so he could not review its detailed argument. He nonetheless considered a Ramesses II destruction of Jericho poorly supported, especially because he found the military logic of such an attack weak.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Should ritual cleanliness matter to modern clergy?
short_answer: No, because ritual purity belongs with ceremonial law, which Christians see as fulfilled in Christ; without a temple, it is not operative for Judaism either.
expanded_answer: Ritual purity is distinguished from moral purity and tied to the ritual law system. Since Christians regard that system as fulfilled in Christ, and since Judaism lacks an operating temple context, clergy today should not be bound by those ritual purity categories.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: To what extent are we responsible for our ideas, given that words and actions are on record?
short_answer: People are responsible for ideas they promote, especially if those ideas lead others astray, but intent and fruit matter.
expanded_answer: People are responsible for ideas they promote when those ideas lead others astray, just as their words and actions matter. Repeating a bad idea to critique it differs from promoting it; intent and the resulting fruit determine the responsibility involved.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What is the rarest tea you have tried?
short_answer: Imperial white tea from a Liverpool tea shop, described as subtle and floral.
expanded_answer: Imperial white tea from a tea tasting in Liverpool is the rarest tea he remembers. The description is qualitative rather than historical: subtle, floral, and distinctive from ordinary teas.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: If Lorenzo Nigro has been quoted as reputable before, why dismiss him now when his conclusions contradict you?
short_answer: He follows Nigro where he believes the data support him, but rejects conclusions he believes have bent under pressure.
expanded_answer: He cites Nigro when he believes Nigro follows the data. He also points to earlier shifts that he attributes to professional pressure, so he does not accept every conclusion simply because he has used Nigro's work before.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: How many early daters are closet late daters?
short_answer: He thinks there are a fair number, but many avoid saying so publicly because they do not want the heat.
expanded_answer: In his view, some public early-date supporters privately lean late. Pressure from donors, grants, or broader backlash can keep academics and translators from saying so openly.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Have you ever been wary of digital books being altered after an author's death because of censorship?
short_answer: Yes. It is already happening in adaptations and could move from altered movies to rewritten books.
expanded_answer: He sees changes to film adaptations as the first step toward later revisions of the books themselves. Digital distribution makes those changes easier after an author can no longer object.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Why didn't Orwell criticize communism directly?
short_answer: Orwell did criticize communism directly in essays, but fiction and allegory communicated the critique more broadly and effectively.
expanded_answer: Orwell did criticize communism directly in essays, but he also understood the power of fiction. Allegory let him communicate the evils of communism more memorably and accessibly than a purely direct political tract would have done.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Did secular Jews significantly contribute to early Bolshevism or communism?
short_answer: Yes, many secular Jews were involved early on, but Jews later became among its first victims.
expanded_answer: In this account, many secular Jews participated in early Bolshevism and later regretted it. Jews also became early victims of the movement they had helped support.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What did Orwell think of New Testament historicity and Jesus' historicity?
short_answer: As far as he can tell, Orwell did not address religious questions much.
expanded_answer: As far as he can tell, Orwell rarely addressed religious questions, including the historicity of the New Testament or Jesus. He makes no more detailed claim about Orwell's theology.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Does censorship come from the government or from publishers?
short_answer: Censorship usually comes from industry and publishers, not primarily from government.
expanded_answer: Publishers and industry structures often decide what can be distributed, promoted, altered, or suppressed. In this answer, they are the usual source of practical censorship.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Do we misunderstand heavenly job roles as well as the scale of heaven and the spirit realm?
short_answer: Yes. In his view, heaven will have many roles suited to it instead of everyone doing the same thing.
expanded_answer: He expects heaven to include many roles, such as listeners, writers, and composers, along with cultural differences in dress. This is his alternative to a flat Sunday-school picture in which everyone performs the same task.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Doesn't self-publishing give anyone the ability to publish anything?
short_answer: That door is starting to close, with platform fees and payout rules hurting niche authors.
expanded_answer: He cites Draft2Digital's new rules as an example: a $20 account fee, what he recalls as a $15 annual charge when earnings remain below $100, and no payout below the $100 threshold. Such rules can make it uneconomical to keep a small or highly specialized book available.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Where are the Egypt in the Bible merch options?
short_answer: The channel has merch options, but they are not advertised much and had not sold recently.
expanded_answer: Merch exists through the channel, including shirts, stickers, and coffee mugs, but it is not regularly promoted. No one had bought merch in over a year because the channel does not pitch it, although mugs are singled out positively.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: If the channel could do less promotion, might that bring back Talbot's Blade?
short_answer: Promotion was only part of the issue; there was pressure for the channel to become strictly Bible-focused.
expanded_answer: The pressure was for the channel to narrow itself toward Bible-only content, with even Egypt tolerated only to a point. Reducing promotion would therefore not solve the underlying disagreement.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: How old was Isaac when he was about to be sacrificed?
short_answer: Scripture does not say, but the guess is 13 to 15 because Isaac could carry wood yet could still be overpowered by Abraham.
expanded_answer: The Bible does not give Isaac's age, so 13 to 15 is explicitly a guess. Isaac was old enough to carry the wood for the offering but probably still young enough for Abraham to overpower him.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Has your view changed on the difference between a hero and a champion?
short_answer: No. A hero fights for a cause, while a champion is simply a representative fighter and may or may not be heroic.
expanded_answer: The distinction remains: a champion represents someone or something in combat, but that does not automatically make the champion noble. A hero is defined more by fighting for a worthy cause, so the two categories can overlap but are not identical.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Does Satan count as a champion?
short_answer: No. In this view, Satan is an intruder and troublemaker rather than a champion fighting for a cause.
expanded_answer: A champion may fight for a bad cause, but must still represent some cause or interest. Satan is instead compared to a squatter who intruded into God's domain and causes trouble, so he does not fit that definition.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What is the evidence for ransom theory?
short_answer: In his view, there is none; ransom theory rests on an argument from silence.
expanded_answer: He gives the theory no positive textual support and dismisses it as an argument from silence.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Did Satan, Lucifer, or other angels help create the earth with God, or did God simply set everything in motion?
short_answer: Neither framing is accepted. God created the earth; angels were spectators and later caretakers, not co-creators.
expanded_answer: The two alternatives form a false dichotomy in this answer. God created the universe, then the heavenly host, and completed the earth. The angels watched that work and later served as caretakers or members of the divine council.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What does `mytho-history` mean?
short_answer: Mytho-history is a real historical core elevated into a dramatic world involving the gods.
expanded_answer: Mytho-history begins with a historical core and lifts it into divine or mythic drama. The Trojan War and the *Iliad* illustrate how a historical conflict can become a mythic narrative.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Can Mesopotamian flood stories be considered mytho-history?
short_answer: Yes. They can contain both mythic development and a historical core.
expanded_answer: Mesopotamian flood traditions can be mytho-historical because mythic development does not exclude a historical seed. In his view, Gilgamesh is another example because an ancient inscription points to a historical figure behind the stories.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Why were the Assyrians so open about brutality toward enemies and captives?
short_answer: Assyrian brutality was strategic terror, a doctrine of fear meant to make conquered peoples pay tribute rather than resist.
expanded_answer: Assyria advertised extreme punishments as part of a doctrine of fear. The threat of another brutal conquest functioned like a protection racket, pressuring subject peoples to submit and pay tribute.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Would an accurate film about Assyrian conquest be too much even for an NC-17 rating?
short_answer: Probably. The violence would be so extreme that even NC-17 would likely not cover it.
expanded_answer: He thinks an accurate depiction would exceed an NC-17 rating because Assyrian conquest deliberately publicized extreme violence.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What is the best candidate for biblical Ai?
short_answer: He still favors Et-Tell, especially if the reported Late Bronze settlement evidence holds up.
expanded_answer: He still favors Et-Tell, with the qualification that he has not reviewed the latest findings. If the reported Late Bronze evidence holds up, it would strengthen Et-Tell as the biblical Ai candidate.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Does Genesis 47:21 say Joseph bought Egypt's private land and put the people into servitude, and do Egyptian records mention anything like this?
short_answer: Yes. Priestly land allotments, later land redistribution, tax records, and the 20 percent tax fit Egyptian evidence.
expanded_answer: In this reading, Joseph acquired the land for Pharaoh, preserved priestly allotments, and imposed a one-fifth tax. Egyptian evidence for priestly lands, later redistribution, and the same tax rate makes that arrangement plausible in its setting.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: How does Deuteronomy 6:4's oneness support the Trinity?
short_answer: It supports one divine being or essence; other passages are needed to establish the plurality of persons.
expanded_answer: The Shema establishes divine oneness, which is compatible with the claim that God is one being or essence. It does not by itself prove the plurality of persons, so the fuller Trinitarian case depends on other biblical passages as well.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What is the strangest objection to a historical Exodus that you have heard?
short_answer: The strangest objection he has heard asks where the Israelites got clothing and shoes, even though they had animals, hides, wool, and simple looms.
expanded_answer: He found the clothing objection especially baffling because a pastoral population could make and replace clothing from hides and wool using basic looms.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Doesn't Deuteronomy 8:4 say their clothing did not wear out?
short_answer: In his reading, they were never short of clothing because it was being replaced; individual garments still wore out.
expanded_answer: He reads the verse as a promise of provision rather than miraculous indestructibility. Israel's clothing did not fail them because they kept having what they needed.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Where can someone read the Mari letters?
short_answer: He recommends Jack Sasson's *From the Mari Archives* as the best English resource.
expanded_answer: He recommends Jack Sasson's *From the Mari Archives* for readers who want the Mari material in English without working through specialist editions.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Can spirit creatures move from place to place, or are they fixed locally?
short_answer: They are not fixed locally, though fallen spirits may be constrained to the earth.
expanded_answer: In this account, spirits are not fixed to one local place. Fallen spirits may be confined to the earthly realm, but they can still move within it.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Can stretching biblical timelines from 6,000 to 50,000 years also allow 4.6 billion years?
short_answer: There are ways to stretch the chronology to something like 50,000 years, but not as easily to 4.6 billion years.
expanded_answer: Some chronological models can stretch biblical genealogical time substantially, perhaps into tens of thousands of years. The same moves do not automatically extend the biblical timeline to billions of years.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Does Genesis 12:3 bless modern Israel or believers?
short_answer: That particular blessing is universal in scope, reaching all families of the earth, though other blessings are specific to Israel or believers.
expanded_answer: In this reading, Genesis 12:3 promises that all families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham. Other promises may apply more specifically to Israel or to believers.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Does Song of Solomon 5:16 contain Muhammad's name?
short_answer: No. The Hebrew term is not an Arabic name, and the form is a common masculine plural.
expanded_answer: The displayed Hebrew analysis identifies the word as a common masculine plural in the phrase translated "wholly desirable." It is not an Arabic proper name or a hidden reference to Muhammad.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: If Jesus says Moses wrote about him, does that imply Moses knew Muhammad's Arabic name?
short_answer: No. Arabic did not exist as a language in Moses' time, so Moses could not have been using an Arabic name.
expanded_answer: The argument fails historically and linguistically because Arabic did not exist in Moses' time in the relevant sense. Therefore, even if Moses wrote prophetically about later figures, this would not mean he encoded an Arabic name in the Pentateuch.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Did Moses write the Pentateuch in Proto-Hebrew or Ancient Hebrew?
short_answer: In this answer, Moses wrote in Amoritic, which later developed toward Proto-Hebrew and Classical Hebrew.
expanded_answer: This answer places the Pentateuch in Amoritic. Proto-Hebrew and Classical Hebrew developed later from that broader linguistic environment.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Did Moses learn Amoritic in Egypt?
short_answer: The Egyptians did not use it generally, but Moses could have encountered Amoritic locally at Avaris where Amoritic names are attested.
expanded_answer: Amoritic was not the normal Egyptian language, but it could be encountered in the Delta setting. The Amoritic names attested at Avaris supply the kind of local environment where Moses could plausibly have learned or heard it.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Is there a verse saying Joseph's family used translators in Egypt?
short_answer: Yes, but Joseph used the interpreter to disguise himself from his brothers; the scene does not show Moses needing one.
expanded_answer: Joseph spoke through an interpreter when his brothers came to Egypt so that he could maintain his Egyptian disguise. The scene does not show that Moses lacked access to a Semitic language.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Didn't Ramesses II move to Thebes when his grandfather became pharaoh?
short_answer: Yes, but the Avaris household staff would have gone too, and Ramesses II had already spent early childhood around Avaris.
expanded_answer: Ramesses II did move to Thebes, but the move would have included the household staff. Since Ramesses had early childhood exposure around Avaris and its staff, the move does not erase the possibility of Semitic-language exposure.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Could Ramesses II have been bilingual?
short_answer: Yes. Bilingualism was common, and Ramesses II's Avaris background makes it plausible.
expanded_answer: Bilingualism was much more common in ancient multilingual settings than many modern people assume. Ramesses II's background around Avaris and its Semitic environment make bilingual ability plausible.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Why did God call Israel holy in Exodus 19:6 and Leviticus 19:2?
short_answer: Holy means set apart; Israel was set apart for God's redemptive plan and to represent him to the world.
expanded_answer: Holiness here means being set apart rather than merely having special access to sacred space. Israel is holy because God set the nation apart for his redemptive purposes and for representing him among the nations.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: If the Ark of the Covenant were still around, would you open it or look inside?
short_answer: Yes. Once the Shekinah glory moved to the temple, the ark no longer had that same sacred status and could be studied as an artifact.
expanded_answer: He would open, photograph, and study the ark as an artifact. His reason is that the ark's special status changed when the Shekinah glory moved to the temple, removing the earlier ritual danger.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What is your theory on where the Ark of the Covenant went?
short_answer: He thinks Nebuchadnezzar II probably destroyed it and melted its gold to pay soldiers.
expanded_answer: He favors a destruction scenario during Nebuchadnezzar II's conquest: sacred furniture was burned in large furnaces so its gold could be recovered to pay soldiers. In his account, the furnaces in Daniel served that purpose, and cherubim from destroyed Israelite sacred furniture were released there.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: How would you explain the violence and war in the Old Testament to a new believer?
short_answer: New believers should be exposed early to the Bible's realistic worldview about evil, judgment, violence, and human fallenness.
expanded_answer: He recommends introducing these passages early. Scripture deals openly with evil, violence, judgment, and fallen societies, so presenting a harmless caricature leaves new believers unprepared for what the text actually contains.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What in nature could be a sign of God's existence to a modern unbeliever?
short_answer: He does not recommend nature arguments; he prefers a case based on Scripture's reliability, historicity, and credibility.
expanded_answer: He considers the cosmological argument too technical to identify the biblical God by itself, while design arguments can become subjective or collapse when someone proposes a naturalistic explanation. He instead recommends building Scripture's credibility through checkable historical claims such as the historical Jesus, the Exodus, or King Jehu.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What is happening in John 7:8-10, and did Jesus lie there?
short_answer: No. In this reading, Jesus went privately to Jerusalem to teach at the temple but did not participate in the Feast of Booths itself.
expanded_answer: In this reading, traveling to Jerusalem differs from joining the feast's eating, drinking, and booths. Jesus avoided the booths where people were looking for him and appeared at the temple, so his statement was technically true. His brothers were not owed a full disclosure of his plans while his appointed time had not yet come.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: Is the shadow ban over yet?
short_answer: No. The channel is still getting far fewer subscribers than before.
expanded_answer: Subscriber growth was about one quarter of its former monthly rate, so he still considered the channel suppressed.

episode_title: Tax Time, There Aint No Reason and There Aint No Rhyme
question: What pizza should I make?
short_answer: Start with a rising-crust cheese pizza, then add extra mozzarella, bell pepper rings, mushrooms, pepperoni, and Parmesan.
