episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Was Egypt all desert sand then, or was it once much greener?
short_answer: For the game's 49 BC setting, a desert landscape is broadly appropriate, though Egypt had been much greener in earlier periods.
expanded_answer: The answer depends on the period. By 49 BC the landscape was largely desertified, but Old Kingdom Egypt still bordered savannas with trees, grass, and wild animals near the Nile. Egypt was especially green and lush in the Neolithic period.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Was there also a practical function difference between peristyle and hypostyle halls?
short_answer: Yes. The peristyle hall sits farther out, while the hypostyle hall lies closer to the holiest area and has more restricted access.
expanded_answer: The architectural distinction also affects temple access. The peristyle hall was farther from the holy of holies and could be entered by higher-status non-priestly groups on certain festival occasions, while the hypostyle hall was closer to the sanctuary and generally restricted to priests.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Were tomb raids already common in the same period people were being buried?
short_answer: Yes. Tomb robbery was very common, even among people connected to the tombs' construction.
expanded_answer: Tomb robbery was extremely old and common in Egypt. People involved in building a tomb, or their relatives, might also tunnel into and rob it, and evidence for robbery contemporary with burial reaches back as early as Dynasty 2.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Did people steal horses from soldiers in Egypt, or only from peasants?
short_answer: Horses usually belonged to the king, so stealing a horse was normally a serious offense carrying the death penalty; stealing a chariot or soldier's equipment was much less serious.
expanded_answer: Most horses belonged to the king, so stealing one was treated as a crime against the king and could carry the death penalty. By contrast, a chariot or a soldier's weapons and armor belonged to the soldier, so stealing those was treated as a much lesser offense.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: How was desertion handled by the army in ancient Egypt?
short_answer: Desertion was handled as elsewhere, usually with the death penalty, because severe punishment maintained military cohesion.
expanded_answer: Desertion was a standard military-discipline issue rather than something unique to Egypt. Armies maintained cohesion by making soldiers fear punishment from their own side more than the enemy, so desertion was normally punished by death.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Was killing a soldier punishable by death?
short_answer: It could be. Murder was punishable by death when a relative or another concerned party brought and proved the charge.
expanded_answer: Murder could bring the death penalty, but Egyptian procedure depended on a private accuser. A relative, friend, or other concerned party had to prosecute the case; if no one remained to bring the charge, the state did not automatically pursue it.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Did being one of the king's soldiers give you special protection in a murder case?
short_answer: No. Royal military service did not protect someone from a murder charge.
expanded_answer: Royal military service did not shield someone from a murder charge. If a qualified accuser brought the charge and proved the murder, the offender could still expect the death penalty.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: What was the purpose of the inner chapel?
short_answer: It housed cult images inside the temple's holiest area.
expanded_answer: The inner chapel lay within the holy of holies near the great seat, plinth, and bark shrine. The god's small cult image could be placed in the bark by day, while the stone naos stored the deity at night.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: When did the state start prosecuting murders directly?
short_answer: Direct state prosecution appears much later than ancient Egypt, probably not until the Islamic period.
expanded_answer: Ancient Egyptian murder cases depended on private prosecution rather than automatic state action. Direct state prosecution appears to be a later development, probably not reaching Egypt until the Islamic period; similar private-prosecution patterns also existed elsewhere.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: What kind of trees are shown in this area?
short_answer: The tall trees are date palms; Egypt also had olive, almond, and acacia trees, though not every tree shown could be identified confidently.
expanded_answer: The tall palms are period date palms, while the identification of some other trees as acacia was uncertain. Egypt also had olive, almond, acacia, and date palms, and date palms spread widely after being imported in the New Kingdom.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Is the same level of tooth decay found where Egyptians got dates from?
short_answer: Yes. Dates came from the Levant, where carbohydrate-rich foods such as sugar, honey, and bread also produced tooth decay.
expanded_answer: Dates came from the Levant, and tooth decay is also found there. Heavy consumption of carbohydrate-rich foods, including sugar, honey, bread, and dates, produces similar dental problems.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Do camels outrun horses only in the desert, or in general?
short_answer: In general. Camels can outrun horses once moving, but they panic too easily to be good war animals.
expanded_answer: The speed claim was not desert-specific: in races, camels can beat horses once they get going. Their speed does not make them ideal for warfare, because camels tend to panic.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: What does "imshi" mean?
short_answer: It is a very rude way of saying "scram," "get lost," or "go away," and should only be used when someone is really annoyed.
expanded_answer: "Imshi" is a rude dismissal meaning roughly "scram," "get lost," or "go away." Polite people do not use it except when genuinely annoyed.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: When ordering in an Egyptian restaurant, should someone say "imshi" after finishing the order?
short_answer: No. Do not say that to a server unless you want the server to spit in your food.
expanded_answer: "Imshi" is insulting rather than a neutral way to end an interaction. Saying it to a waiter invites a hostile response.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Is it wise to tip generously in Egypt?
short_answer: It depends. Tip generously for unusually good service, but ordinary transactions call for the customary gratuity or modest bakhshish.
expanded_answer: Generous tipping is appropriate for unusually good service, but ordinary situations are context-dependent. Restaurants and hotels may already include gratuities, while public bathrooms and small service interactions often call for modest bakhshish rather than large tips.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: What if someone identifies as a doctor to avoid harassment in Egypt?
short_answer: Most people probably could not verify the claim, but faking a doctorate would be lying.
expanded_answer: Most people would be unable to verify the claim, but that would not make it acceptable: faking a doctorate would be lying. Such a claim would also offer little protection in dangerous or official encounters.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Should toilet paper be brought to Egypt or bought there?
short_answer: Bring it and pack it in luggage so travelers have the kind they want.
expanded_answer: Packing toilet paper ensures travelers have the type they prefer, and customs would not care about it. The recommendation also reflects his personal practice of carrying a roll while traveling in Egypt.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: How much water should you bring to Egypt?
short_answer: None. Buy bottled water there because it is easy to find.
expanded_answer: Do not pack water: bottled water is widely available at Egyptian hotels, airports, and convenience stores. Travelers should budget for it, and even locals drink bottled water.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Should travelers rely on Canadian dollars for a trip to Egypt?
short_answer: No. Convert Canadian funds to U.S. currency before traveling; U.S. dollars are easier to exchange and use in Egypt.
expanded_answer: Canadian dollars were discouraged for direct use in Egypt. The practical recommendation was to exchange them for U.S. currency in Canada before the trip, because U.S. dollars are accepted more readily and can be exchanged at Egyptian airports.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Could Alexander the Great have had a relationship with the Cleopatra shown in the game?
short_answer: No. They lived in different periods, separated by roughly three centuries.
expanded_answer: Alexander belongs to the fourth century, while the game's Cleopatra belongs to the first century, making such a relationship chronologically impossible. The earliest use of Cleopatra as a family name was left uncertain, but that did not change the period mismatch.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Is Bayek's being the Medjay for all Egypt under the pharaoh historically accurate?
short_answer: The game compresses the role: Medjay were spread across Egypt as local leaders, guards, constables, and police.
expanded_answer: After the Second Intermediate Period, Medjay were distributed throughout Egypt. They remained an ethnicity and served as community leaders, guards, constables, and police. Bayek's national role compresses those distributed local functions into one character.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Is the game's depiction of Cleopatra correct?
short_answer: Only in part: in his assessment, the drunkenness and drug use fit Cleopatra, but the costume did not.
expanded_answer: In his assessment, details such as drunkenness and drug use fit Cleopatra, but the visual design did not. The dress and headgear were not period and looked wrong compared with surviving images of Cleopatra.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: What would Cleopatra's proper attire have been?
short_answer: Probably a dress with a beaded overdress and a headband like the one on the Sphinx of Thutmose II.
expanded_answer: A more plausible look would be a dress, probably with a beaded overdress, and a headband resembling the one on the Sphinx of Thutmose II. The headband would have a cobra on the front, with its tail or body passing over the top of the head.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Were rabbits indigenous to ancient Egypt?
short_answer: Yes. Rabbits were native there and appear in place names and divine associations.
expanded_answer: Egyptian place-name and religious evidence includes areas named after the rabbit or hare and associated with the rabbit goddess Wenut. The hare nome was one example supporting rabbits' indigenous presence.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Did the king own all the horses in Egypt?
short_answer: The king owned most horses, though not literally every horse.
expanded_answer: Some horses could be privately owned, but the vast majority in Egypt belonged to the king. That royal ownership explains why stealing a horse was treated so seriously.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Are aprons period for ancient Egypt?
short_answer: Not as Egyptian dress, as far as he knew, though Greek influence might make them plausible in the Ptolemaic period.
expanded_answer: He did not know of aprons as normal Egyptian dress, and they do not appear in statuary or domestic-life figurines. Greek influence might make a Ptolemaic-period exception possible.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: How often were ancient Egyptian houses plastered like this?
short_answer: Fairly often. Mudbrick houses were commonly plastered, painted, and decorated.
expanded_answer: Plaster was not restricted to exceptional buildings: mudbrick houses were fairly often plastered, painted, and decorated. The particular house shown was also magnificent by Egyptian standards.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Are camels smart?
short_answer: Not especially. They can be trained, but horses are smarter.
expanded_answer: Camels are not especially bright, though they can be trained and respond to certain commands. They function as herd animals but are less intelligent than horses.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Are hippos menaces?
short_answer: Yes. Hippos are highly dangerous, attack boats and swimmers, and kill more people in Africa than crocodiles or snakes.
expanded_answer: Hippos are among Africa's most dangerous animals. They are aggressive, can outrun people when charging, attack boats and swimmers, and kill more people than animals such as crocodiles or snakes.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Did Egyptians eat hippopotamus meat?
short_answer: Probably. Egyptians were unlikely to waste that much meat once a hippo was killed.
expanded_answer: The evidence is uncertain, but Egyptians probably ate hippopotamus meat rather than waste such a large animal. Hippos were difficult to kill, kings are shown hunting them as a sign of prowess, and the meat is apparently considered tasty.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Was Menes killed by a hippo?
short_answer: No reliable record shows that Menes was killed by a hippo; the story is a myth.
expanded_answer: The story should not be treated as firm history. It is a myth, and no actual record proves that Menes was killed by a hippo.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Where do you find hippos now?
short_answer: Hippos are still found across Africa, including around the Blue and White Niles.
expanded_answer: Hippos remain widely distributed in Africa. The Blue Nile and White Nile regions are two areas where they can still be found.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: How did Egyptians hunt hippos?
short_answer: They used spears, getting close enough for the hippo to attack and striking it repeatedly until it died.
expanded_answer: Hippo hunting was done with spears rather than safely from long range. Hunters got close enough for the animal to attack, then drove in as many spears as possible until it died.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Were pyramids found everywhere in Egypt?
short_answer: No. Pyramids were not distributed everywhere across Egypt.
expanded_answer: Pyramids were not found everywhere in Egypt. The brief exchange followed the observation that pyramids should not have been visible from the character's location in the game.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Would the sphinx statues originally have been painted?
short_answer: Yes. The sphinx statues would originally have been painted.
expanded_answer: The sphinx statues would have been painted rather than left as plain stone. The answer then pointed to blue-green faience tiles in a Step Pyramid gallery as another surviving use of color.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Why does the Step Pyramid look like a ziggurat?
short_answer: It does not closely resemble a ziggurat and is much larger; for about 300 years it was the tallest human-made structure.
expanded_answer: The comparison was rejected because the Step Pyramid does not closely resemble a ziggurat and is much larger. It remained the tallest human-made structure for about 300 years, until Sneferu's pyramids.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Is the Step Pyramid the one where Ron Wyatt tried to read an Egyptian inscription?
short_answer: Yes. His attempted reading was badly mistaken.
expanded_answer: This was the pyramid associated with Ron Wyatt's attempted reading, which was criticized as badly mistaken. Wyatt read a throne hieroglyph as though it depicted a pyramid-building machine.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Does the Step Pyramid look like a Mayan temple?
short_answer: Only in the limited sense that Mayan temples can also be stepped pyramids.
expanded_answer: Both can be stepped pyramids, creating a limited resemblance. The major difference is that Mayan examples have a temple on top, while the Step Pyramid does not.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Is the Pyramid of Unas underground?
short_answer: No. A surviving mound should still be visible from the surface.
expanded_answer: The Pyramid of Unas may appear as a rubble mound in that area, but it is not simply invisible underground. Because a surviving mound remains, it should still be visible from the surface.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Are stories about scorpions getting into your shoes in hotel rooms exaggerated?
short_answer: Mostly yes. It is possible, but the stories are dramatized.
expanded_answer: A scorpion can get into a hotel room or shoe, but the stories are dramatized. He had never encountered a scorpion or snake in an Egyptian hotel room; he had found small chameleons in hotel rooms and seen fast centipedes on temple floors. Checking shoes is still wise.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: What is the difference between the spellings "Zoser" and "Djoser"?
short_answer: "Zoser" is an antiquated nineteenth-century spelling, while "Djoser" is the modern spelling of the same royal name.
expanded_answer: The two spellings refer to the same king. "Zoser" reflects an antiquated nineteenth-century pronunciation and spelling, whereas "Djoser" is the modern scholarly form.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 5)
question: Is the idea that shabtis were an early replacement for sacrificing the dead king's administrators a myth?
short_answer: Yes. The replacement theory is a myth.
expanded_answer: The idea makes an appealing story, but it is not correct. Shabtis should not be explained as an early replacement for sacrificing the dead king's administrators.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: How should we understand the "judgment of the gods" in Exodus 12:12?
short_answer: In his reading, the passage judges Egypt's rulers and human power structure rather than idols or spiritual beings.
expanded_answer: Exodus 12:12 is the only plague text that explicitly speaks this way, so he did not extend the claim to every plague. He compared "gods" with Moses being made "like a god" to Pharaoh, a figure with power of life and death. Because the firstborn plague strikes heirs and human power structures, he understood it as judgment on rulers and authorities rather than statues or spiritual beings.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Is Avaris in the game?
short_answer: He did not know yet and would have to see whether the game includes it.
expanded_answer: He did not know whether Avaris appeared in the game. He suggested checking and said it would be interesting if it did.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What kind of event could turn Egypt's stored water black during the plagues?
short_answer: He suggested something like petroleum or oily discharge into the river as the closest natural comparison.
expanded_answer: He proposed a petroleum-like discharge or oil slick seeping into the river as the natural analogy that came to mind. For the jars, he said modern readers may miss the ritual-purity setting: stone and wooden jars were expected to make drawn water ritually clean, but if the wells were contaminated, the water drawn in those clean vessels would still come out as the bad, blood-like ooze.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Do you think the Nile literally became blood, or just took on blood-like qualities?
short_answer: He favored the latter: it resembled blood rather than becoming literal blood with real corpuscles.
expanded_answer: He favored the water taking on the attributes or appearance of blood, not becoming literal blood with red corpuscles. He also noted that the image of the Nile turning to blood is not unique to Exodus, citing Egyptian-style language such as the prophecy of Ipuwer where the Nile is said to turn to blood while people still drink from it.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What is your view of Lake Nasser from an egyptology standpoint?
short_answer: He called it mixed: helpful in some ways, destructive in others.
expanded_answer: Lake Nasser and the dam were both a benefit and a loss. The dam supplies power, regulates the Nile, and prevents destructive flooding that once reached major temples such as Karnak, making many sites available year-round. At the same time, he said the reservoir destroyed or badly affected archaeological sites south of Aswan, so it is not a simple gain for egyptology.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What was the other place with a temple of Yahweh that you wanted to see?
short_answer: Leontopolis had one and Elephantine had another, though Elephantine is probably too far south to appear in the game.
expanded_answer: Leontopolis, near Heliopolis, should have a temple of Yahweh. Elephantine had another Yahweh temple, although it was probably too far south for the game map. He hoped the game would reach the Leontopolis area.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Is the Red Pyramid actually red?
short_answer: Sort of. It used to have reddish casing stones, but those stones have been stripped away.
expanded_answer: It was named for reddish casing stones, originally red granite, but those stones are now gone. He compared it with the White and Black Pyramids, whose color names also refer to casing stones that have since been stripped away.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Why were the casing stones removed from pyramids?
short_answer: Islamic caliphs stripped them for reuse, especially as palace flooring.
expanded_answer: The casing stones were small enough to remove and reuse, so later rulers quarried them from the pyramids rather than cutting new stone. In his example, Islamic caliphs cut them down to pave palace floors.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Where should the Red Pyramid be relative to the Step Pyramid?
short_answer: It is at Dahshur. The game's general distance was plausible, but the specific placement was wrong and other pyramids block a direct view from the Step Pyramid.
expanded_answer: Dahshur lies within the broader visual range of Saqqara, and the game's general distance was roughly accurate. The problem was the specific monument and placement: several pyramids stand between the Red Pyramid and the Step Pyramid, blocking a direct view.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Would the Red Pyramid have flooded like the game shows?
short_answer: No. Dahshur is dry, high ground, although some other pyramids do have flooded chambers.
expanded_answer: The Red Pyramid at Dahshur would not have flooded this way because the site is dry and on high ground. Some pyramids do have this problem. He gave Taharqa's pyramid as an example, where the high water table floods the burial chambers and entry requires scuba gear.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Were elaborate puzzle mechanisms or labyrinths common in Egyptian pyramids?
short_answer: No. Only a few pyramids had labyrinths; most floor plans were straightforward.
expanded_answer: Game-like puzzle mechanisms were not period-accurate. He estimated that only two or three pyramids had labyrinths, while most used straightforward plans because complex interiors were difficult to build.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: If Old Kingdom Egyptians did not have metal axes, how did they cut trees down?
short_answer: They used stone axes because metal axe hafting technology had not yet developed.
expanded_answer: Old Kingdom Egyptians did have axes, just not the later kind of hafted metal axes. Because they lacked the technology to mount a metal blade into a shaft in that way, they used stone axes for cutting trees.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: How would horses be so common in a desert like this?
short_answer: They would not be; the game's abundance of horses is "movie magic."
expanded_answer: The answer was brief: horses would not have been that common in the desert. Their abundance was treated as game-world convenience rather than historical realism.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Are the nomes on the game map accurate representations of Egypt's actual nomes?
short_answer: No. They are not close, and the geography is distorted enough to make the map hard to recognize.
expanded_answer: The game's nomes are not even close to accurate geographically. The map is distorted enough that he was having trouble recognizing where things were, and he joked that using it as a guide in Egypt would be a recipe for getting very lost.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Are horses ritually pure?
short_answer: No. Horses are not ritually pure.
expanded_answer: Horses are not ritually pure. The comment came while he was moving through Memphis and discussing temple scenery, so he did not elaborate beyond the clear negative answer.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Is Ptah shown as a mummy the way Osiris is?
short_answer: Yes. Ptah is depicted as a mummiform creator god.
expanded_answer: Ptah is shown mummiform, and the game had correctly shown his typical scepter combination. Ptah is a creator god who creates through will and speech; this Memphite theology contrasts with rival Heliopolitan theology about Re.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Can you explain the etymology of Egypt?
short_answer: It comes through Greek, though he was working from memory and kept the explanation brief.
expanded_answer: The name comes through Greek and, from memory, connects with the Greek form of a city name. He was careful that he did not remember every original form off the top of his head, but he rejected the simplified explanation being offered in chat.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What would you say to Christians who think they should not play video games at all?
short_answer: He considered a blanket prohibition legalistic and advised Christians to avoid immoral games and use good sense about entertainment.
expanded_answer: In his view, Christians should avoid immoral games. He considered a blanket rule against all video games a human rule and therefore legalistic. He advised using good sense and choosing entertainment that is morally fitting and glorifies God.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Do the god-flagpoles go all the way back to the Old Kingdom, and what wood were they made from?
short_answer: They go back at least to the Old Kingdom, but the possible follow-up about the wood was not answered.
expanded_answer: The flagpole symbol goes back at least to the Old Kingdom as far as the evidence allows, even though few Old Kingdom temples survive. Because the word `netjer` is already ancient, he thought the divine flagpole symbol may go back into the Early Dynastic period or earlier. The transcript's possible follow-up about which wood was used is garbled, and the response does not answer it.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What makes a video game immoral?
short_answer: In his view, killing in a game is not inherently immoral; the issue is whether the game requires acts such as murdering innocents.
expanded_answer: He distinguished murder from every act of killing. In his view, combat against enemy combatants in a war game is not automatically immoral. A game that requires the player to murder innocent people would be different.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What language family does Egyptian belong to?
short_answer: Egyptian belongs to the Afroasiatic language family.
expanded_answer: Egyptian is part of the Afroasiatic language family, using the older wording "Afro-Semitic" in the transcript. The language family spans the ancient Near East and northern Africa and cannot be classified as purely African or purely Semitic.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Would Swahili (transcript unclear) count as Afroasiatic?
short_answer: He did not know the language being asked about.
expanded_answer: The language name is unclear in the transcript, and he did not know it well enough to answer. He then moved back to evaluating the game's Memphis and temple architecture, so the supported answer remains limited.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Do little gates like this appear in Egypt too?
short_answer: Yes. Similar decorated gates can appear in temenos walls and connected temple walls.
expanded_answer: Small decorated gateways can appear as part of temenos walls, giving an example near the temple of Khonsu at Karnak. They can be short or taller, often decorated with a winged disk, and the game was right to connect the gate to a wall rather than leaving it isolated.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What is a good way to start learning Coptic?
short_answer: He recommended learning from someone who knows Egyptian, named Lambdin as the gold-standard textbook, and mentioned Crum for the dictionary.
expanded_answer: He warned that Coptic is often taught poorly when instructors treat knowledge of Greek as sufficient, because Coptic is structurally its own Egyptian language. For study materials, he considered Bentley Layton's book decent, called Thomas Lambdin's Sahidic Coptic introduction the gold standard, and recommended Crum's dictionary despite its age.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Who is Petro?
short_answer: He described Petro as the leader of a Gnostic cult called Valley of Healing and directed viewers to Rob's channel for more.
expanded_answer: In his account, Petro led a Gnostic cult called Valley of Healing, and federal authorities had investigated it. He did not give a full account in this stream and directed viewers to Rob's channel for more detail.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Did ancient Egyptians raise sheep?
short_answer: Yes, though cattle were preferred.
expanded_answer: Egyptians raised sheep, although cattle were their preferred animal. The transcript gives no further detail.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Did Egyptians use wool?
short_answer: Generally not, because wool is too hot for Egypt.
expanded_answer: No in practical terms: wool was too hot for Egypt. The transcript support is brief, so the expanded answer is correspondingly limited.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Is mummy tummy likely in the Sinai?
short_answer: He considered it less likely than on the Nile, yet advised treating the Sinai with the same caution.
expanded_answer: He considered mummy tummy less likely in the Sinai because people there use well water rather than Nile water. Even so, he recommended the same caution because poor hand-washing could still create risk.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Can I get hepatitis C in Egypt?
short_answer: He said hepatitis C should not be the concern and recommended hepatitis A/B protection plus a tetanus shot.
expanded_answer: He said hepatitis C should not be the concern for a traveler in Egypt and advised protection against hepatitis A and B, along with a tetanus shot. In his description of the hepatitis vaccine series, the first two shots protect and the third is a booster.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Was the Nile sacred in the same way the Ganges is regarded as sacred?
short_answer: No. The Nile was treated as divine, but not as perpetually holy or clean in that Hindu sense.
expanded_answer: The Nile could be regarded as divine or connected with a deity, but not sacred and perpetually clean in the same way the Ganges is treated in Hindu practice. He also noted that Egypt had one major arterial river, unlike a setting with multiple rivers where one can be singled out as sacred.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Aren't deities by definition sacred or holy?
short_answer: He distinguished a god's sacred temple presence from a natural embodiment like the Nile or the ground.
expanded_answer: Holiness depends on context: a god's presence in temple cult or sacred space is not the same as a natural embodiment in the environment. He compared the Nile as the embodiment of Hapi and the ground as Geb; Egyptians could associate them with gods without treating every bit of river water or ground as temple-holy.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: How prestigious was it to be a bronze smith in ancient Egypt?
short_answer: It was an important and respected craft within the craftsman class.
expanded_answer: Bronze smithing belonged to the craftsman class, alongside trades such as decorating, tomb cutting, and carpentry. It was important and respected while remaining part of a craft stratum rather than an elite office.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What probably darkened the land of Egypt during the plague of darkness?
short_answer: He suggested a sandstorm mixed with fire and ash.
expanded_answer: He suggested a sandstorm that had picked up fire and ash, possibly from burning grasslands or lake regions in the Sahara. From his own experience with sandstorms, he emphasized that such storms can make houses disappear behind the sand, block the sun, and even strip paint from a car.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Did ancient Egyptians usually ride camels or horses?
short_answer: Neither, normally. Chariots pulled by horses were the transportation of choice, while camel riding was not normal except for merchants.
expanded_answer: Egyptians generally did not ride either animal in the way the question imagines. Horses were used with chariots, and chariots were the preferred elite transportation, while camel riding was not normal except in cases such as merchants.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Can you explain the temple of Yahweh at Tell el-Yahudiyeh a bit?
short_answer: It was on a mound near Leontopolis, had Semitic pottery and a simple temple footprint, and was politically difficult to re-excavate.
expanded_answer: Tell el-Yahudiyeh means "tell of the Jew" and lies near Leontopolis, on the northeastern outskirts of modern Cairo near Heliopolis. Petrie excavated a simple Yahweh temple there, with Semitic pottery and a basic plan of walls, pillars, and a holy of holies. The site is hard to study because renewed excavation became politically too sensitive.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Is Tell el-Yahudiyeh a possible place where Mary and Joseph went to escape Herod?
short_answer: He considered it one of five possible locations and one of the better candidates.
expanded_answer: The temple was in operation until about AD 50, so he considered Tell el-Yahudiyeh one of five possible destinations for Mary and Joseph in Egypt and one of the better candidates. He connected its Yahweh worship to Israelites who settled there after the Babylonian invasion and said more information would require older excavation reports such as Petrie's book.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: If someone raised two million dollars, would you excavate at Tell el-Yahudiyeh?
short_answer: He would love to, but the real problem would be getting a politically sensitive license.
expanded_answer: He would love to excavate Tell el-Yahudiyeh, but the hard part would be securing permission because the site is politically toxic. He added that a very large amount of money might open doors in practice, while still framing the license as the real barrier.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: How did Christianity change the culture of Egypt, and are there book recommendations on the topic?
short_answer: Christianity became culturally dominant especially in Lower Egypt and shaped education and church leadership from Alexandria outward; no book recommendation was given.
expanded_answer: Christianity became the standard culture especially in Lower Egypt, while parts of the south remained pagan much longer. Alexandria became a major center of Christian learning, with its catechetical school training many bishops for the wider Christian world. The response did not name a book on the topic.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Are there book recommendations on Egypt's forced cotton production under Islam?
short_answer: He was not an expert on that period and did not have book recommendations.
expanded_answer: He was not an expert on early Islamic Egypt or forced cotton production, so he did not want to recommend specific books. He acknowledged that books on early Islamic Egypt exist, but he did not know which ones to name.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What cultural or social norms changed after Christianity was introduced to Egypt?
short_answer: Paganism and Christianity coexisted uneasily, with changes such as less expensive Christian burial customs.
expanded_answer: Christianity and paganism existed side by side with tension, even in Christian-majority places like Alexandria. One concrete social change he named was burial: Christian burials tended to be less expensive and less focused on elaborate funerary provision than pagan burials.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Can we definitely say Ramesses II was the pharaoh of the exodus?
short_answer: Yes. If there was an exodus at all, Ramesses II is the only serious fit.
expanded_answer: Falk argued that if the exodus happened, Ramesses II is the only viable candidate. He pointed to the Merneptah Stele shortly after Ramesses II, the abandonment history of Avaris in the 19th Dynasty, and the fact that Ramesses II dominates that dynasty chronologically; combined with Israel building the city of Ramesses, he said no serious alternative remains.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Why are there so few records from the latter half of Ramesses II's reign?
short_answer: The period may have been uneventful or deliberately kept quiet; very few records survive after about year 25.
expanded_answer: The surviving record becomes very thin after about year 25. Apart from a few letters exchanged with the Hittites and a few temple dedications, little remains. Diplomatic correspondence would omit compromising information, so it does not resolve whether the period was uneventful or deliberately kept quiet.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: What is a swamp puppy?
short_answer: It is just a nickname for an alligator or crocodile.
expanded_answer: "Swamp puppy" is simply a nickname for an alligator or crocodile. The stream immediately returned to game navigation, so no further explanation is supported there.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 6)
question: Are there any theories about which pharaoh Joseph interpreted dreams for?

short_answer: The extended tour starts in Sinai, and the wider trip includes Aswan, Thebes, Abydos, Cairo, and Tanis.
expanded_answer: The extended tour begins with Sinai, a modern governorate rather than an ancient nome. Other listed stops or regions include Aswan, Thebes, Abydos, Cairo, and Tanis.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: When did the Sphinx lose its nose?
short_answer: The exact date is uncertain, but it seems to have happened in the Islamic period.
expanded_answer: The exact date is unknown, though the loss appears to have happened during the Islamic period. The Sphinx is recorded with its nose until roughly the 500s, so it kept the nose through most of the Egyptian monarchy.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Will the Egypt tour stay at the hotel near the pyramids, and what is its name?
short_answer: He did not know the hotel details yet, and that information can change late in tour planning.
expanded_answer: He did not yet know the hotel and might not know until late in planning, because the choice can change with the tour's size. He expected it to be nice, since Egyptian tourism depends heavily on hotel accommodations.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Will you be streaming or filming during your Egypt tour?
short_answer: They hope to, though internet limits may make recording and uploading more practical than livestreaming.
expanded_answer: They hope to stream or film, depending on conditions during the tour. If the internet cannot support a livestream, they may record segments and upload them during the trip.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Do we know what restaurants the Egypt tour will eat at?
short_answer: No. The tour company handles those arrangements, though he knows places he likes to visit on his own.
expanded_answer: The tour company will choose the restaurants, and he did not yet have the list. He sometimes likes to sneak out for food and knows places in Egypt, including Luxor, so travelers who stay close to him may find meals outside the formal plan.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: What do you consider Egypt's greatest wonder?
short_answer: His preference is the temples and tombs over the pyramids.
expanded_answer: People often visit Egypt for the pyramids, but his own priority is the temples and tombs, especially the temples. He singled out the Ramesseum and Dendera; Dendera retains much of its color and has a decorated ceiling, roof access, and an underground chamber for secret rituals.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Is this what ancient naval combat was like?
short_answer: Somewhat. Ramming was common, ships had battle rams, and fire arrows or burning pitch could be used against flammable sails.
expanded_answer: Ramming was a common naval tactic, and ships could carry battle rams. Fire arrows were often aimed at flammable sails. Rather than burning in flight, they could be tipped with heated pitch that ignited a target on impact.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: What triggers Dr. Falk more: Assassin's Creed inaccuracies or hearing Amenhotep III in 1446 BC?
short_answer: He chose the chronology error; artistic liberties are acceptable in fiction until people confuse fiction with fact.
expanded_answer: He found the Amenhotep III chronology error more irritating. Game designers are artists and may take liberties in fiction; the problem starts when people confuse fiction with fact.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Why were the Egyptians softer and meeker than empires such as the Assyrians, Hittites, and Mitanni?
short_answer: Egypt usually wanted tribute through a lighter hegemony, while Assyria and some others pursued tighter control through fear and violence.
expanded_answer: In Falk's account, Egypt usually maintained a hegemony and sought tribute or loot rather than direct administration. Assyrians, Hittites, Persians, and others pursued tighter control and replaced governors. Assyria in particular used violence to frighten people into compliance and keep tribute flowing.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Was any later eastern empire more brutal than Assyria?
short_answer: No empire clearly surpassed Assyria overall, though the Persians had moments of comparable brutality.
expanded_answer: No later eastern empire clearly surpassed Assyria in his comparison, although the Persians were sometimes equally brutal. Persians often offered cities a treaty before fighting, an approach he also compared with later Roman practice.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Is there any villain-origin explanation for why the Assyrians were so brutal?
short_answer: No. In his account, economics and competition for resources drove Assyrian brutality.
expanded_answer: Assyria competed with other Mesopotamian city-states for resources and became more effective and brutal than its neighbors. It then carried that local-bully strategy wherever it expanded.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Did Egypt have contact with West Africans?
short_answer: Not with West Africans directly, though Egypt did have contact with Nubia, Punt, and nearby sub-Saharan regions.
expanded_answer: Egyptian contacts extended to Nubia and Punt, including regions of Sudan and Ethiopia south of the fourth cataract, as well as some sub-Saharan groups west of Egypt near Libya. They did not extend as far as West Africa.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Are there any period examples of Egyptian women wearing hair like Halet's?
short_answer: He knew of no period examples from Egypt.
expanded_answer: He knew of no period Egyptian examples of women wearing Halet's hairstyle. The transcript gives no further detail.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: What is Set's good coming?
short_answer: Set's good coming is power; his bad coming is violent storms.
expanded_answer: Set could grant what Falk jokingly called "phenomenal cosmic power." His bad coming brought severe, destructive storms.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Was there any god or entity with only a bad coming?
short_answer: Apophis comes closest, though he treated Apophis more as a demon than an ordinary god.
expanded_answer: Apophis is the closest example, though Falk treated him more as a demon than an ordinary god. His role in myth is to try and fail to eat the sun disk.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: What are Osiris's good and bad comings?
short_answer: The good coming is entry into Osiris's fields and apotheosis, while the bad coming is rejection and the heart being eaten.
expanded_answer: Osiris's good coming allowed entry into the fields of Osiris and apotheosis, along with what Falk sarcastically described as working there as a slave for the rest of one's natural life. His bad coming was rejection at the weighing of the heart; as judge, Osiris decided whether the heart was too heavy and would be given to Ammit.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Is there a metaphysical reason Egyptian gods have dual natures?
short_answer: It seems to be simply how Egyptian religion developed.
expanded_answer: Egyptian religion simply seems to have developed that way. The transcript offers no deeper metaphysical mechanism.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Who eats the heart at the weighing?
short_answer: Ammit does, a female hybrid demon with crocodile, lion, and hippo features.
expanded_answer: The heart-eater is Ammit, a female demon. She is a hybrid of crocodile, lion, and hippopotamus, seen in some temples, tombs, and Book of the Dead papyri, with the specific function of eating the heart at the weighing.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Is Sobek the crocodile figure meant when Ammit has a crocodile head?
short_answer: No. Sobek is the most important crocodile deity, but Ammit is a separate hybrid creature.
expanded_answer: Sobek is not the only crocodile-related divine figure, even if he is the most important crocodile deity. Ammit is separate: a three-part hybrid with a crocodile head, lion foreparts, and hippopotamus rear parts.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Which common stereotypes about ancient Egypt irritate you most?
short_answer: He pointed to exaggerated lost-knowledge claims, alien pyramid ideas, and especially the claim that the pyramids were granaries.
expanded_answer: The first irritation he named was the claim that Egypt had extraordinary scientific knowledge now lost to modern people. Alien-pyramid ideas also annoyed him, but the pyramid-as-granary claim stood out most; he named Ron Wyatt as a promoter and Ben Carson as someone who repeated it.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: If a temple were broken like that, would it lose value in Egyptian eyes?
short_answer: The transcript does not give a clear yes-or-no answer; it only notes that temples did break.
expanded_answer: Temples did break from time to time, but gameplay dialogue cut off the answer before he said whether damage reduced a temple's value in Egyptian eyes. The transcript therefore supports no confident yes or no.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: What do you think of the idea that Joseph and Imhotep were the same person?
short_answer: He dismissed the idea outright.
expanded_answer: He called the Joseph-Imhotep identification ridiculous. The game crashed before he gave any longer explanation, so the transcript preserves only that direct dismissal.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Will the tour drink lotus tea at a seer's house?
short_answer: No. Not on the tour, though he knows a place to get blue lotus perfume.
expanded_answer: Lotus tea at a seer's house is not part of the tour. He did say that he knows a good place to buy blue lotus perfume.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Is the pronunciation of "iron" standard in your area?
short_answer: Yes. He said it is standard in his area and identified himself as Canadian.
expanded_answer: He said the pronunciation is standard where he lives and identified himself as Canadian. The transcript gives no narrower regional or linguistic explanation.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Do you like Tim Hortons?
short_answer: Yes, especially its doughnuts, though he said he eats them too often.
expanded_answer: He likes Tim Hortons a little too much, especially its doughnuts. Although he believes he should not eat them, he still does.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 8)
question: Are those papyrus boats accurate?
short_answer: Largely yes. Papyrus boats were real but usually temporary seasonal craft, unlike more permanent wooden boats.
expanded_answer: The papyrus boat shown was broadly accurate because Egyptians did make boats from papyrus. These were temporary seasonal craft, not permanent vessels: they did not necessarily need much pitch, were meant to last only a few months at most, and differed from expensive permanent wooden boats.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What was your time at Abu Simbel like?
short_answer: He avoided the standard rushed bus trip by staying overnight, giving him more time at Abu Simbel near the restricted Sudanese border zone.
expanded_answer: The usual same-day trip reaches Abu Simbel around midday, allows only an hour or two at the site, and must leave before the protected road closes. He traveled out the previous day, stayed overnight, and photographed the temple and Milky Way under exceptionally dark skies. Two packs of wild dogs fought around him while he worked, and he heard crocodiles nearby. He found Abu Simbel beautiful and recommended staying overnight, though it was too distant for his planned tour schedule.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Is perch as good as monkfish?
short_answer: No. He preferred monkfish, though he also liked perch.
expanded_answer: The perch served at Abu Simbel was fresh from Lake Nasser and beautifully prepared, but monkfish remained his clear preference.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What are the main endonyms for Egypt?
short_answer: The usual one is "the Two Lands," while "Kemet" appears more rarely.
expanded_answer: An endonym is a people's name for themselves. Egypt's most common self-designation was Tawy, "the Two Lands," referring to Upper and Lower Egypt; Kemet appears in some cases but much less often.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: How did the Hyksos come to power?
short_answer: They rose into a power vacuum after the 13th Dynasty lost control, then expanded from the Delta.
expanded_answer: The Hyksos were Semitic 15th Dynasty rulers based in the northern Delta. After 13th Dynasty authority withdrew toward Thebes, they filled the resulting absence of authority and later expanded; no evidence of an initial military invasion was presented.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: How are Baal and Seth similar personality-wise?
short_answer: Their personalities differ; their stronger similarity is functional, since both are storm gods.
expanded_answer: Baal is the hero god of the Ugaritic Baal cycle who defeats Mot and Yam and restores order, while Seth has a broader Egyptian role as a god of power, might, and Lower Egypt. Their overlap is functional rather than personal: both are storm gods associated with power and strength.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What is a good resource for Egyptian mythology?
short_answer: He recommended Wilkinson's Gods and Goddesses of Egypt as accurate, well illustrated, and still available.
expanded_answer: Wilkinson's book is substantial and still obtainable. Its accuracy and strong illustrations were the reasons for his recommendation.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Was Seth a chaos god?
short_answer: No. Seth represents unbridled power and can have chaotic effects, but "chaos god" is a misnomer.
expanded_answer: Seth's power is unrestrained rather than chaos itself. Falk compared it to an atomic bomb or a storm striking the Delta: the force can produce chaos and destruction without making Seth simply the god of chaos.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Does that mythology book refute December 25 or crucifixion claims about Osiris, Isis, or Horus?
short_answer: The book does not address those claims; Falk called the December 25 claim silly and pointed to his own video for more detail.
expanded_answer: Wilkinson's book does not spend time on those claims because, in Falk's view, serious academics do not treat them as live issues. He specifically called the December 25 claim silly and referred viewers to a separate video; the crucifixion claim was not discussed separately.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: At what age did Egyptians practice circumcision, and was it limited to adults?
short_answer: The age is unclear; adults are attested, children may also have been circumcised, and the practice may have been elective rather than universal.
expanded_answer: The evidence does not establish a clear age rule. Adult circumcision is attested, children may also have undergone it, and the practice may have depended on voluntary participation rather than a culture-wide requirement.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: How did people at Deir el-Medina have children if they were stuck there?
short_answer: It was a sizable community where people grew up, married, and had children within the village.
expanded_answer: Deir el-Medina was a sizable multigenerational village, not an isolated barracks. Residents grew up together, worked in the same community, married local partners, and raised families there.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: During the Amarna period, were the Hurrians part of the Mitanni Empire?
short_answer: Yes. Amarna letter EA 24 is a Hurrian-language letter from Mitanni king Tushratta to Amenhotep III.
expanded_answer: EA 24 is written in Hurrian rather than Akkadian or a Canaanite dialect. In its opening, Tushratta identifies himself as king of Mitanni and Amenhotep III's father-in-law, reflecting the Mitanni-Hurrian setting and royal marriage diplomacy. Mitanni's continued existence in this material also contradicts David Rohl's placement of the Amarna material with King Saul, when Mitanni should no longer exist in that chronology.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What is David Rohl's motivation for his revised chronology?
short_answer: In Falk's view, Rohl's motive is celebrity and attention, not whether the chronology is right.
expanded_answer: Rohl was a former rock musician and successful record producer who later studied Egyptology and published revised chronologies. Falk said Rohl knew the chronology was wrong but kept promoting it because the books sold well and evangelical churches invited him to speak and paid his travel expenses.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Is David Rohl a more malicious con man than Ron Wyatt?
short_answer: No. Falk called Rohl a charlatan, but considered Wyatt worse because Wyatt wrapped his claims in alleged divine revelation.
expanded_answer: Falk distinguished Rohl, whom he called a charlatan and con man, from Wyatt, whom he considered a more serious religious fraud. The key difference was that Wyatt claimed messages, angelic revelation, or divine endorsement, while Rohl's main harm was confusing Christians with a bogus chronology.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Were there military revolutions in the ancient Near East like guns in the 16th century?
short_answer: Yes. Major examples include chariots, bits and bridles, and shifts from stone to bronze and then iron weapons.
expanded_answer: Chariots and bits and bridles changed warfare drastically. Metallurgy was also revolutionary, moving from stone and flint weapons to bronze and eventually iron during the long span of Egyptian history.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Was there ever a copper age in Egypt or the ancient Near East like there was in Europe?
short_answer: No. The copper there naturally smelted with arsenic contamination, so the region moved straight into bronze use.
expanded_answer: The region bypassed a distinct Copper Age because the available copper naturally included arsenic contamination and therefore smelted into arsenic bronze. Tin could later be added deliberately, but bronze appeared as soon as smelting began.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Did Ron Wyatt ever explicitly claim to be a prophet?
short_answer: Not explicitly, but Falk said Wyatt's other claims effectively amounted to that.
expanded_answer: Wyatt did not simply announce "I am a prophet," but claimed messages from God, angelic communication, prophecies, and personal divine speech. Falk treated that combination as functionally claiming prophetic authority while avoiding the explicit label.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Did arsenic bronze give weapons poison damage?
short_answer: No. Falk joked that infection would kill someone long before arsenic poisoning did.
expanded_answer: Arsenic bronze would not give a weapon game-like poison effect. The likely danger was an infected wound, which he joked would kill long before arsenic poisoning mattered.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Did ancient Egyptian scribes use wooden desks to hold their scrolls?
short_answer: No. Egyptian scribes wrote with a board across their laps rather than at wooden desks.
expanded_answer: Scribes sat cross-legged, placed a board on their laps, laid the papyrus over it, and wrote there. Wood was also too precious to use for a desk like the one shown in the game.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What makes an Egyptian burial site a necropolis?
short_answer: A necropolis is a "city of the dead" containing multiple tombs.
expanded_answer: The term combines roots meaning "dead" and "city" and normally applies to a place with multiple tombs. Abydos, Saqqara, Giza, and the areas around pyramids were given as examples.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Did Egyptians seal servants in tombs like Mesopotamians?
short_answer: No. The subsidiary burials accumulated over time, and their occupants died naturally rather than being sacrificed.
expanded_answer: Older literature sometimes treated 1st- and 2nd-Dynasty subsidiary burials as sacrificed retainers. The graves instead accumulated over time and the occupants are understood to have died naturally, so they were not servants sealed into a ruler's tomb.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What was the maximum number of horses tied to an Egyptian chariot?
short_answer: No absolute maximum was established; Egyptian chariots generally used two horses.
expanded_answer: Egyptian chariots normally used a pair of horses. The answer did not establish an absolute upper limit or discuss a larger team.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: How would you respond to claims that Yahweh was part of a Canaanite pantheon?
short_answer: Falk found the northern Canaanite case unpersuasive and preferred a Kenite or Midianite hypothesis.
expanded_answer: His objection concerned Yahweh's origin, since a culture could later add any god to its pantheon. Falk rejected treating Baal, El's son in the Ugaritic cycle, as a placeholder for Yahweh. He had not seen Yahweh named in Ugaritic documents and found the Kenite or Midianite view more consistent with the biblical texts.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Why were there so many priests in Egyptian cities, and how religious was Egypt compared with other ancient Near Eastern civilizations?
short_answer: Egypt was intensely religious at all levels, with elite temple religion and private household shrines.
expanded_answer: Religion was a central part of Egyptian culture, which helps explain the many priests shown in the city. The elite had more time and wealth to devote to religion, but it also reached lower social levels through household shrines and idols in private homes.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Were there militant holy orders in Egypt?
short_answer: No. Priests and soldiers could be the same people at times, but not as fused militant religious orders.
expanded_answer: An individual could be both a military man and a priest, but the roles were not institutionally conflated. Egypt therefore did not have militant holy orders in the sense of fused religious-military organizations.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What determined whether someone got snake pits, the lake of fire, Ammit, or other dangers in the afterlife?
short_answer: It depended more on how prepared a person was for the afterlife than on a fixed punishment schedule.
expanded_answer: These dangers were risks faced by inadequately prepared dead people rather than necessarily assigned punishments. The less prepared someone was for the afterlife, the more vulnerable that person was to the lake of fire, Ammit, and other threats.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Why would a living king's use of a sacred bark count as blasphemy?
short_answer: It crossed the line between a king as divine in potential and a god in actuality.
expanded_answer: Kings could be treated as divine in potential during life, but not as gods in actuality until death. A sacred bark signaled an actual god, so a living king using that imagery crossed a boundary, especially after Amun's priesthood sharpened the distinction between kingly and divine power.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Where did Egypt's gold come from?
short_answer: Mostly from Nubia, Kush, and Punt, within a wider trade cycle.
expanded_answer: Most of the gold came from Nubia, Kush, and Punt, especially the hills of Kush and Nubia. Egypt also sent bronze tools to Punt, received gold and malachite, smelted the malachite into copper, and made more trade goods until Punt developed its own smelting.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Did pharaohs get deified with cults?
short_answer: They were deified after death, with funerary temples and cults that revered the dead king as a god.
expanded_answer: Funerary temples could depict dead pharaohs as godlike and include sacred-bark imagery. That cultic reverence followed death rather than belonging to the king's ordinary life.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What did pharaohs do in the afterlife if Osiris ruled there?
short_answer: Kings joined Amun-Re's bark and served there instead of laboring in Osiris's fields.
expanded_answer: Ordinary people went to the fields of Osiris and worked, while kings joined the bark of Amun-Re. Falk jokingly called it an eternal cruise, then clarified that the kings technically served Amun-Re on the bark.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Would pharaohs have to go through the night journey over and over, and what if Apophis got them?
short_answer: The danger was possible, but Falk hoped Bastet would be on the bow doing her job.
expanded_answer: Apophis could threaten the repeated night journey in this mythic framework. Falk hoped Bastet would be on the bow performing her protective role, though he allowed that an attack was possible.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Did pharaohs fish?
short_answer: No. Fishing was a lower-class activity; pharaohs instead hunted animals such as hippos and ducks.
expanded_answer: Commoners fished, while pharaohs pursued elite hunting activities such as hunting hippos or shooting ducks. Fishing itself was considered beneath the king's status.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: How did ancient Egyptians fish?
short_answer: They used both nets and rods with lines.
expanded_answer: Egyptians used two methods in this brief answer: nets and rods with lines.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Were heaps of tax records historically consistent with ancient Egypt?
short_answer: Yes. Egypt left many tax documents, and the general tax rate was about 20 percent, with variation.
expanded_answer: Large amounts of Egyptian tax documentation survive, so the game's piles of records fit the setting. Taxes generally worked out to roughly 20 percent, though the amount could be somewhat higher or lower depending on how a person was assessed.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Are hippos pack animals?
short_answer: Not in the usual sense; hippos congregate in herds, so "herd animal" is more precise.
expanded_answer: Hippos do congregate in groups, but the answer classifies them as herd animals rather than pack animals.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Were boat theft and piracy historically plausible for the period?
short_answer: Yes. Boat theft was common, and piracy is attested from the Iron Age.
expanded_answer: Stealing boats fit the setting, and piracy was not a modern invention. Known piracy was dated back to the Iron Age.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Will there be good stargazing sites in Egypt, and how do Aswan and Sinai compare?
short_answer: Aswan should be one of the tour's better sites; Sinai may be better away from lights, but that comparison was not based on first-hand experience.
expanded_answer: Aswan is good near the water but less so deeper in town, and it was likely the best stargazing available on the planned tour. Sinai could be darker away from developed areas, though Sharm el-Sheikh may be bright and Falk had not visited to verify it; in his experience Abu Simbel was best because it had almost no electric light.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What were Egyptian wigs made of, and how did wigs relate to lice?
short_answer: They could use animal hair, horse tails, or beaten flax; shaving the head and wearing a wig helped address lice.
expanded_answer: Human hair was not typical. Wigs could be made from animal hair, including horse-tail hair, or from beaten flax, materials that human lice would not favor; women commonly shaved their heads entirely and wore wigs.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Does an Egyptian woman's wig imply that she is rich?
short_answer: Yes. Wigs were expensive, while ordinary women were more likely to put up with lice.
expanded_answer: A wig could indicate wealth because wigs were expensive. Ordinary women would generally tolerate lice rather than afford that kind of display item.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: What do we know about the First Dynasty?
short_answer: Not much. The Palermo Stone gives yearly events, and otherwise the evidence mainly identifies rulers and rough reign lengths.
expanded_answer: The First Dynasty is poorly documented. Apart from the Palermo Stone's yearly event notices, the surviving information mostly establishes who reigned and approximately how long, with little else in written records.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: When was Avaris settled by Semites?
short_answer: The earliest evidence for Semitic settlement at Avaris is around Dynasty 10.
expanded_answer: The settlement evidence discussed begins with Dynasty 10; no earlier evidence was identified.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Were gladiators historically plausible in Egypt?
short_answer: Yes. Gladiators were present by the third century BC, and Egypt picked the practice up from the Romans.
expanded_answer: Gladiators fit the setting because evidence for them goes back to the third century BC. Egypt adopted the practice from the Romans rather than developing it as a purely native institution.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Was Crocodilopolis a real town?
short_answer: Yes. It was a real place and a Sobek center associated with crocodiles.
expanded_answer: Crocodilopolis was a real town centered on the temple of Sobek, the crocodile god. Falk also joked that the name itself hints at its crocodile association.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Were Semites in Avaris as far back as the late third millennium BC?
short_answer: Yes. Dynasty 10 falls in the very late third millennium BC.
expanded_answer: The Dynasty 10 evidence places Semitic settlement at Avaris in the very late third millennium BC.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Would wolves be historically plausible in this Egyptian setting?
short_answer: No. The closest equivalents would be jackals or domesticated dogs, not wolves.
expanded_answer: Wolves would not fit the Egyptian setting. The closest animals were jackals or domesticated, greyhound-like dogs, and pelts like those shown would not be practical desert clothing.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: How wealthy were the Medjay?
short_answer: Usually not very wealthy unless they were corrupt, despite their local authority.
expanded_answer: The Medjay were community leaders but generally did not accumulate much wealth unless they were corrupt. Falk joked that any extra money probably went toward wine instead of becoming lasting wealth.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Were two-versus-two gladiator fights common?
short_answer: Yes. Gladiatorial events mixed and matched groups of fighters.
expanded_answer: Two-against-two matches fit gladiatorial practice because events could combine different groups of fighters. Animal fights were different: lions were usually added when organizers wanted someone killed.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Would people be able to defeat lions with weapons in the arena?
short_answer: That was considered a fair fight, but the animals usually won.
expanded_answer: An armed person facing a lion counted as a fair fight in arena terms. The animals still won more often than not.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Would gladiators have used real swords?
short_answer: Yes. There was no such thing as a fake sword in this context.
expanded_answer: Gladiators used real swords. Falk dismissed the idea of a fake sword as meaningless in this context.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Why did Isis reassemble Osiris's body?
short_answer: To prevent him from entering the afterlife missing pieces.
expanded_answer: Reassembly restored Osiris's body before the afterlife. Without it, he could still enter, but his spirit or restored body would lack any pieces that had not been recovered.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Was prostitution common in Egypt?
short_answer: Yes. Falk described it as the last resort for a destitute woman without a trade who could not become a concubine.
expanded_answer: He said connections were not strictly required if a woman had learned a trade such as garment making or weaving and was good enough to earn a living from local crafts. For a destitute woman without those skills who could not become a concubine, prostitution was the last resort; he regarded concubinage as the less desperate option.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Are Benu herons extinct now?
short_answer: No clear present-day answer was given; they were only said to have survived into Ptolemaic Egypt.
expanded_answer: Benu herons still existed in Ptolemaic Egypt and were described as three to four feet tall, the largest flighted bird in Egypt, and only slightly smaller than condors. Their present-day status was not stated.

episode_title: Dr. Falk plays Assassin's Creed Origins (part 9)
question: Who would win in a fight, Horus or Ra?
short_answer: Falk called it a tough question and did not choose a winner.
expanded_answer: He gave no winner or comparison and only called it a tough question.

episode_title: Special Live Stream: "All the Stars as Angels" Q&A
question: Will the novels be adapted into a visual-novel video game?
short_answer: No. A separate visual novel is in development, but it is not based on these books.
expanded_answer: These novels will not be adapted into a visual-novel game. A separate visual-novel project is in development, but these books probably would not fit that format well.

episode_title: Special Live Stream: "All the Stars as Angels" Q&A
question: Will the audiobooks use multiple voice actors?
short_answer: No. That would be far too expensive, and the audiobook market is currently unstable.
expanded_answer: Audiobook production is already expensive, while publisher and platform contract changes make the market uncertain. Using multiple actors would raise the cost from about $3,000 into the tens of thousands, so no multi-actor production is planned.

episode_title: Special Live Stream: "All the Stars as Angels" Q&A
question: If you had an extra $3,000 right now, could you make an audiobook?
short_answer: Possibly, but probably not a good one; publisher and contract uncertainty also leaves release unresolved.
expanded_answer: An extra $3,000 might fund an audiobook, though probably not a good one. Most of book one had already been recorded and still needed editing, but no release was promised while the publishing and contract situation remained unclear.

episode_title: Special Live Stream: "All the Stars as Angels" Q&A
question: Are the novels rated PG-13?
short_answer: Roughly yes: mild profanity and some violence, but no gratuitous or graphic content.
expanded_answer: A PG-13 description fits the books' light or occasional profanity, some violence, drinking, and characters who behave like adult non-Christians. The content is not gratuitous or graphic, and some events happen without being described.

episode_title: Special Live Stream: "All the Stars as Angels" Q&A
question: Why be hopeful about influencing culture when there is no major marketing campaign behind the novels?
short_answer: Authors now have to build traction slowly themselves and hope a growing catalog plus reader reviews can move the series forward.
expanded_answer: Neither his traditional nor indie books received a real marketing campaign, so authors now have to do much of that work themselves. His hope is a long game: build a catalog, ask readers for reviews, keep putting the work into the culture, and offer better fiction than the darker material he sees dominating the market.

episode_title: Special Live Stream: "All the Stars as Angels" Q&A
question: Why are stars used analogically for angels or divine beings?
short_answer: Visible heavenly lights provide a natural analogy for divine beings and heavenly life.
